lose coverage. eligibility will depend on each person's work, income, education, community-service activity and qualifying exemptions. under the connecticut department of social services' [official h.r.1 guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/dss/all-programs/dss-benefits-and-hr1/hr1-for-members/hr1-work-rule-changes), an affected adult can satisfy the new rule by earning at least $580 a month, working at least 80 hours a month, completing at least 80 hours of community service, or taking part in an approved work or training program for at least 80 hours. enrollment at least half-time in an education program can also qualify. the guidance says combinations of qualifying activities may be used to reach 80 hours, so the rule is broader than a simple requirement to hold a conventional job. the same dss page lists categories that are exempt, including parents or caregiver relatives of a child under 14, pregnant or postpartum people, foster and former foster youth, american indian or alaska native people, certain veterans, and people who are medically frail. people recently released from jail or prison, people in drug or alcohol treatment, and some people experiencing a short-term hardship may also qualify for an exemption. the exemptions matter because a missed work-hour target does not by itself establish that someone is ineligible for husky d; the agency must apply the full eligibility rules to the person's circumstances. dss says it is building ways to confirm eligibility from records the state already has, a process commonly called ex parte verification. ct mirror reported that the department is using that approach to reduce the paperwork required from people whose information already demonstrates that they qualify. the state has also launched [medicaidmattersct.org](https://www.medicaidmattersct.org/) as an information resource. dss's h.r.1 materials direct residents to community action agencies for help understanding the new work rules and reporting qualifying hours. the policy debate is also about money. connecticut has used $115 million from an emergency response fund to help offset the expiration of federal subsidies for affordable care act plans, according to ct mirror. lamont said the state would first concentrate on helping eligible residents use the benefits that remain available and did not promise state dollars to replace the medicaid cuts. that leaves an unresolved question for lawmakers and the administration: whether connecticut will later spend state money to protect coverage for people who are eligible under current state rules but cannot meet the new federal conditions. for stamford, monday's event put the national medicaid changes in a local setting. the gathering included stamford mayor caroline simmons, stamford health officials and city health-and-human-services staff, according to wfsb. their role is primarily outreach: helping residents understand what will change, who may be exempt and what documents they may need. the event did not change the federal effective date or create a new coverage category. the immediate deadline is jan. 1, 2027, when the work and community-engagement rules take effect. the dss faq also says husky d adults will renew every six months instead of every 12 months beginning jan. 1, and applicants will face a shorter period of retroactive coverage. residents who rely on husky d should use the official dss guidance, respond to renewal notices and seek help from a community action agency before assuming that a new rule ends their coverage. the practical outcome will depend on how the state verifies exemptions, counts qualifying activity and handles people whose circumstances change during the transition. connecticut health health ct ct-i91-windsor-ejection-2026-10-01.excerpt: A person was taken to Hartford Hospital with serious injuries after being ejected in a two-car crash that closed southbound I-91 in Windsor Thursday evening.
ct-i91-windsor-ejection-2026-10-01.text: person seriously injured after ejection in windsor i-91 crash a person was taken to hartford hospital with serious injuries after being ejected in a two-car crash that closed southbound i-91 in windsor thursday evening. one person was seriously injured thursday evening after being thrown from a vehicle in a two-car crash on interstate 91 south in windsor, connecticut state police said. the collision closed a section of the highway during the evening commute and remained under investigation overnight. connecticut department of transportation officials said the crash was reported at about 5:15 p.m. between exits 36 and 35b. the agency reported the southbound closure while state police and emergency crews worked at the scene. the reported closure covered both a windsor interchange and the adjoining southbound segment, making the incident a significant travel disruption for drivers using the corridor. state police told the connecticut post that the person ejected from the vehicle was taken to hartford hospital by windsor emergency medical services with serious injuries. authorities did not release the person's name, age or condition beyond that description. they also did not identify the other driver or disclose whether anyone else was hurt. multiple state police units responded, according to the connecticut post's account of the investigation. the newspaper reported that the scene was still active around 9:15 p.m., several hours after the crash was first reported. police had not announced a cause, and the available reports did not say whether speed, impairment, weather, a medical event or another factor played a role. those possibilities remain unconfirmed and should not be treated as explanations. the transportation disruption continued into the night. the connecticut post reported heavy traffic near the closure at about 9:23 p.m., citing the department of transportation. patch later reported that the highway reopened late thursday night. the closure limits reported by ctdot were the same in both accounts: southbound i-91 between exits 36 and 35b. patch reported early friday that windsor ems transported the injured person to hartford hospital and that connecticut state police were investigating. patch also noted that the reports did not identify the person or explain what caused the crash. wfsb, which first reported the closure, separately described the incident as a two-vehicle crash and attributed the road information to ctdot and the serious-injury information to state police. for windsor and neighboring communities, the immediate concern was the combination of a serious injury scene and a highway shutdown during a busy travel period. the reopening restored the route, but it did not and [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/01/i-91-south-closed-windsor-after-crash/). new-england new-england new england ct windsor windsor, connecticut connecticut windsor i-91 traffic connecticut ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.excerpt: Kosta Diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him.
ct-kosta-diamantis-sentenced-2026-09-30.text: former connecticut official sentenced to 7 years after fleeing to greece kosta diamantis was sentenced in absentia for extortion, bribery and false-statement convictions tied to school-construction contracts; federal authorities are still seeking him. former connecticut school-construction official konstantinos “kosta” diamantis was sentenced wednesday to 84 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release, but he was not in the bridgeport courtroom to hear the punishment. the 70-year-old former state official had fled to greece before sentencing, and the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of connecticut said law enforcement is seeking him. the federal announcement is at https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-state-official-sentenced-7-years-federal-prison-school-construction-extortion-and. u.s. district judge stefan r. underhill imposed the sentence for convictions involving extortion, bribery, conspiracy and false statements. a federal jury in bridgeport found diamantis guilty in october 2025 on 21 counts: two counts of extortion, two extortion-conspiracy counts, two bribery counts, two bribery-conspiracy counts and 13 counts of making false statements to federal agents, according to the justice department. connecticut public reported that the case grew out of diamantis’s work as the state’s former deputy budget director and director of the office of school construction grants and review. that office administered grants for connecticut public-school construction projects seeking state funding. prosecutors said diamantis used the position to demand and receive payments from contractors while helping them obtain or preserve work. the justice department identified projects involving a school project in tolland, state reimbursement work for new britain and renovations at hartford’s bulkeley high school. the release says one contractor paid diamantis with cash and checks and hired his daughter at an inflated salary; those details describe the conduct underlying the convictions, not new untested allegations. the sentence came after an unusual break in the normal criminal-justice process. diamantis had been scheduled to appear for sentencing in september but did not attend. ct mirror reported that his lawyer told the court diamantis had left the united states and was in greece, where he holds dual citizenship. the later sentencing could proceed without him, but his absence leaves the practical question of how and when he will be taken into custody. federal officials have not announced that he has returned to the united states. the financial consequences are not settled. the justice department said judge underhill will determine restitution after additional court proceedings. that decision could identify losses that the government says were caused by the scheme, but the sentencing announcement did not give a final restitution amount. the unresolved figure matters because the projects at issue involved public school construction and state reimbursement, placing the case's consequences beyond the contractors and former official who appeared in court. the prison term was also shorter than the range sought by prosecutors. ct mirror reported that the government recommended a guideline range of 121 to 151 months, while the judge imposed 84 months. the difference does not change the convictions or the three-year supervised-release term, but it will be part of the record as prosecutors pursue diamantis and the court addresses restitution. ct mirror’s sentencing report is at https://ctmirror.org/2026/09/30/kosta-diamantis-still-a-fugitive-sentenced-to-84-months/. the case is not finished for the other people involved in the investigation. the justice department said contractors identified as duffy, monarca and roy pleaded guilty to related charges and are awaiting sentencing. the investigation was conducted by the fbi and irs criminal investigation, and federal prosecutors said the bribery scheme involved multimillion-dollar school-construction projects. connecticut public’s account of the sentencing, including the fact that diamantis remained outside the country, is at https://www.ctpublic.org/news/2026-09-30/kosta-diamantis-cts-disgraced-former-deputy-budget-director-sentenced. for connecticut, the public-interest question now extends from the sentence to the systems that allowed a senior official overseeing school-building money to steer contractors while concealing conduct from investigators. the court has established criminal responsibility through the jury’s verdict and the sentence; it has not yet completed restitution proceedings or resolved diamantis’s custody. those next steps will determine how much money is recovered, whether the former official is returned to face the prison term and what accountability reaches the related contractors. new-england new-england new england ct bridgeport bridgeport, ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: The new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services.
ct-leap-attendance-grants-2026-09-30.text: connecticut awards $6.2m to 29 districts to improve student attendance the new grants expand a home-visiting program that state officials say helped drive four straight years of lower chronic absenteeism, but the latest awards will still have to translate into local services. connecticut is awarding approximately $6.2 million to 29 school districts and regional education organizations for a home-visiting program aimed at bringing chronically absent students back into regular contact with their schools. the grants, announced sept. 30 by gov. ned lamont and education commissioner charlene russell-tucker, are being distributed through the learner engagement and attendance program, known as leap. the money comes from a $7 million state budget line item. about $800,000 will support statewide infrastructure such as home-visitor training, program implementation and data collection, according to the [connecticut governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-and-commissioner-russell-tucker-announce-state-grants-to-expand-program). leap pairs trained school staff and community partners with students and families. the visits are intended to identify the practical or personal barriers behind missed school days and connect families with services that can make regular attendance possible. the program began in 2021 with federal pandemic-relief money, initially serving 15 districts. it later expanded to 25, and this round brings the state’s reach to 29 districts for the 2026-27 school year. the recipients include some of connecticut’s largest districts. waterbury is slated to receive $525,000, hartford $500,000, bridgeport $475,000 and new haven $425,000. stamford will receive $350,000, while smaller awards go to districts including east windsor, east haven, plainfield and jamestown. middletown’s $125,000 award was reported separately by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-school-system-getting-6-figure-grant-aimed-boosting-attendance), which described the grant as funding for the same statewide leap effort. state officials say connecticut’s chronic-absenteeism rate fell from 23.7% in the 2021-22 school year to 16.4% in 2025-26. the governor’s office calculated that change as nearly 35,000 more students attending school regularly than at the earlier point. the figures describe statewide movement and do not establish that leap alone caused the decline; the announcement calls the program one part of a broader attendance strategy. there is earlier research behind the state’s decision to continue the program. the center for connecticut education research collaboration, a partnership involving the state education department and connecticut colleges, studied leap’s first 15 districts. its [published evaluation](https://portal.ct.gov/ccerc/current-projects/leap) found attendance gains after home visits, including an average increase of nearly 15 percentage points six months after visits for students served during the 2021-22 school year. the study also reported different effects by grade level and district, which matters because the new grant round includes a broader mix of communities than the initial cohort. connecticut says home visitors have conducted about 88,000 visits and reached roughly 53,000 students since leap began. those totals are cumulative program figures supplied by the state, not an independent count released with the new awards. the current announcement also does not provide a district-by-district attendance target or a deadline for demonstrating results. the immediate test will be local execution. districts will need to recruit or assign visitors, train them, coordinate with community organizations and turn conversations with families into help with transportation, health, housing, counseling or other barriers when those needs are identified. if the grants produce lasting attendance gains, connecticut will have a stronger case for making the home-visiting model a durable part of school operations after the pandemic-era funding that launched it has faded. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut student attendance chronic absenteeism leap public schools education funding

ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.excerpt: A $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help Connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity.
ct-middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansio.text: middletown veterans cemetery expansion will add 1,510 cremation plots a $584,250 federal grant, paired with $294,250 in state money, will help connecticut expand its only state-operated veterans cemetery as cremation burial space nears capacity. connecticut will expand the state veterans cemetery in middletown with 1,510 new burial plots for cremated remains, state officials announced friday. the project will use a $584,250 grant from the u.s. department of veterans affairs alongside $294,250 that connecticut has already allocated, adding capacity at a cemetery that serves veterans and eligible family members from across the state. the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-funding-to-expand-the-connecticut-state-veterans-cemetery-in-middletown) was also covered locally by [middletown patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/middletown-ct/middletown-veterans-cemetery-expansion-add-cremation-burial-plots). the work is planned for a parcel next to the existing cemetery at 317 bow lane. the property was formerly used by connecticut valley hospital and was recently transferred from the state department of mental health and addiction services to the department of veterans affairs, which is overseeing the expansion. the location allows the state to extend an existing cemetery rather than wait for a separate site to be developed. under the state’s announcement, the federal money will pay for the cremains burial plots and related site work, including an entrance gate, fencing, landscaping, irrigation components, concrete-block storage bays, site furnishings and supporting infrastructure. the state funding will support demolition of cottage 22, a vacant connecticut valley hospital building on the property. connecticut has not announced a completion date for the construction. the expansion is aimed at a specific capacity problem. the [connecticut department of veterans affairs](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the middletown cemetery currently has 14,718 burial plots and 3,000 columbarium niches. state officials estimate that the existing supply of in-ground cremation plots will be exhausted around january 2028 without additional space; with the expansion, those plots are projected to remain available through at least december 2033. that timing matters because the cemetery offers several distinct choices for families. the project concerns in-ground burial of cremated remains, while casket burials and above-ground columbarium niches are separate options. the state says extending the cremation-plot supply through 2033 would bring the estimated depletion dates for all three options into alignment, giving officials time to plan a future cemetery intended to serve veterans and their families over the longer term. the middletown site was established in 1985 and is the largest state-operated veterans cemetery in connecticut, according to the department of veterans affairs. the department’s [cemetery-services page](https://portal.ct.gov/dva/cemetery-and-memorial-services) says the site is the final resting place for more than 16,000 veterans and family members. connecticut also maintains the colonel raymond f. gates cemetery in rocky hill, which is reserved primarily for veterans residing at the state’s residential and skilled-nursing facilities, and provides perpetual care for spring grove veterans cemetery in darien, which is closed to new burials. the funding announcement follows a longer state effort to secure land and keep the middletown facility eligible for federal cemetery support. a [2023 state bond authorization](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/opm/bud-capital-budget/agendas/cy-2023/agenda%5fdec15%5f2023.pdf) set aside $3 million for land acquisition and improvements connected to the department of veterans affairs cemetery program. a subsequent state planning document said the middletown cemetery was expected to approach capacity within several years, while an [environmental scoping notice](https://portal.ct.gov/ceq/das/scoping-notice/dva-cemetery-expansion) identified the bow lane expansion area and estimated that existing space could be depleted in about 4.6 years. for connecticut veterans’ families, the immediate result is a planned increase in local burial capacity, not a new benefit or completed construction project. the state and federal awards still have to be translated into demolition, site preparation and cemetery improvements. the announcement does not specify the construction schedule or the final operating date for the new plots. the department of veterans affairs will remain responsible for project oversight and for coordinating burial services while the expansion proceeds. connecticut veterans veterans ct middletown middletown, connecticut connecticut middletown veterans cemeteries department of veterans affairs

ct-new-haven-quantumct-hub-opening-2026-.excerpt: The 4,500-square-foot center at 101 College Street will connect Yale and UConn researchers with students, startups and industry as the state builds a quantum-technology corridor.
ct-new-haven-quantumct-hub-opening-2026-.text: new haven opens quantumct hub as connecticut bets on quantum-tech economy the 4,500-square-foot center at 101 college street will connect yale and uconn researchers with students, startups and industry as the state builds a quantum-technology corridor. a new research and startup hub opened tuesday night in downtown new haven, giving connecticut’s long-running quantum-technology effort a physical base for collaboration among universities, entrepreneurs and industry. the ribbon-cutting at 101 college street marked the opening of a 4,500-square-foot center operated by quantumct, a nonprofit created to help move quantum research toward commercial uses. the [new haven independent report published by ct mirror](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/07/quantumct-innovation-hub-new-haven-101-college/) said the first-floor space is intended for researchers, students and entrepreneurs. its practical role is less about housing a finished quantum computer than about creating a place where people can share research, train workers, develop partnerships and build companies. a planned project at nearby 2 church street is expected to provide additional room for companies that grow out of the broader innovation district, but that facility is not the same as the hub that opened this week. the initiative joins two different connecticut strengths. yale researchers have built a long record in quantum information processing, while the university of connecticut has developed a research group focused in part on quantum sensing, according to the ct mirror report. uconn said in a july account of the federal award that about 65 of its researchers were working in quantum-related areas, with that number expected to rise to 70. quantum sensing uses unusual properties of matter at very small scales to measure things such as temperature, distance and magnetic fields with exceptional sensitivity. the new center also gives a local address to a funding strategy that has grown rapidly. the national science foundation [listed connecticut’s quantum technologies engine](https://www.nsf.gov/news/nsf-awards-12-new-regional-innovation-engines-fuel-research) among 12 new regional innovation engines announced in july. nsf said each team would initially receive $15 million over two years, with the possibility of as much as $160 million over a decade if it meets defined milestones. the connecticut team is led by uconn and is built around a coalition that includes universities, nonprofits and private-sector partners. state officials have made a separate, sizable commitment. uconn reported that connecticut pledged $61 million to support a quantum corridor headquartered in new haven, while the governor’s broader downtown investment announcement described a $50.5 million innovation-cluster package for infrastructure and facilities. the figures refer to overlapping parts of a multiyear strategy rather than a single check delivered at tuesday’s ceremony. a [new haven board of alders record](https://newhaven-ct.legistar.com/legislationdetail.aspx?fulltext=1&guid=f6aa0ae3-8682-4c53-8b30-9167845acacb&id=8045400&options=&search=) describes the city’s role in an innovation cluster linking quantum technology, bioscience, artificial intelligence and advanced computing. that public investment is meant to solve a familiar problem in emerging technology: strong research does not automatically produce local companies, skilled workers or durable jobs. quantumct’s model puts academic researchers, students and potential employers in the same network and gives early-stage businesses a place to find partners. the state’s own record describes the goal as supporting research and development, entrepreneurship and the translation of discoveries into products and services; those are objectives, not evidence that the corridor has already delivered a particular number of jobs or companies. private investment is beginning to test whether the strategy can work. the ct mirror report noted that d-wave acquired yale-founded quantum circuits for $550 million earlier this year and that d-wave is considering expanding the new haven workforce. that transaction is a company decision, not a guarantee for the region, but it illustrates why state and university leaders see a connection between basic research and commercial infrastructure as important. the hub is designed to shorten that distance without claiming that every research project will become a business. for new haven, the immediate change is visible and concrete: a new shared space in the downtown bioscience district, alongside a growing cluster of laboratories and offices. for students and workers elsewhere in connecticut, the longer-term question is whether the investment creates accessible training and jobs beyond the universities. for taxpayers, the relevant test will be whether quantumct meets the federal benchmarks attached to the nsf award and whether the state’s facilities support companies that can remain in connecticut. the opening therefore marks a beginning, not a finished quantum economy. quantumct still has to build its research, workforce and business networks, and the nsf funding can expand only if the initiative meets its milestones. connecticut now has a headquarters, a federal award and a substantial state-backed plan; the next measure of success will be what researchers, students and companies actually build from that foundation. connecticut business business ct new haven 101 college street, new haven, connecticut connecticut new haven quantum computing ct-prediction-markets-exit-crackdown-202.excerpt: State officials say three of nine companies targeted over unlicensed sports wagering have stopped offering prediction-market services in Connecticut, but the scope of at least one departure remains disputed.
ct-prediction-markets-exit-crackdown-202.text: three prediction-market operators halt connecticut sports contracts amid state crackdown state officials say three of nine companies targeted over unlicensed sports wagering have stopped offering prediction-market services in connecticut, but the scope of at least one departure remains disputed. connecticut regulators say three of the nine prediction-market operators targeted in the state's september crackdown have stopped offering sports-event contracts to residents, giving the state's campaign against a fast-growing form of online wagering its first reported retreat. the development affects platforms that let users buy and sell contracts tied to sports outcomes, while leaving six other named operators in communication with the department of consumer protection. the [connecticut office of the governor](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-announces-new-actions-against-illegal-prediction-markets-offering-sports-wagers) said the department of consumer protection issued nine cease-and-desist orders in september. the agency's list included polymarket, coinbase, crypto.com, robinhood, prophetx, novig, webull, gemini and underdog predict. the orders directed the platforms to stop advertising, promoting or making unlicensed online gambling available to connecticut residents. they also required the platforms to let connecticut customers withdraw funds held on their services. the new development was reported by connecticut news outlets after dcp commissioner bryan cafferelli said three operators had heard the state's message and were leaving. [ct insider reported](https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) that officials identified the three as prophetx, gemini and webull. the story said the department remained in contact with polymarket, coinbase, crypto.com, robinhood, novig and underdog. a related [news-times report](https://www.newstimes.com/politics/article/connecticut-prediction-market-companies-leave-ct-22460358.php) clarified that webull intended to continue its other services in connecticut and was responding specifically to the order concerning prediction markets. that distinction matters because “leaving connecticut” can describe several different actions: shutting down a company's entire business in the state, removing only sports contracts, or restricting particular products through geolocation. the news-times report said an analyst disputed the characterization of prophetx's withdrawal, while webull said it was still operating other services. the public statements reviewed for this report therefore support a narrower conclusion: state officials say three operators have stopped or are stopping the targeted sports-market activity, but the exact product-by-product status is not independently established for every company. connecticut's position is that sports prediction markets are wagers, not investments insulated from state gaming rules. the governor's september announcement said the state believes the contracts can take bets from people under 21, people on the voluntary self-exclusion list and participants wagering on connecticut college sports. officials also said the platforms do not operate under the technical, integrity and consumer-protection standards required of licensed sportsbooks. those are the state's allegations and regulatory conclusions; the companies have argued that their event contracts are financial products governed by federal law. the fight has regional and national significance because prediction markets have expanded beyond election-style questions into contracts on game winners, point spreads and player statistics. connecticut's release said one platform reported nearly $250 million in college-football trading volume on the first day of the 2026 season. the state is trying to preserve a more limited legal market created in 2021, when connecticut authorized sports wagering through licensed partners connected to draftkings, fanduel and fanatics, while maintaining an age minimum and responsible-gambling rules. the enforcement campaign also sits alongside a court dispute. connecticut sued kalshi in august seeking to block what the attorney general described as unlicensed sports betting. in its [august 26 announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/connecticut-sues-kalshi-to-stop-illegal-unlicensed-sports-betting), the attorney general's office said a federal judge had denied kalshi's request for a preliminary injunction and that kalshi had appealed to the second circuit. the kalshi litigation is separate from the september orders to the nine operators, but it could help determine how far state gambling laws reach when a platform describes its products as federally regulated event contracts. for connecticut users, the immediate practical question is access to specific sports markets and the ability to withdraw money, not whether all prediction-market products have disappeared. the department said it is still communicating with six operators, and the state has not announced a final resolution with each of them. further cease-and-desist actions, company notices, court rulings or public compliance records will be needed to show whether the remaining platforms restrict their sports offerings or continue to challenge connecticut's interpretation of state law. connecticut gambling gambling ct hartford connecticut connecticut gambling prediction markets consumer protection sports betting

ct-realpage-rent-pricing-case-2026-10-06.excerpt: A federal antitrust lawsuit backed by Connecticut and other states survived RealPage's effort to have the case thrown out, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent setting in court.
ct-realpage-rent-pricing-case-2026-10-06.text: connecticut realpage rent-pricing case will continue after court ruling a federal antitrust lawsuit backed by connecticut and other states survived realpage's effort to have the case thrown out, keeping allegations about algorithmic rent setting in court. connecticut's antitrust case against realpage will continue after a court rejected the company's attempt to have the rent-pricing lawsuit thrown out, attorney general william tong's office announced tuesday. the ruling keeps alive a multistate challenge to software that prosecutors say helped landlords use nonpublic market information to coordinate apartment prices. the [connecticut office of the attorney general](https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2026-press-releases/court-sides-with-attorney-general-tong-in-realpage-case) said connecticut, the u.s. department of justice and other states sued realpage in 2024. the case alleges that realpage sold revenue-management software to property managers, collected sensitive information about rents, discounts and available units, and used that information to recommend prices. state officials further allege that the system encouraged property managers to accept recommendations automatically, reducing the incentive to compete for renters. those are allegations, not findings that realpage or the landlords violated the law. the ruling is a decision about whether the claims can proceed, not a final judgment on liability or a determination that any particular connecticut tenant was overcharged. realpage has not been found liable in the state announcement, and the public release did not identify the judge or provide a full copy of the order. the litigation also includes six large landlord defendants named in a january 2025 amended complaint: greystar real estate partners, blackstone's livcor, camden property trust, cushman & wakefield, pinnacle property management services and willow bridge property company. the attorney general's office said the coalition alleges those companies worked with realpage and each other by sharing competitively sensitive information and using common pricing tools. a prior state announcement identified greystar, pinnacle and willow bridge as companies operating in connecticut, giving the case a direct connection to renters in the state. two of those landlord matters have already taken a different path. tong's office said connecticut joined other attorneys general in settlements totaling $7 million with livcor and $7 million with greystar. under those agreements, the companies agreed to stop using nonpublic data from other landlords to set rents. the settlements do not resolve the remaining case against realpage or answer the broader question of how algorithmic pricing affects apartment markets. the [justice department's case page](https://www.justice.gov/atr/case/us-and-plaintiff-states-v-realpage-inc) identifies the case as *u.s. and plaintiff states v. realpage, inc.* and lists connecticut among the state plaintiffs. its docket materials include the 2024 complaint, an amended complaint and filings related to proposed judgments involving several landlord defendants. the federal record shows the case has generated separate resolutions and ongoing claims rather than one single proceeding with one outcome for every defendant. the dispute matters in connecticut because rent-setting decisions can affect the starting price, renewal price and discounts offered at multifamily properties, even when the software company and property owner are not household names to tenants. the state's case does not establish how much any connecticut renter paid because of the alleged conduct, and the attorney general's announcement did not provide a statewide damages estimate. it does show what the state is seeking: an order preventing realpage and participating property managers from sharing nonpublic information and working together to inflate rents. renters should not treat the tuesday ruling as an immediate rent reduction or a payment announcement. a surviving lawsuit can move into further litigation, settlement discussions or trial, and the public sources reviewed for this report do not establish a final remedy or timeline. for now, connecticut remains one of the states pursuing the case, while the next major developments will come through court filings, additional settlements or a final decision on the allegations. connecticut housing housing ct hartford connecticut connecticut housing rent antitrust realpage

ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.excerpt: The grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities.
ct-recreational-trails-grants-2026-10-01.text: connecticut awards $10.5m for 50 recreational-trail projects the grants will support construction, accessibility work, planning and maintenance, with half of the selected projects serving distressed municipalities or environmental-justice communities. connecticut is awarding approximately $10.5 million to 50 projects intended to build, repair, connect and improve recreational trails across the state, gov. ned lamont and the department of energy and environmental protection announced thursday. the awards come through the connecticut recreational trails grant program after a competitive review by deep and the connecticut greenways council. the money was previously allocated by the state bond commission, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-state-grants-for-recreational-trails). the program supports more than new stretches of pavement: the 2026 list includes construction, rehabilitation, bridge replacement, accessibility upgrades, trailhead and parking improvements, planning and design, equipment, outreach and long-term maintenance. that mix means the award will produce different kinds of results in different communities. winchester received $749,000 for construction intended to complete the sue grossman still river greenway. new haven received $274,730 for planning and design at the east rock park college woods inclusive community trail, while naugatuck received $400,000 to design a connector for the naugatuck river greenway between naugatuck and waterbury. bridgeport received $180,000 for planning and design of the old mill green pathways project, and east hartford received $200,000 to design a gap closure on the east coast greenway. the geographic spread is one reason the grants matter beyond individual trailheads. other awards include $505,000 for a multi-use connector in avon, $495,000 for an accessible bridge and trail at steep rock association’s hidden valley preserve, $492,874 for the university of connecticut’s trails and active-living program, and $498,400 for the connecticut forest and park association’s blue-blazed trail system and woodland conservation corps. the full award table also includes projects in eastern connecticut, the shoreline, the hartford region and the northwest hills. twenty-five of the 50 projects are in, or serve, municipalities the state classifies as distressed or environmental-justice communities. that designation does not mean every project has the same scope or construction schedule, but it signals that the review process gave weight to communities that have not always had equal access to outdoor recreation. the state says the awards are designed to improve public access while supporting recreation, active transportation, conservation and local connections. there is already evidence of substantial demand for the network. connecticut’s trail census, a uconn program that uses infrared counters and volunteer-supported data collection, recorded more than 2.7 million trail uses at 27 monitored locations during 2025, the state release said. the [uconn ct trails program](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/) maintains the census and a public trail-finder system; its 2025 count report is listed in the program’s [research archive](https://cttrails.uconn.edu/pubs/reports/). counter totals measure recorded uses at monitored sites, not every trip on every trail, so they should be read as an indicator rather than a statewide attendance total. the program also arrives as connecticut continues to treat trails as public-health and economic infrastructure. deep describes more than 2,000 miles of multi-use trails in state parks and forests alone, while the governor’s office said outdoor recreation contributes about $6 billion annually to the state economy and supports more than 50,000 jobs. those figures come from state and federal economic accounts cited in the announcement, not from an independent assessment of this grant round. the next phase will be local implementation. planning awards still require design work, permits and decisions about routes, access and maintenance before construction can begin. construction awards will need to be matched with contracting, scheduling and long-term upkeep. for residents, the practical question is when each town or organization can turn its award into a safer crossing, a more accessible trail, a completed connection or a maintained public route. the grant list provides the funding commitments; project timelines will depend on the recipients and the state’s agreement process. new-england new-england new england ct hartford connecticut connecticut recreational trails deep outdoor recreation public access infrastructure

ct-shore-line-east-service-expansion-202.excerpt: The expanded CTrail schedule adds afternoon and evening trips between New Haven and New London, including a connection for riders arriving from New York.
ct-shore-line-east-service-expansion-202.text: shore line east adds four weekday trains as new schedule begins the expanded ctrail schedule adds afternoon and evening trips between new haven and new london, including a connection for riders arriving from new york. ctrail shore line east’s expanded weekday schedule began monday, adding four trains between new haven and new london and shortening some of the long gaps that have shaped travel along connecticut’s shoreline. the change affects commuters and other riders using stations from new haven to southeastern connecticut, with new afternoon and evening options in both directions. the new schedule adds two eastbound trains from new haven union station to new london. train 1628 leaves at 2:55 p.m. and reaches new london at 4:05 p.m.; train 1640 leaves at 6:03 p.m. and arrives at 7:13 p.m., according to the [official shore line east schedule effective oct. 5](https://shorelineeast.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/sle-october-5th-schedule_edit.pdf). both trains serve the line’s stations, including branford, guilford, madison, clinton, westbrook and old saybrook. two new westbound trains fill part of the return-trip gap. train 1683 departs new london at 4:40 p.m. and reaches new haven union station at 5:49 p.m. train 1693 leaves new london at 7:28 p.m. and arrives in new haven at 8:37 p.m. the official timetable also shows several existing trains with adjusted numbers or times, so a rider who remembers an older departure should check the current schedule rather than rely on the previous timetable. the 6:03 p.m. eastbound trip is especially relevant to passengers connecting from the new haven line. the new timetable lists a connection from metro-north super express train 3542, which leaves new york’s grand central terminal at 4:11 p.m. and stamford at 4:55 p.m. before reaching new haven. connecticut officials had described the connection as a way to make an evening trip toward the shoreline more practical, but the state’s schedule warns that connecting-service times are not guaranteed. the service increase follows an additional $3 million for the connecticut department of transportation in budget adjustments approved during the 2026 legislative session, according to [gov. ned lamont’s announcement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/09-2026/governor-lamont-announces-additional-shore-line-east-rail-service-coming-on-october-5). the governor’s office said the schedule was shaped by customer-satisfaction survey responses and feedback to train and customer-service staff. the goal was to target periods when riders had fewer choices, not to redesign the line’s route or add new stations. the expansion is meaningful because shore line east remains below its pre-pandemic service and ridership levels. the [new haven register reported](https://www.nhregister.com/connecticut/article/ct-shore-line-east-more-trains-amtrak-22422965.php) that the four additions bring the line to 24 weekday trains, compared with 36 before the pandemic, and that ridership was about 247,000 last year versus roughly 660,000 in 2019. those figures provide context for the change: the new trips improve the timetable without restoring the line to its earlier frequency. shore line east connects new haven with new london and stops at state street and union station in new haven, as well as branford, guilford, madison, clinton, westbrook, old saybrook and new london. the corridor serves shoreline communities that rely on rail for work, school, medical appointments and connections to the broader new haven and new york markets. the added evening departures may be most useful to people whose schedules do not fit the older midday gaps or the limited late-day choices. the line’s operator says passengers should use the interactive trip planner or current timetable before traveling, particularly when connecting to metro-north or amtrak. the published schedule notes that amtrak trains listed for shore line east accept only a ctrail monthly pass or ten-trip ticket, and passengers must reserve a seat through amtrak’s ridereserve program. the immediate test for the expansion will be whether the new trips make those connection windows dependable enough to bring more riders back to the corridor. connecticut transportation transportation ct new haven shore line east corridor, connecticut connecticut shore line east ctrail commuter rail new haven new london transportation

ct-south-windsor-flock-camera-removal-20.excerpt: The Town Council voted 6-3 to take down eight automated license-plate readers within 60 days and purge the data, putting privacy concerns ahead of keeping the system as a police tool.
ct-south-windsor-flock-camera-removal-20.text: south windsor votes to end flock contract and remove license-plate readers the town council voted 6-3 to take down eight automated license-plate readers within 60 days and purge the data, putting privacy concerns ahead of keeping the system as a police tool. south windsor will end its contract with flock safety and remove the town’s automated license-plate readers after the town council voted 6-3 monday night. the resolution calls for the town manager to terminate the agreement, take down the readers within 60 days and purge the data collected through the system, according to the [journal inquirer’s report](https://www.ctinsider.com/journalinquirer/article/south-windsor-ct-flock-cameras-removed-22465434.php). the decision followed an oct. 5 public hearing on the eight cameras. the journal inquirer reported that residents from south windsor and neighboring communities spoke in favor of removal, with privacy and fourth amendment concerns dominating the testimony. no one at the hearing spoke in favor of keeping the system, the newspaper reported. a council straw poll after the hearing produced a 20-2 vote for removal, although the formal council action was the 6-3 vote that sets the town’s policy. mayor craig zimmerman said he initially supported the program but changed his position after meeting with officials inside and outside south windsor. he told the journal inquirer that the cameras could help police, but that he was not comfortable with the contract’s limits on control and accountability for the data. deputy mayor andrew paterna similarly framed the vote as a question about mass surveillance rather than distrust of south windsor police. the three council members who opposed removal emphasized the public-safety value of the technology. councilor audrey delnicki described flock and similar systems as another tool available to law enforcement, while councilor michael ouellette said he trusted the police chief and department to handle the data appropriately, according to the journal inquirer. councilor elizabeth pendleton said she was initially undecided before voting to remove the cameras because a private company operated the system and had access to extensive personal data. south windsor’s own april 6 council minutes show how the system was designed to work before monday’s vote. police chief kristian lindstrom described four bidirectional locations that scanned roadways in both directions and said the system had been operating for nearly 11 months. the minutes say ordinary data was stored for 30 days unless it was retained longer for an investigation, and that officers used individual accounts with trackable credentials. those details came from a presentation months before the council chose to end the program, not from an audit of the vote or a finding that south windsor officers misused the system. the [town minutes](https://www.southwindsor-ct.gov/sites/g/files/vyhlif8416/f/minutes/4-6-26_minutes-town-council-regular-meeting_2.pdf) provide that earlier official account. the local decision arrives as connecticut’s new automated-license-plate-reader rules take effect. the connecticut office of legislative research says public act 26-14, effective oct. 1, generally limits retention to 21 days and restricts public agencies and vendors to listed uses, including specific criminal investigations, warrant searches, missing-person cases and stolen-vehicle recovery. the law also bars certain forms of monitoring and data use, including investigations tied to immigration enforcement. the [legislative summary](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/rpt/pdf/2026-r-0089.pdf) describes the statewide framework, but it does not require south windsor to keep its local system operating. flock spokeswoman courtney terlecki told the journal inquirer that agencies own their data, access is limited to authorized users and searches create permanent audit trails. south windsor’s vote does not decide whether other connecticut towns will keep similar systems, but it adds another local test of whether the investigative benefits are worth the privacy and governance concerns. the journal inquirer has reported that the town began using the readers in 2025 after the council approved the program in a 2023 executive session. for residents, the immediate change is operational: the readers are scheduled to come down, the contract is to be terminated and the collected data is to be purged. if south windsor officials later propose bringing the technology back, the journal inquirer reported that the town would need another public hearing and another public vote. that leaves the next steps—contract timing, physical removal and confirmation of deletion—as the parts of monday’s decision that still have to be carried out. connecticut public-safety public safety ct south windsor south windsor town hall, south windsor, connecticut connecticut south windsor flock safety automated license plate readers privacy police technology public safety

ct-southington-fema-safer-grant-12-firef.excerpt: The FEMA award could add 12 firefighters and expand around-the-clock coverage, but the Town Council must still accept the grant and decide how to pay for the positions after federal support ends.
ct-southington-fema-safer-grant-12-firef.text: southington fire department wins $3.03 million staffing grant, but town approval is still pending the fema award could add 12 firefighters and expand around-the-clock coverage, but the town council must still accept the grant and decide how to pay for the positions after federal support ends. southington’s fire department has been awarded a $3.03 million federal grant that could add 12 firefighters to the department, a potentially significant change for a town that has relied on a mix of career staff, volunteers and mutual aid from neighboring communities. the award was announced by the department in late september and reported locally this week, but it is not yet a hiring authorization: the town council must review and accept the grant before the plan can move forward. the money comes through the federal emergency management agency’s staffing for adequate fire and emergency response program, commonly called safer. fema describes safer as a competitive grant program intended to help fire departments increase the number of firefighters, meet minimum staffing standards and achieve 24-hour coverage. its guidance says hiring awards can support the traditional missions of fire departments as well as stronger protection from fire and related hazards. [fema’s safer program guidance](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_gpd-fy-2023-safer-faqs.pdf) provides that broader context. southington officials and department representatives say the local award would address a long-running staffing problem. the southington outsider reported that the department’s volunteer ranks have fallen from more than 100 people about 14 years ago to roughly 20 now, according to captain daniel comen, who wrote the grant application. that decline has left the station at 35 clark street staffed only on weekdays, the publication reported. the new grant is intended to make that station available around the clock. the operational goal is more than adding names to a roster. comen told the southington outsider that the department now has as many as seven firefighters on duty and can fall to six, while the grant-supported plan would raise the regular daily level to 11, with a low point of 10. the department says that additional coverage could make it easier to send a crew to an emergency without leaving another station short-handed. the department also expects the staffing change to reduce its dependence on neighboring towns for routine coverage. southington currently calls on mutual-aid partners in meriden, bristol, new britain, plainville and cheshire when it needs to maintain station coverage while responding to a larger fire, according to comen’s account in the southington outsider. he said the department’s goal is to reduce routine mutual-aid requests by about half. that is a department target, not a guaranteed result of the award, and actual response times will depend on hiring, training, scheduling and call volume. the award is unusually large by the department’s accounting. southington fire department officials told patch that it was the only fiscal-year 2025 safer award announced for a connecticut department at the time, the largest announced in new england, the second-largest in the northeast and the 11th-largest nationally. those rankings are based on awards announced so far, rather than a permanent ranking of every fire department or a measure of fire outcomes. the quinnipiac post reported the same pending-review status and described the award as one of the largest in the region based on the department’s figures. the unresolved issue is what happens after the federal grant period. patch reported that the award would offset the cost of hiring the 12 firefighters, but that local officials and taxpayers would ultimately have to decide whether to keep funding the positions when federal money runs out. the southington outsider also reported that the department expects the added staffing to reduce overtime costs, but potential savings do not by themselves establish the town’s future payroll obligation. the town has not yet announced a final implementation schedule or long-term cost decision. the next formal checkpoint is the town council’s review and acceptance of the grant. patch reported that the council’s next regular meeting is scheduled for oct. 12 at the john weichsel municipal center, while the southington outsider reported that the department expected the grant to be considered at a meeting on oct. 13. the differing dates show why the agenda and the council’s official action should be checked before treating the award as final. until the council acts, southington has a federal staffing opportunity, not 12 newly hired firefighters. connecticut public-safety public safety ct southington southington, connecticut connecticut southington firefighters fema safer grant emergency response mutual aid local government

ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.excerpt: A Region 12 bus carrying students left South Grand Street and struck a building Thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation.
ct-suffield-school-bus-crash-2026-10-01.text: suffield school bus crash sends 11 to hospitals with minor injuries a region 12 bus carrying students left south grand street and struck a building thursday morning; police said the cause remains under investigation. eleven people were taken to two local hospitals with minor injuries thursday after a small school bus carrying students left the roadway and struck a building in suffield, connecticut. the crash brought police, fire and ambulance crews to south grand street and left investigators working to determine why the bus veered off the road. suffield police said officers responded to the area of 425 south grand st. at about 9:49 a.m. after receiving a report of a motor-vehicle crash with possible injuries. their preliminary account said the bus was traveling north toward mountain road when it left the right shoulder and collided with a building beside the street. police did not announce a mechanical problem, medical event, weather factor or other cause. the bus came from regional school district 12, which serves communities in the shepaug valley. nbc connecticut reported that students were aboard, while the suffield volunteer ambulance association said 15 people, including the driver, were on the small bus. the association said 10 students and the driver were transported for evaluation. authorities did not release the students’ ages or identify the hospitals. the ambulance response required help from several nearby agencies. the ambulance association said it sent three ambulances staffed by paramedics, while enfield ems and the windsor locks lions club ambulance provided additional units. north central cmed helped coordinate the transports and contacted receiving hospitals to confirm that they could accommodate the patients. that coordination also shaped how the students were handled after the crash. according to the ambulance association’s statement reported by patch, responders tried to keep the students together when possible so school staff and families could receive information more easily. region 12 personnel came to the scene to assist the students, and emergency officials said the response was managed through the area’s normal mutual-aid system. the ambulance association also pushed back on online descriptions of the incident as a mass-casualty or multi-casualty event. it said the scene required significant coordination but did not meet that designation. that distinction describes the emergency-management classification, not the seriousness of the reported injuries: police and ambulance officials said everyone taken for treatment had minor injuries. hearst connecticut media reported that the bus was carrying shepaug valley school students on the way to a fair and that a region 12 official said the vehicle was driven by a properly licensed teacher. that account adds context to the trip but does not resolve the central unanswered question of what caused the bus to leave south grand street. police interviewed people involved and said the investigation was continuing. south grand street was closed while the scene was investigated and later reopened, according to local reports. no charges or citations had been announced in the available accounts. for families and residents, the immediate outcome was that the 11 people transported for care had reported minor injuries; the longer-term questions concern the crash sequence, the condition of the building and any findings by police or the school district. sources: [suffield police department details reported by patch](https://patch.com/connecticut/suffield/crash-reported-south-grand-street-suffield), [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/11-people-sent-to-hospitals-after-school-bus-crashes-into-building-in-suffield/3780574/), [wfsb](https://www.wfsb.com/2026/10/01/school-bus-crashes-into-building-suffield-police-confirm/), and [hearst connecticut media](https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/journalinquirer/article/region-12-school-bus-crash-suffield-ct-south-grand-22457938.php). new-england new-england new england ct suffield suffield, connecticut connecticut suffield school bus region 12 traffic crash public safety

ct-tv-to-table-trail-launch-2026-10-06.excerpt: The new tourism guide highlights more than 60 Connecticut restaurants and chefs featured on national food programs, with a Stamford launch hosted by Waterbury native Scott Conant.
ct-tv-to-table-trail-launch-2026-10-06.text: connecticut launches tv-to-table trail linking food-show fame to local restaurants the new tourism guide highlights more than 60 connecticut restaurants and chefs featured on national food programs, with a stamford launch hosted by waterbury native scott conant. connecticut has turned its television food cameos into a statewide tourism itinerary. gov. ned lamont and the connecticut office of statewide marketing and tourism announced the launch of the [connecticut tv-to-table trail](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-announces-tv-to-table-trail) on oct. 5, inviting visitors to go from watching a chef or restaurant on screen to visiting the place where the food is made. the program is built as a promotional guide rather than a single road route. the state’s [ctvisit directory](https://ctvisit.com/articles/connecticut-tv-table-trail) presents the trail as a map of restaurants and food destinations that have appeared on television, giving travelers a way to search for stops across connecticut. the launch announcement says the featured businesses include chefs who have appeared on chopped, beat bobby flay, diners, drive-ins and dives, best bite in town, guy’s grocery games and cupcake wars. the breadth is part of the pitch. the [hour reported](https://www3.thehour.com/food/article/connecticut-tv-table-trail-22454768.php) before the launch that more than 60 eateries were included, spread across fairfield, hartford, new haven, new london, tolland and other connecticut counties. the list ranges from greenwich restaurants such as colony grill and corbo’s southside deli to bridgeport’s merritt canteen, fairfield’s rawley’s drive-in and new haven’s da legna x nolo. those examples make the trail less about one celebrity destination and more about connecting familiar local businesses with a statewide audience. the launch took place at the stamford museum and nature center and featured connecticut native scott conant, a james beard award-winning chef, restaurateur, cookbook author and longtime television personality. according to [ct insider’s preview of the launch](https://www.ctinsider.com/food/article/connecticut-tv-to-table-trail-scott-conant-22427700.php), the event included tastings and a live cooking competition, with one invited guest serving as a judge alongside conant. the governor’s release says contestants used conant’s martone street tomato sauce with ingredients from farms in easton and shelton. conant’s role gives the state’s marketing effort a recognizable host, but the trail’s value depends on the restaurants that visitors can actually reach. a tv appearance can create curiosity; a directory can turn that curiosity into a trip to a diner, pizzeria, seafood restaurant or bakery in a different part of the state. for communities outside the major tourism centers, that is a way to attach national exposure to an existing local business without pretending that every stop offers the same kind of dining experience. the trail also fits a pattern in connecticut’s tourism strategy. the state has previously promoted themed experiences such as the connecticut pizza trail and the connecticut christmas movie trail. the tv-to-table guide uses the same basic idea—organize scattered attractions around a shared theme—but shifts the focus from a single food category or season to restaurants that already have a story connected to television. for visitors, the immediate next step is to use the ctvisit map to choose stops and then check each business directly for hours, reservations, menus and accessibility. the published material describes the trail as a discovery and marketing tool; it does not promise a uniform pass, discount, ranking or required sequence. that distinction matters because the businesses remain independent restaurants and food destinations, not branches of one state-run attraction. the launch gives connecticut a new way to package local food culture, but it does not by itself show how many additional diners the trail will bring. that will depend on whether travelers use the map beyond the initial publicity and whether participating businesses can convert television recognition into repeat visits. for now, the program offers a current, statewide list of places where a familiar television story can become an in-person meal. connecticut connecticut connecticut ct stamford stamford museum and nature center, stamford, connecticut connecticut tourism restaurants food television ct-uconn-blue-emergency-phones-injunctio.excerpt: A judge declined to issue an immediate shutdown order but set an Oct. 9 hearing on a parent’s request to keep the campus emergency phones operating while the dispute proceeds.
ct-uconn-blue-emergency-phones-injunctio.text: uconn parent asks court to halt storrs blue-light phone removals a judge declined to issue an immediate shutdown order but set an oct. 9 hearing on a parent’s request to keep the campus emergency phones operating while the dispute proceeds. a parent of a university of connecticut student is asking a state court to pause the university’s removal of blue-light emergency phones from the storrs campus, opening a new legal fight over whether a physical emergency network can be retired as cellphones and safety apps become more common. the court declined to grant an immediate, before-hearing injunction, but scheduled a remote preliminary hearing for oct. 9 at 9:30 a.m., according to reporting by [nbc connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/uconn-parent-sues-school-to-stop-removal-of-blue-light-emergency-phones/3780793/) and [hearst connecticut media](https://www.newstimes.com/news/education/article/uconn-blue-emergency-phones-lawsuit-22457637.php). billyjoe contreras filed the application oct. 1 in connecticut superior court, citing concerns about campus safety. his request would bar uconn from disconnecting, disabling, removing or decommissioning the existing blue-light phones and associated safety lights at storrs while the case is pending. he also asks the university to continue maintaining and operating the system. the immediate request was an ex parte application, meaning contreras sought temporary relief before a full hearing with the university; the judge’s decision leaves the phaseout dispute open rather than deciding whether the phones must ultimately remain. in an affidavit described by hearst, contreras argues that a student’s personal phone may be unavailable, uncharged, lost, stolen or unusable during an emergency. his filing says removing a nearby fixed device without an equivalent replacement could create a gap in access to help. that is an allegation and safety argument from the plaintiff, not a court finding. the oct. 9 proceeding is expected to give the parties a chance to discuss whether they can resolve the issue; if they cannot, the court may schedule a later evidentiary hearing. uconn has defended the phaseout as a technology and cost decision. nbc connecticut reported that the university says it received only two legitimate blue-phone calls in the past five years: one reporting a car crash and another from someone who believed they were being followed, a concern the university said was unfounded. the school told nbc that modernizing the system would cost about $6 million and that annual operating expenses exceed $70,000 as aging equipment requires more repairs. the university is not planning to remove every phone. uconn has said it will keep devices in locations where cellular coverage is weaker and is assessing which sites meet that test. for other students, the school points to personal cellphone calls, text-to-911 and the livesafe app, which can connect users to the university’s emergency communications center by text, video or phone. students interviewed by nbc said those tools do not entirely replace a clearly marked device that can be activated without finding or unlocking a personal phone. uconn’s own [division of university safety page](https://police.universitysafety.uconn.edu/emergency-blue-phones/) describes the existing storrs system as a network of phones located throughout campus: a user presses a button, describes the emergency to a dispatcher and a police officer is sent to the location. that design matters to the dispute because the devices serve students, employees and visitors who may not have a working phone immediately available. the university’s current public description explains how the system operates, but it does not establish how many storrs phones will remain after the review. the question of usage is still developing. a sept. 28 entry in [uconn’s public-records log](https://publicrecords.uconn.edu/requests/fpo-26-639-09-28-26-819-am/) shows an open request seeking the number of emergency blue phones at storrs as of aug. 31, the largest number ever installed and a year-by-year count of calls over the prior 25 calendar years. those records could add context to the university’s five-year figures, but the request itself is not a response from the school and does not yet provide the requested data. the next legal milestone is the oct. 9 remote hearing. until then, the court has not ordered uconn to stop its work, and the university’s plan to retain some phones in weak-service areas remains the stated approach. the case will turn on evidence about the remaining devices, their reliability and use, the alternatives available at each location and the practical safety consequences of removing them. for the storrs community, the immediate issue is not whether cellphones are widespread; it is whether that coverage is sufficient at every place and moment where a person may need help. new-england new-england new england ct storrs storrs, connecticut connecticut uconn storrs ct-woodbridge-karales-homicide-suicide-2.excerpt: Jo Ann and William Karales were found after an employee requested a welfare check at their Orchard Road home; police said the incident was isolated and posed no known danger to the public.
ct-woodbridge-karales-homicide-suicide-2.text: medical examiner rules woodbridge couple’s deaths a homicide-suicide jo ann and william karales were found after an employee requested a welfare check at their orchard road home; police said the incident was isolated and posed no known danger to the public. the deaths of a woodbridge couple found inside their orchard road home have been ruled a homicide-suicide, according to findings from connecticut’s office of the chief medical examiner and statements from local police. jo ann karales, 66, died from a shotgun wound to the neck and her manner of death was classified as homicide, the medical examiner’s office told news organizations. william karales, 71, died from a gunshot wound to the head and his manner of death was classified as suicide. nbc connecticut reported the findings after the couple’s bodies were taken to the medical examiner’s office in farmington. the couple was found friday, oct. 2, after an employee of their business told police the homeowners had not shown up for work and could not be reached. woodbridge police were called to the home at about 11:49 a.m. for a well-being check, according to the department’s account reported by nbc connecticut and [ct insider](https://www.ctinsider.com/connecticut/article/woodbridge-joann-william-karales-murder-suicide-22462568.php). officers entered through a rear window and found both people dead inside, police said. the connecticut state police western district major crime squad assisted woodbridge investigators with processing the scene. police initially described the matter as an isolated incident and said there was no known danger to the surrounding community. the medical examiner’s findings answered how the two people died but did not publicly establish what led to the shooting. police had initially declined to characterize the deaths while the examination and investigation were pending. as of monday, authorities had not disclosed a motive or described any other person as a suspect. the distinction matters: the medical examiner’s ruling classifies the manners of death, while the investigative record may still be incomplete. the deaths also affect a small connecticut company with a local employment connection. ct insider reported that william and jo ann karales operated sea lark enterprises, the woodbridge-based business behind soap lift, a product designed to keep bar soap raised so water can drain away. the report said the business grew from an operation william karales started in his long island garage and eventually shipped products beyond connecticut. ct insider also reported that the company worked with the amity transition academy, a program serving students with intellectual disabilities, to provide paid packaging work. that background gives the case a community dimension beyond the orchard road investigation: the couple’s deaths leave questions for relatives, employees and people who knew the business through that employment partnership. woodbridge police extended condolences to the karales family and thanked the state police major-crimes investigators who assisted. the department’s public statements, as reported by nbc connecticut, did not announce additional arrests or charges. further information would have to come from investigators or the medical examiner as the case record develops. connecticut public-safety public safety ct woodbridge orchard road, woodbridge, connecticut connecticut woodbridge new haven county homicide-suicide office of the chief medical
