ct-yale-tony-reno-death-2026-10-02.excerpt: Reno led Yale to five Ivy League championships and 83 wins during a 14-year tenure that reshaped the Bulldogs’ place in the FCS.
ct-yale-tony-reno-death-2026-10-02.text: former yale football coach tony reno dies at 52 reno led yale to five ivy league championships and 83 wins during a 14-year tenure that reshaped the bulldogs’ place in the fcs. tony reno, the former yale football coach who guided the bulldogs through five ivy league championships, has died at 52, yale athletics announced friday. the news reached the new haven campus less than eight months after reno stepped down from the program for health reasons. the [yale memorial](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/10/2/in-memoriam-former-football-head-coach-tony-reno.aspx) described a coach whose influence extended beyond wins and losses into the lives of the students he mentored. the associated press, in [reporting carried by the boston globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/02/sports/reno-yale-football/), said no cause of death was given. reno’s record places him among the most successful coaches in yale’s long football history. he went 83-49 over 14 seasons, according to yale and the ap, and ranks second in career victories behind carm cozza. his teams won ivy league titles in 2017, 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2025. yale also beat harvard in seven of the final nine meetings under reno, giving his tenure a particularly strong mark in the rivalry that anchors the program’s season each fall. the final championship season added a new chapter. yale’s official account of reno’s tenure says the 2025 bulldogs finished 8-2 in the regular season and 6-1 in league play, earning the ivy league’s first automatic berth in the ncaa football championship subdivision playoffs. yale then rallied from a 28-point deficit to beat youngstown state 43-42 in the opening round before losing 21-13 to eventual national champion montana state. the bulldogs finished no. 13 in the final fcs rankings. that run gave the program a national stage while preserving the ivy league’s academic and athletic identity. reno left the job in february, when he said his health situation made stepping down the right decision for yale football. in its [announcement at the time](https://yalebulldogs.com/news/2026/2/17/tony-reno-steps-down-as-head-coach-of-yale-football.aspx), the university said reno had led the program since january 2012 and had helped establish a foundation for the next coach. he had spent more than a decade on yale’s staff before becoming head coach, including work under jack siedlecki on the 2006 ivy championship team. kevin cahill took over the program after a national search. the numbers tell only part of why the announcement is significant to yale and the region. yale said six bulldogs won the asa s. bushnell cup as ivy league player of the year during reno’s tenure, while five yale players were selected in the nfl draft over the past seven years covered by the university’s february review. the school also credited reno’s teams with success in the classroom and community. in its memorial, yale emphasized his standards for student-athletes and the relationships he built with players, colleagues and alumni rather than presenting the coaching change simply as a succession story. reno’s connection to the area ran through both new haven and massachusetts. yale identified him as a massachusetts native, and the university’s account of his career says he spent his early yale years as an assistant before returning to lead the bulldogs. his family remained part of the program’s public story: the ap reported that he is survived by his wife, toni, and their children, dante, angelina and vince. dante was yale’s quarterback during the 2025 championship season, when the bulldogs made their first fcs postseason appearance. for yale, the immediate task is continuing a program that reno left with a conference title, a playoff win and a clear competitive identity. for new haven, his death closes the chapter on a coach who spent much of his career tied to the city and its university. yale’s tribute makes clear what will be measured now: not only how the bulldogs perform under cahill, but how much of reno’s emphasis on mentorship survives in the players who follow him. new-england new-england new england ct new haven new haven, connecticut connecticut new haven yale college football ivy league tony reno

ma-blandford-wildlife-corridor-2026-10-0.excerpt: The new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the Mass. Pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western Massachusetts.
ma-blandford-wildlife-corridor-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts protects 580 acres in blandford wildlife corridor the new public conservation land links more than 39,000 acres across the mass. pike while adding habitat and outdoor recreation space in western massachusetts. massachusetts conservation agencies and the nature conservancy have completed a project protecting more than 580 acres in blandford, creating new public land on both sides of interstate 90 and strengthening a wildlife connection through the western massachusetts hills. the [massachusetts executive office of energy and environmental affairs](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-protects-over-580-acres-for-wildlife-and-outdoor-recreation-in-blandford) announced the project oct. 2. [western mass news](https://www.westernmassnews.com/2026/10/03/more-land-added-chester-blandford-stare-forest/) independently reported the same acreage and the new designations. the protected property is divided into a 360-acre masswildlife blandford wildlife management area and a 218-acre addition to chester-blandford state forest. the former christmas tree farm crosses the mass. pike and connects more than 39,000 acres of already protected land, according to state officials and the local report. that makes the project more than a stand-alone open-space purchase: it closes a gap in a larger landscape where animals can move between habitat on opposite sides of one of new england's busiest highways. the land is open to the public for outdoor recreation, although the announcement did not provide a separate trail map, parking plan or operating schedule for the new management area. residents and visitors will need to rely on updates from masswildlife and the department of conservation and recreation for practical access information as management details are posted. the property contains mature and young forest, agricultural grasslands, wetlands and four brooks: sanderson, cushman, finley and peebles. those waterways are part of the westfield river watershed. state agencies said the conservation work will help protect water quality and nearby drinking-water supplies, while preserving cold-water fish habitat used by species such as eastern brook trout. the corridor also has a direct transportation-safety dimension. the state says masswildlife, dcr, massdot and the nature conservancy have been working to understand how animals cross roads and highways. at the blandford site, massdot and the nature conservancy are monitoring a culvert under i-90, where black bears, bobcats, coyotes, river otters and other wildlife have been documented passing through, according to the state announcement. keeping that route connected can help animals reach food, water and seasonal habitat while giving planners evidence for future crossing improvements. the project includes habitat that can support the new england cottontail, massachusetts' only native rabbit, which state officials describe as vulnerable to habitat loss. protecting connected forest and grassland does not guarantee that the rabbit or any other species will expand here, but it preserves the kind of varied landscape wildlife managers say is necessary for movement and adaptation as conditions change. blandford's acquisition is part of a broader state conservation strategy. massachusetts' biodiversity goals call for doubling the pace of land and water protection, with targets of conserving 30 percent by 2030 and 40 percent by 2050. the administration said its proposed mass ready act includes $304.5 million for land-protection programs and $20 million tied to biodiversity goals; those are proposed investments, not funds this project alone received. for the hilltowns, the immediate result is a permanently protected stretch of forest, streams and open land that can serve both residents and wildlife. the agencies involved still have to translate the acquisition into day-to-day public access and long-term habitat management. the new designations give them the protected footprint; future agency plans will determine how visitors use it and how the corridor is monitored over time. massachusetts environment environment ma blandford blandford, massachusetts massachusetts blandford conservation wildlife outdoor recreation

ma-boston-native-deisseroth-nobel-2026-1.excerpt: Karl Deisseroth, a Harvard graduate and Stanford professor, shares the 2026 medicine prize for pioneering optogenetics, which lets researchers control selected nerve cells with light.
ma-boston-native-deisseroth-nobel-2026-1.text: boston-born scientist shares nobel for turning light into a brain-research tool karl deisseroth, a harvard graduate and stanford professor, shares the 2026 medicine prize for pioneering optogenetics, which lets researchers control selected nerve cells with light. a boston-born scientist whose education included harvard university is one of three researchers awarded the 2026 nobel prize in physiology or medicine for work that changed how scientists study living brains. karl deisseroth, a stanford university professor, shares the prize with peter hegemann of humboldt university of berlin and georg nagel of the university of würzburg. the nobel assembly cited their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a method that uses light-sensitive proteins to activate or inhibit selected cells. the [official nobel announcement](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/press-release/) is the primary record of the award. the boston connection is biographical but meaningful: deisseroth was born in the city and earned his bachelor's degree from harvard in 1992 before completing his medical and doctoral training at stanford, according to the [associated press report published by wbur](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/10/05/nobel-prize-medicine-karl-deisseroth-boston-brain-research) and a [national academy of sciences biography](https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/karl-deisseroth-4gxnxv/). the award therefore links a major international science story to the region's longstanding role in training scientists and physicians, even though deisseroth now works in california. optogenetics addresses a basic problem in neuroscience: observing a brain signal is not the same as showing that a particular group of cells caused a behavior or symptom. traditional electrical stimulation can affect nearby circuits, while drugs spread through tissue and may act on many cell types. deisseroth's contribution was to help make a more targeted experiment possible by placing microbial proteins called opsins on selected mammalian neurons and using pulses of light to control them. [stanford's account of the work](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2026/10/karl-deisseroth-nobel-prize-physiology-medicine) describes the method as a way to switch individual nerve cells on or off in a living brain. the prize recognizes a sequence of discoveries rather than a single invention. hegemann and nagel studied light-sensitive proteins in single-celled algae. their work showed that channelrhodopsin can open a channel when exposed to blue light, producing an electrical impulse. deisseroth then helped adapt the underlying idea for neuroscience by getting light-sensitive proteins expressed in nerve cells and developing a way to deliver light through very thin optical fibers. that combination made it possible to test how defined circuits influence movement, emotion and behavior in living animals, instead of relying only on broad stimulation or observation. stanford says optogenetics is now used in thousands of laboratories worldwide. the university's [technical explainer](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2026/10/opsins-optogenetics-explainer-karl-deisseroth) says researchers can use different opsins and light wavelengths to increase or suppress activity in selected cells. that precision has helped scientists investigate disorders including parkinson's disease and depression in animal models. those experiments are not the same as an approved treatment for people, and the nobel recognition does not mean optogenetic therapy is ready for routine clinical use. it means researchers have a sharper way to test cause and effect in complex neural systems. the work also has a direct new england academic thread. deisseroth's harvard degree came before his stanford research career, and one of his early graduate students, feng zhang, later became a professor at the massachusetts institute of technology, according to stanford's account. that connection is part of a broader regional research ecosystem, but it should not be confused with the location of the prizewinning laboratory: deisseroth's current appointments are at stanford's schools of medicine and engineering, and the other two laureates are based in germany. for patients and families affected by neurological or psychiatric illness, the practical significance is still prospective. the technique can identify circuits involved in disease and help researchers evaluate possible interventions, but it does not by itself establish safety, effectiveness or availability of a human treatment. stanford describes the field as a foundation for understanding how the brain works and for exploring future therapies. the distinction matters because laboratory control of genetically modified cells in animals is far removed from a treatment that could be prescribed in a clinic. the nobel assembly announced the medicine prize monday in stockholm, beginning a week of awards that also includes prizes for physics, chemistry, literature and peace. the 2026 medicine prize carries 12 million swedish kronor, according to the ap report. deisseroth told reporters that he had been working late when the nobel committee called and that his next immediate task was making school lunches for his children. the personal detail does not change the science, but it underscored the unusual local angle of a global award: a boston native's name is now attached to one of modern neuroscience's most influential research tools. the next questions are scientific rather than ceremonial. researchers will continue testing what optogenetics can reveal about healthy neural circuits and disease, while determining which findings can eventually be translated into safe human therapies. for new england readers, the clearest verified takeaway is narrower: deisseroth's boston roots and harvard training are part of the story, while the nobel-winning work itself grew from an international chain of discoveries and is being advanced today at stanford and laboratories around the world. massachusetts science science ma boston boston and harvard university, massachusetts massachusetts boston harvard university nobel prize neuroscience optogenetics stanford university

ma-bridgewater-state-students-struck-202.excerpt: Steven Mayle, 44, was arraigned on charges including attempted murder after prosecutors said video showed him steering into two students during Homecoming weekend.
ma-bridgewater-state-students-struck-202.text: bridgewater state crash case moves forward as driver held without bail steven mayle, 44, was arraigned on charges including attempted murder after prosecutors said video showed him steering into two students during homecoming weekend. steven mayle, 44, of east weymouth, was arraigned monday in brockton district court in connection with the saturday crash that injured two bridgewater state university students during homecoming weekend. the plymouth county district attorney's office said mayle was held without bail and ordered to undergo a further competency evaluation at bridgewater state hospital. he is scheduled to return to court oct. 23 for a dangerousness hearing, according to the office's announcement as reported by the [fall river reporter](https://fallriverreporter.com/man-held-without-bail-after-allegedly-striking-two-bridgewater-state-students-authorities-looking-for-driver-in-road-rage-incident-prior-to-crash/). prosecutors brought two counts each of attempted murder, assault with intent to murder and leaving the scene of personal injury, along with one count each of reckless operation of a motor vehicle and a marked-lanes violation. those are allegations, not findings of guilt. the case remains at an early stage, and mayle is entitled to the presumption of innocence while the court addresses his competency and the commonwealth's request to keep him in custody. the underlying incident happened about 10:45 a.m. saturday on burrill avenue near the university's moakley center. two students were taken to area hospitals. earlier reporting said one had serious but non-life-threatening injuries and the other had minor injuries. the crash occurred as the campus hosted homecoming activities, a setting that brought a large number of students, families and visitors to the bridgewater campus. assistant district attorney samantha mullin told the court that surveillance video showed mayle traveling at high speed, turning, jumping a curb and striking both students. [cbs boston reported](https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/steven-mayle-bridgewater-state-students-struck-suv/) that mullin described the incident as targeted. that characterization is the prosecution's account of the video and is not a judicial finding. the university previously said there was no evidence the driver had singled out those particular students, a distinction that leaves the alleged deliberate movement of the vehicle separate from any established motive. mayle's defense attorney disputed that the act was deliberate or malicious and said his client was experiencing a severe mental-health crisis, cbs boston reported. a clinician who evaluated mayle before the arraignment recommended additional evaluation and testified that he appeared unaware of the charges, according to that report. the court's competency process will address whether mayle can understand the proceedings and assist in his defense; it does not decide whether the collision occurred or whether the criminal charges can ultimately be proved. investigators are also examining an alleged road-rage encounter in east bridgewater that preceded the campus crash. the [fall river reporter](https://fallriverreporter.com/man-held-without-bail-after-allegedly-striking-two-bridgewater-state-students-authorities-looking-for-driver-in-road-rage-incident-prior-to-crash/) reported that police are seeking the driver of a white suv who may have encountered mayle near a railroad crossing. a witness told police that a man believed to be mayle approached the suv and displayed a knife before driving toward bridgewater. that account remains part of an active investigation, and the suv driver's version had not been reported. bridgewater state, bridgewater police and east bridgewater police are investigating the sequence of events. the university's earlier statements said the driver had no affiliation with the school and that the campus police department was coordinating with municipal investigators. the students' names have not been released, and the public reports do not establish a broader threat to the campus or provide a final account of their recovery. the next confirmed court date is oct. 23. until then, the competency evaluation, dangerousness proceedings, additional witness accounts and any later release of evidence are likely to shape the case. the charges describe the seriousness of the alleged conduct, but the final legal outcome will depend on evidence presented in court rather than on the preliminary descriptions from prosecutors, police or news reports. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma bridgewater bridgewater state university, bridgewater, massachusetts massachusetts bridgewater bridgewater state university campus safety attempted murder charges homecoming

ma-cambridge-civic-assembly-shotspotter-.excerpt: A lottery-backed panel will study gunshot detection and park cameras over four Saturdays before sending recommendations to the City Council.
ma-cambridge-civic-assembly-shotspotter-.text: cambridge puts shotspotter debate before 40 residents in first civic assembly a lottery-backed panel will study gunshot detection and park cameras over four saturdays before sending recommendations to the city council. cambridge is moving its argument over gunshot-detection technology and public surveillance into a new phase: a 40-person civic assembly selected through a resident lottery. the city scheduled the selection for monday, oct. 5, at city hall, describing the process as the first municipal civic assembly in massachusetts and one of the first in new england. the [city of cambridge’s announcement](https://www.cambridgema.gov/news/2026/09/cityofcambridgetohostcivicassemblylotteryselectionnightonoctober5) said the panel will study the issues and develop recommendations for the city council rather than make a binding decision itself. the assembly’s assignment is deliberately narrow but consequential. members will consider whether, how and under what conditions cambridge should use gunshot-detection systems such as shotspotter and overnight video surveillance in public parks. the city’s [civic assembly guide](https://www.cambridgema.gov/civicassembly) says participants will examine effectiveness, cost, privacy, civil liberties, equity and public trust, then weigh evidence and lived experience before writing recommendations. final authority remains with the elected council. the selection process was designed to make the panel broader than the group that normally attends a council meeting. in september, the city mailed invitations to about 15,000 randomly selected households from a pool of roughly 56,000 cambridge households. more than 400 people entered the lottery, according to the city, and every neighborhood was represented among the applicants. residents 16 and older were eligible to volunteer, with additional outreach aimed at neighborhoods most affected by gun violence. the city is also paying residents for the time required to do the work. the assembly will meet for four full saturdays — oct. 24, nov. 7, nov. 21 and dec. 5 — with a $1,000 stipend and accommodations that include child care, interpretation and translation, according to the city’s september launch announcement. independent experts and community members with different perspectives are expected to brief the panel. the process is being organized with fide north america and supported by community partners, including researchers at the massachusetts institute of technology. the experiment follows a year of sharp disagreement over shotspotter. cambridge day reported that the city council voted 5-2-2 in may to end the city’s use of the system within 90 days. the technology uses acoustic sensors to flag sounds that may be gunfire, a design supporters associate with faster emergency response and critics associate with privacy, accuracy and over-policing concerns. those competing claims are part of what the assembly is being asked to examine; the city’s materials do not predetermine an outcome. the debate changed again after the july 4 fatal shooting of xavier bautista, a cambridge department of public works employee. nbc boston reported that the council later voted 6-3 to reactivate shotspotter for at least 90 days while the resident review took place. that sequence left cambridge with a live policy question rather than a settled one: whether to keep a controversial detection network, impose new safeguards, or pursue other public-safety approaches. for residents who were not selected, the process is still meant to be public. the city says briefings, agendas, speaker lists, minutes and other materials will be posted online, and community members can submit comments for the assembly and the city to consider. the city’s timeline says selected participants will be notified by oct. 10, with recommendations due to the council in december. the council will then decide how — or whether — to incorporate them into future surveillance and public-safety policy. that timetable gives cambridge a structured way to test a difficult local question before making a longer-term commitment. it also creates a record residents can inspect: who was selected, what evidence the panel heard, which safeguards it recommends and where disagreement remains. the immediate result of the lottery is therefore only the beginning. the more consequential measure will be whether four saturdays of representative deliberation produce guidance the council and the wider community consider credible. ma-canton-hickory-lane-fire-2026-10-05.excerpt: The Hickory Lane home was destroyed after a Sunday blaze and a Monday-morning rekindle; officials said the cause remained under investigation and the fire was not believed to be suspicious.
ma-canton-hickory-lane-fire-2026-10-05.text: canton house fire injures resident, kills dog and sends firefighter to hospital the hickory lane home was destroyed after a sunday blaze and a monday-morning rekindle; officials said the cause remained under investigation and the fire was not believed to be suspicious. a house fire in canton injured the home’s sole occupant, killed a pet dog and destroyed the residence before the fire rekindled hours later, sending a firefighter to a hospital for precautionary treatment. the first blaze began around 3:45 p.m. sunday at 11 hickory lane, according to the [canton fire department’s account reported by the boston globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/05/metro/canton-fire-destroys-home-hospitalizes-occupant-and-firefighter/). firefighters arrived to find heavy flames moving from an enclosed rear porch into the roof and attic of the two-story home. the crews initially tried to fight the fire from inside, but moved to a defensive exterior operation after the roof began to sag and partially collapse. canton fire chief jamie meier said the fire was already well developed when crews arrived, the globe reported. the structure was ultimately considered a total loss. the resident was found injured outside the house and taken to a boston-area hospital. officials said the injuries were burns that were not believed to be life-threatening. a labradoodle was found dead inside the home. [nbc boston](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/canton-massachusetts-fire-injures-resident/4025904/) reported that the resident was expected to be ok, while the fire department said the property itself could not be saved. firefighters also faced a water-supply problem involving a nearby hydrant that was not working properly, according to the accounts. that detail matters because crews were dealing with a fire that had already reached the upper portions of the building and a roof that was becoming unsafe for interior operations. the reporting does not say how long the hydrant problem lasted or whether it changed the final damage assessment. the danger continued after the initial fire was knocked down. the home had been boarded up when firefighters were called back at about 3 a.m. monday, oct. 5, after the fire rekindled. [wcvb](https://www.wcvb.com/article/firefighter-hospitalized-after-fire-rekindles-at-canton-home-where-resident-suffered-burns/74024607) reported that the rear of the house was gone and the front was unstable, leaving crews to work from outside while smoke and flames moved through the structure. during the second response, a firefighter who became short of breath was taken to milton hospital as a precaution. a camper with a fiberglass shell and propane tanks at the back of the property also caught fire, and the heat melted vinyl siding on a neighboring home, according to the globe. no additional injuries were reported in the accounts reviewed for this story. the cause had not been finalized. the [boston 25 report](https://cmg-cmg-tv-10020-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/news/local/crews-return-canton-home-after-fire-rekindles-overnight/wq4qiws6r5g4lal6vduj2p2mhm/) on the rekindle said investigators were still working to determine what started the original fire, and the station described the monday return as an ongoing investigation. the globe reported that officials did not believe the fire was suspicious and that investigators considered embers from a portable fire pit on the back porch a possible origin. those statements describe a preliminary assessment, not a final cause determination. for canton residents, the incident is a reminder that a fire can remain dangerous after visible flames are knocked down, particularly when a roof or attic has been compromised. the immediate consequences in this case include a displaced resident, a destroyed home, damage to a neighboring property and a firefighter injury. the available reports do not identify the resident or provide a detailed medical update, and they do not say whether the state investigation has reached a final conclusion. the next step is the completion of the fire investigation by canton officials and the massachusetts state fire marshal’s office. until that work is finished, the confirmed facts are the injuries, the pet death, the total loss of the home, the overnight rekindle and the precautionary hospitalization of the firefighter; the precise ignition source remains unresolved. massachusetts public-safety public safety ma canton 11 hickory lane, canton, massachusetts massachusetts canton ma-clean-water-trust-infrastructure-awar.excerpt: The latest Clean Water Trust package directs low-interest financing and grants to Gloucester, Provincetown, Manchester-by-the-Sea, Revere, Nantucket and Harwich.
ma-clean-water-trust-infrastructure-awar.text: massachusetts water board approves $80 million for wastewater, pfas and stormwater projects the latest clean water trust package directs low-interest financing and grants to gloucester, provincetown, manchester-by-the-sea, revere, nantucket and harwich. massachusetts’ clean water trust board approved $80,141,116 in new grants and low-interest loans on oct. 7, directing fresh financing toward wastewater treatment, sewer expansion, drinking-water protection and utility cybersecurity projects in communities across the state. the award list reaches from gloucester and provincetown to manchester-by-the-sea, revere, nantucket and harwich. the [massachusetts clean water trust announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/clean-water-trust-approves-801-million-in-new-grants-and-loans-at-its-october-meeting) identifies the package as a mix of state revolving fund loans and smaller targeted grants, rather than a single statewide construction program. the largest commitment is a $50 million loan to gloucester for secondary treatment and facility upgrades at the city’s water pollution control facility. the loan carries a 1.5% interest rate. gloucester says on its [project funding page](https://gloucester-ma.gov/1573/funding) that the work is being financed primarily through the massachusetts clean water state revolving fund, with the treatment upgrades tied to the facility’s long-term compliance and water-quality obligations. the trust’s [oct. 7 board materials](https://www.mass.gov/doc/board-materials-1072026/download) describe replacement of aged systems and the addition of secondary treatment in accordance with the city’s federal discharge permit and an environmental protection agency consent decree. provincetown is slated to receive a $13,901,116 loan at 1.5% for phase 6b of its sewer collection-system expansion. the board materials say the phase would extend service into nine currently unsewered subareas and serve 513 properties. that award follows the town’s announcement that it had received more than $2 million in separate state grants for infrastructure, planning and public safety, including a massworks award for sewer service near nelson avenue. together, the decisions show how provincetown is assembling several funding sources for a townwide sewer buildout while connecting infrastructure planning to future housing capacity. manchester-by-the-sea’s $13.44 million, 2% drinking-water loan is aimed at pfas treatment at the lincoln street well. according to the board materials, the well has an approved withdrawal rate of 0.38 million gallons per day and supplies about 40% of the town’s water. the planned process combines greensand pressure vessels for iron and manganese treatment with granular activated carbon for pfas. the town’s [pfas information page](https://manchester.ma.us/777/pfas) says officials have been testing the lincoln street well and gravelly pond under state and federal requirements since 2021; the new award finances a treatment project, but it does not by itself establish a new contamination finding or change public-health guidance. revere’s awards address a different pressure: inflow and conveyance in a sewer system subject to a consent decree. the trust approved two planning loans, worth $1.25 million and $500,000, for continued assessment and project planning. the board documents say the work includes evaluating inflow removal, the waitt park pumping station and force main project, and alternatives for reducing combined-sewer overflow risk. revere also received a $250,000 sewer overflow and stormwater reuse municipal grant, making the city the only community in the package listed for both planning loans and a stormwater grant. the remaining awards are smaller but touch different parts of municipal water management. nantucket received a $750,000 loan at 2% through the community septic management program. harwich received a $50,000 cybersecurity improvement grant for drinking-water infrastructure. the trust says its programs are run with the massachusetts department of environmental protection through state revolving funds, which operate as an environmental infrastructure bank supported by the commonwealth and the u.s. environmental protection agency. for residents, the immediate news is a financing commitment, not a promise that every project will be built on the same timetable. each borrower still has to move through its own design, permitting, contracting and construction steps, and the board’s approval does not settle the final cost or schedule of local work. the state says the trust has loaned roughly $10.4 billion since its creation in 1989 and estimates that 97% of massachusetts residents have benefited from its assistance. the new round’s practical effect will be measured locally: in gloucester’s treatment capacity, provincetown’s sewered properties, manchester-by-the-sea’s drinking-water safeguards and revere’s effort to control sewer and stormwater flows. massachusetts environment environment ma ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-09-2.excerpt: A planned change to the state’s financial-monitoring process would move public warnings earlier for private institutions that may not have resources to meet student obligations for 18 months.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-09-2.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 a planned change to the state’s financial-monitoring process would move public warnings earlier for private institutions that may not have resources to meet student obligations for 18 months. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities found to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice in december, no later than dec. 31. the planned change is part of an update to the state’s financial assessment and risk monitoring process, or farm, and is intended to give students, employees and communities more time to plan before the spring semester is well underway. the [massachusetts board of higher education’s sept. 29 farm update](https://www.mass.edu/bhe/documents/2026-9-26-farm-update.pdf) describes the requirement as a fiscal-year 2027 enhancement. [wbur reported](https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools) on the board discussion. the notice would not mean that a college had decided to close, and the state did not identify a new institution as being in that position in the materials reviewed for this report. instead, the proposed timing would make a school’s financial risk public when the department of higher education determines that it may not have sufficient resources to fulfill its obligations to enrolled and admitted students for the next 18 months. that distinction matters: the policy is designed to provide an earlier warning and a chance to arrange transfers or teach-outs, not to announce that every school receiving a notice will shut down. the board of higher education and the department already operate an annual system for screening the finances of private institutions. the [department’s farm overview](https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp) says the process is intended to identify institutions at risk of imminent closure and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities. under the planned enhancement, the public notice would arrive in december rather than after colleges have moved deeper into the academic year and students have made deposits or settled into spring plans. the board’s update says the earlier notice is meant to avoid spring postings that are less useful for planning. wbur reported that board chair chris gabrieli said current rules allow determinations after dec. 1, the annual threshold date used to evaluate whether an institution can continue through the current and following academic year. department commissioner noe ortega told the board that the proposed dec. 31 deadline would help officials support students while institutions are still making decisions about the future. the state’s existing legal framework requires more than a warning. under [massachusetts general laws chapter 69, section 31b](https://malegislature.gov/laws/generallaws/parti/titlexii/chapter69/section31b), a private institution must immediately notify the board about known liabilities or risks reasonably likely to cause an imminent closure or interfere with obligations to current and admitted students. if the board determines that an institution may be at risk, the school must provide information for the review and prepare a contingency plan. that plan must address how students can complete their programs, how records would be preserved, student-loan information, financial and accreditation disclosures, and refunds for eligible student deposits. the proposed december notice is one part of a broader effort to start that planning earlier. the farm update says the department wants to condense contingency planning from three phases to two, with earlier work on transfer agreements and curriculum maps for programs that have specialized accreditation, licensure requirements or few transfer options. it also calls for earlier detail on community communications and employee-reduction plans if a closure occurs. all institutions, regardless of whether they are currently in the farm process, would be encouraged to develop transfer memorandums of understanding and curriculum maps with partner schools. the department also says it needs more capacity to assess financial risk. the board document outlines plans to procure outside accounting and financial-services consultants as needed and to explore additional full-time positions, including audit expertise. the stated rationale is that worsening market conditions may put more institutions at risk while the department relies heavily on information supplied by colleges rather than independently verified data. the planned support would supplement, not replace, the department’s existing review process. the issue has become more immediate in massachusetts after anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst announced in april that they planned to close amid financial struggles, according to wbur. the department’s public farm page says it is working with hampshire to help students complete degrees or transfer by the end of 2026, while the state has also listed anna maria among institutions involved in recent financial-assessment communications. those cases illustrate why the timing of a warning can affect more than enrollment: students may need to compare credits and programs, faculty and staff may need to seek work, and host communities may have to plan for the loss of an institution. the next step is implementation of the fiscal-year 2027 farm enhancements and continued board oversight. the public materials do not name colleges that would receive a december notice, and they do not establish that a closure is imminent at any particular campus. for students and families, the practical takeaway is to watch both their institution’s financial communications and the department’s [public notifications page](https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp), where massachusetts posts notices related to institutional financial condition and risk. earlier disclosure could give affected students more choices, but it cannot remove the financial pressures facing small private colleges. massachusetts education education ma massachusetts massachusetts higher education college closures financial oversight student transfers farm

ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.excerpt: Higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two Massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring.
ma-college-closure-risk-notice-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts colleges may have to disclose closure risk by dec. 31 higher-education officials are planning an earlier public-warning deadline for financially distressed private colleges after two massachusetts schools announced plans to close last spring. massachusetts higher-education officials are planning to require private colleges and universities judged to be at risk of imminent closure to post a public notice by dec. 31, an effort to give students, employees and surrounding communities more time to respond to a financial crisis. the proposed timing was described by outgoing department of higher education commissioner noe ortega during the board of higher education's sept. 29 meeting, according to wbur and the state house news service (https://www.wbur.org/news/2026/09/30/massachusetts-private-colleges-higher-ed-closing-risk-schools). the change would not mean that every school posting a notice is certain to shut down. under the state's financial assessment and risk monitoring, or farm, system, an institution is considered at risk of imminent closure when the commissioner determines that it may be unable to continue operations or substantially meet its obligations to enrolled and admitted students through the current and following academic year. the massachusetts department of higher education says the system is intended to identify risks, monitor mitigation plans and reduce disruption to students, families, faculty, staff and host communities (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/farm.asp). the state already requires colleges to alert the board of higher education about known financial liabilities or risks that could lead to an imminent closure or prevent the institution from fulfilling its obligations. the department's farm materials say those immediate notifications are confidential, while public notice is part of a later process if the institution's financial condition remains sufficiently uncertain after review and risk-mitigation planning. the department also requires private institutions to post annual financial reports and plain-language summaries on their websites. the proposed dec. 31 date is meant to make the public-warning process more predictable. wbur reported that current regulations use dec. 1 as the annual threshold measurement date for deciding whether a college can meet its obligations for the rest of the current academic year and the next one, while the board currently has flexibility about when after that date to make a determination. board chairman chris gabrieli said a december determination would reduce the risk that students and staff learn about a potential closure only after they have made plans for the spring semester. the discussion follows two massachusetts closures announced near the end of the last academic year. anna maria college in paxton and hampshire college in amherst cited financial difficulties in announcing plans to close, wbur reported. hampshire's public notice from the department of higher education says the college planned to end academic programming at the end of 2026 while continuing academic programs, residential support and transition services for enrolled students through dec. 31 (https://www.mass.edu/strategic/documents/2026-04-14-hampshire-noitce-posting-for-dhe-website.pdf). the notice also says the department could not confirm that hampshire had enough resources to sustain current operations and fulfill obligations through the current and subsequent academic years; that is a regulatory finding, not a claim that every massachusetts college faces the same condition. massachusetts has been building this oversight system since the sudden 2018 closure of mount ida college. the department says 24 colleges and universities closed, merged or began winding down between 2014 and 2022, and that the 2019 farm law and later regulations were designed to improve financial monitoring and closure planning. those rules can require a contingency plan covering student deposits and records, and in some cases a bond or letter of credit to help protect those obligations. the department's current process describes screening from november through april, review of risk-mitigation plans from june through october, and determinations and contingency planning in november and december. officials also said the board plans to add staff and use outside firms to strengthen financial assessments, while revising required training for private-college trustees. the goal, gabrieli said, is to give students time to identify transfer options, give faculty and staff a reasonable period to seek other work, and reduce the shock to communities that depend on a campus. the timing matters this fall because ortega's term as commissioner ended sept. 30 and josé luis santos began serving as interim commissioner on oct. 1, according to the department (https://www.mass.edu/). the public-warning deadline remains a planned policy change rather than a newly announced closure list. the next questions are whether the board of higher education formally adopts the dec. 31 timetable, which institutions are identified through the annual farm review, and what mitigation or teach-out plans follow. until those steps occur, students should not read the proposed deadline as evidence that a particular college is about to close; it is an attempt to move information earlier when the state does determine that a school's finances may threaten its ability to serve students. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma boston massachusetts massachusetts higher education college closures financial stability department of higher education students

ma-cranberries-school-meals-2026-10-06.excerpt: A new state partnership with Ocean Spray will put reduced-sugar dried cranberries made entirely from in-state fruit into participating K–12 meal programs this fall.
ma-cranberries-school-meals-2026-10-06.text: massachusetts-grown cranberries are headed for school cafeterias a new state partnership with ocean spray will put reduced-sugar dried cranberries made entirely from in-state fruit into participating k–12 meal programs this fall. massachusetts students will soon have a locally grown snack option in school cafeterias as the state works with ocean spray cranberries inc. to bring dried cranberries made entirely from massachusetts fruit into participating k–12 meal programs. the [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-announces-massachusetts-grown-cranberries-for-schools-across-the-state) describes the partnership as part of the commonwealth’s broader farm-to-school effort and says the first product will be available to participating districts in october. the program is designed around the way public schools already buy food. the massachusetts department of elementary and secondary education awarded ocean spray a contract to process reduced-sugar dried cranberries for districts that participate in the u.s. department of agriculture foods distribution program. that means the initiative is not a statewide retail launch or a requirement that every school add cranberries to its menu. districts will decide whether and when to order through the existing distribution system. for the 2026–27 school year, districts will order through gold star foods, the state-contracted warehouse and distributor in canton. the standard delivery fee will be waived, according to the state, a practical detail that can matter to food-service directors working with tight budgets and storage schedules. the products will be available exclusively to massachusetts k–12 school districts through that program, so families will need to check their own district’s menu or food-service notices to know whether the snack is being served. the first item is a fruit punch flavored craisins dried-cranberry pouch scheduled to arrive in october. a raspberry lemonade flavored version is planned for february 2027. both are part of ocean spray’s reformulated 1.16-ounce school platform and were developed to meet updated usda requirements for added sugars in school meals. ocean spray’s [school nutrition materials](https://www2.oceanspray.com/foodservice/segments/schools) describe the company’s broader k–12 food-service line, while the state announcement supplies the massachusetts-specific terms. the state says the fruit punch product contains 12 grams of sugar, compared with 24 grams in ocean spray’s original dried-cranberry product, and that each pouch provides a half-cup of fruit under the product’s serving calculation. the massachusetts sourcing requirement is the central feature of the agreement. ocean spray has verified that 100% of the cranberries used in the two school products will be grown and harvested in the commonwealth. that connects a familiar packaged food to farms in southeastern massachusetts, where cranberry production is concentrated. the [massachusetts department of agricultural resources’ october proclamation](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-proclaims-october-as-massachusetts-cranberry-month) identifies cranberries as the state’s official berry and marks the start of the annual harvest season. the state’s education announcement says cranberries are massachusetts’ top agricultural food commodity crop, supporting more than 6,400 jobs and generating more than $1.7 billion in economic impact, with about 11,500 acres of commercial bogs. those figures are presented by the state as a measure of the industry’s importance; they do not mean that the new school contract will produce a comparable share of that economic activity. the immediate effect is narrower: it gives districts another locally sourced item they can purchase through a familiar federal food channel. the partnership also illustrates why processing and distribution are as important as farming in local-food programs. fresh cranberries are seasonal, while a shelf-stable dried product can be portioned, shipped and stored for school service. by using ocean spray’s processing operation and the usda foods network, the state is trying to fit a massachusetts crop into the operational requirements of cafeterias rather than asking every district to build a new local supply chain from scratch. the rollout comes as massachusetts continues its universal free school-meals program and as state officials promote local procurement as a way to support farmers while improving school food. the cranberry products are not a new benefit that changes student eligibility, and the announcement does not say how many districts will participate. the next measurable step will be district orders and menu postings this fall, followed by the second flavor’s planned arrival in february. for growers, schools and families, the test will be whether a state-specific product can move from a seasonal crop into regular, affordable cafeteria service. massachusetts agriculture ma-cranberry-harvest-quality-2026-10-02.excerpt: The state is celebrating October as Cranberry Month while UMass Amherst’s final 2026 forecast warns of very poor keeping quality for the crop, adding a food-supply and farm-management challenge to the seasonal harvest.
ma-cranberry-harvest-quality-2026-10-02.text: massachusetts cranberry harvest opens with industry facing poor keeping-quality forecast the state is celebrating october as cranberry month while umass amherst’s final 2026 forecast warns of very poor keeping quality for the crop, adding a food-supply and farm-management challenge to the seasonal harvest. massachusetts is beginning its annual cranberry harvest under two competing headlines: state officials are promoting october as cranberry month, while the university of massachusetts amherst’s cranberry station says the 2026 crop has a very poor keeping-quality forecast. the warning does not by itself predict the size of the harvest or say that every bog will be affected in the same way. it does mean growers and buyers are entering the season with a documented concern about how well harvested fruit will hold after it leaves the bog. gov. maura healey proclaimed october as massachusetts cranberry month on oct. 1 at makepeace farms in wareham, where the massachusetts department of agricultural resources gathered with growers and local officials to mark the start of the harvest. the department says massachusetts has about 11,500 acres of commercial cranberry bogs, concentrated in southeastern massachusetts, cape cod and the islands. its announcement is available at https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-proclaims-october-as-massachusetts-cranberry-month. the state describes cranberries as massachusetts’ leading agricultural food commodity crop. the department estimates the industry supports more than 6,400 jobs and generates more than $1.7 billion in economic impact. those are statewide economic estimates supplied by the administration, not a measure of this year’s harvest revenue. the same announcement says cranberry growers help protect more than 60,000 acres of undeveloped open space, making the industry relevant to land use and conservation as well as food production. the quality warning comes from umass amherst’s cranberry station, the university extension and research program serving the state’s growers. its june 12 final 2026 keeping quality forecast describes the massachusetts crop’s keeping quality as “very poor.” the station lists that forecast at https://www.umass.edu/agriculture-food-environment/cranberry/news. keeping quality is different from total acreage, yield or price: a forecast about storage performance does not establish how many berries will be harvested or what consumers will pay for them. that distinction matters during a month built around the crop’s public identity. cranberries move from working bogs into fresh and processed-food markets, but the available state announcement does not provide a final 2026 production total or explain how the umass forecast will affect individual growers, processors or retail supply. the practical questions will emerge through the harvest and post-harvest handling: how much fruit meets buyers’ quality standards, how quickly it must be moved, and whether growers face added costs to protect the crop. massachusetts has also been investing in the infrastructure behind cranberry farming. the agricultural department says it has directed more than $9 million since 2020 to 157 projects through its cranberry bog renovation enhancement grant program. those projects, according to the department, have modernized 533 acres and supported irrigation, water management, specialized equipment and automation. the stated goals are to improve productivity and environmental performance while reducing operating costs; the announcement does not claim that the grants will offset this year’s quality concerns. the region’s former cranberry land is part of a separate environmental story. gbh reported that the barnstable clean water coalition bought 64 acres of retired cranberry bogs in 2023 and is testing restored wetlands, ponds and marshes as ways to remove nitrogen before it reaches cape cod waters. that project is not a measure of the commercial harvest, but it shows why bogs matter beyond the crop: working farms, retired agricultural land, groundwater and coastal ecosystems are connected in southeastern massachusetts. the gbh report is at https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-10-01/gbh-daily-into-the-bog. october’s proclamation gives growers a public platform at the same moment the umass forecast raises a less celebratory question about the crop’s durability. state officials are emphasizing a farming tradition that they say stretches back more than 200 years, while researchers and growers must manage the immediate realities of quality, water and operating costs. later harvest and market records will show whether the poor keeping-quality forecast translates into measurable losses or simply requires more careful handling for a crop that remains central to the south coast’s agricultural economy. massachusetts ma-employee-ownership-stipends-2026-10-0.excerpt: A new state program will cover half the eligible cost of feasibility studies, valuations, legal work and transaction planning for companies considering ESOPs or worker cooperatives.
ma-employee-ownership-stipends-2026-10-0.text: massachusetts offers businesses up to $25,000 to explore employee ownership a new state program will cover half the eligible cost of feasibility studies, valuations, legal work and transaction planning for companies considering esops or worker cooperatives. massachusetts is offering financial help to businesses that want to determine whether employee ownership could provide a path for succession, job retention or long-term growth. the healey-driscoll administration announced tuesday that the massachusetts center for employee ownership, or massceo, has launched a technical-assistance stipend program that will cover 50% of eligible pre-conversion costs. the [state announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-launches-new-program-to-help-businesses-explore-employee-ownership) says companies can receive as much as $25,000 for an employee stock ownership plan project or $12,500 for a worker-cooperative project. the money is intended for the work that comes before a sale or conversion. eligible expenses include feasibility studies, business valuations, legal services and transaction planning. massceo will connect applicants with qualified consultants it selects, while businesses apply on a rolling basis subject to available funding. that structure matters: the new program helps an owner investigate whether a transition is workable, but it does not announce that the state will finance the purchase of a company or guarantee that an application will be approved. the two main models named by the state give workers different forms of ownership. in an esop, a trust generally holds company stock for employees through a retirement-plan structure. in a worker cooperative, employees become members and use a democratic governance model to make decisions about the business. the [massceo program page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-center-for-employee-ownership) describes both as options alongside employee-ownership trusts, another structure in which employees are the intended beneficiaries of a continuing trust. the choice affects financing, governance, taxes, retirement benefits and how much decision-making authority workers receive, so the stipend is aimed at professional analysis rather than a one-size-fits-all conversion. massachusetts has been building a public infrastructure around that analysis. the u.s. department of labor’s [employee ownership initiative overview](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/about-ebsa/our-activities/programs-and-initiatives/employee-ownership-initiative/tools-and-resources/employee-ownership-states) identifies the massachusetts center for employee ownership as an office created through the state’s 2022 economic-development legislation and notes that the center has a 19-member advisory board. a [2025 annual report filed with the massachusetts legislature](https://malegislature.gov/reports/29314/%28144%29%20cy25%20massceo%20annual%20report.pdf) says the center’s statutory mission includes education, outreach, research, grants and efforts to increase the number of employee-owned companies. the new stipend puts one part of that mission into a direct service for business owners. for a closely held massachusetts company, the issue is often less about a corporate label than about what happens when an owner wants to retire, sell or step away. a conventional sale can move a company’s headquarters, jobs or decision-making outside the community. an employee-ownership study can test whether the existing workforce, management team and finances could support another route. that possibility is a policy goal, not a reported outcome of this program: the state has not announced how many companies will convert or how many jobs the stipends will preserve. the program also leaves important questions for applicants. the state announcement does not set out a single application deadline, a statewide award target or a total program budget; it directs businesses to massceo’s information page and says assistance depends on available funding. owners will need to confirm eligibility, the list of approved providers and which costs qualify before committing to a study. a business that receives help to explore an esop or cooperative can still decide that the structure is not financially or operationally suitable. that review phase is the immediate news for massachusetts businesses. the state is lowering the price of specialized advice at the point when an owner is deciding whether employee ownership is realistic, while leaving the ultimate decision with the company and its workers. applications and program details are available through [massceo](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massachusetts-center-for-employee-ownership); the center’s contact information lists kevin kuros as director and identifies the massachusetts office of business development as its home. any later conversion, financing agreement or change in company ownership would be a separate development that should be reported on its own terms. massachusetts business business ma boston massachusetts massachusetts employee ownership small business esop worker cooperatives succession planning

ma-faulkner-hospital-crash-2026-10-01.excerpt: Patricia McGrath, 68, died after the Oct. 1 collision in Jamaica Plain; authorities say the crash remains under investigation and no criminal charges have been filed.
ma-faulkner-hospital-crash-2026-10-01.text: boston woman identified after suv crashes into faulkner hospital campus patricia mcgrath, 68, died after the oct. 1 collision in jamaica plain; authorities say the crash remains under investigation and no criminal charges have been filed. patricia mcgrath, a 68-year-old dorchester resident, has been identified as the woman who died after an suv struck her outside brigham and women’s faulkner hospital in jamaica plain, according to the [suffolk county district attorney’s office, as reported by whdh 7news](https://whdh.com/news/woman-killed-when-car-slammed-into-hospital-building-in-jamaica-plain-identified/). the crash happened thursday, oct. 1, near the hospital’s dialysis unit, where boston police said mcgrath was sitting on a bench. the vehicle continued from the pedestrian area into the hospital campus and hit the wall of the belkin house, a separate building at the faulkner complex, around 10:45 a.m. the collision damaged a gas line. mcgrath was taken for treatment and later died, while two people who were inside the suv were also injured and brought to the hospital, [cbs boston reported](https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/3-injured-car-crash-faulkner-hospital/). the available reports do not identify the two occupants or describe the severity of their injuries beyond their transport for medical care. the damaged gas line turned the crash into a wider campus safety response. faulkner hospital said the belkin house was evacuated as a precaution while crews worked with national grid and the boston fire department. the main hospital building was reported safe and operating at the time, and national grid shut off gas service to the rest of the hospital after the collision. four boston ems members were also evaluated for possible gas exposure, cbs boston said. the incident temporarily affected the area around the medical campus. emergency responders and the damaged building created traffic impacts, according to the hospital statement cited by cbs. that matters in jamaica plain because faulkner serves southwest boston and nearby suburbs as a community teaching hospital, and the crash occurred beside a facility that was continuing to provide care while the scene was secured. the reports do not establish how long the belkin house evacuation lasted or whether the building sustained damage beyond the gas-line impact. authorities have described the collision as an accident rather than a deliberate act. boston police sent homicide detectives and the department’s fatal-collision team to the scene, a response that reflects the death and the need to reconstruct what happened, not a public finding that a crime occurred. as of the victim-identification update on oct. 2, the district attorney’s office said no criminal charges had been filed. the investigation remained open. the public record still leaves key questions unanswered. none of the cited reports explains why the suv left its path, whether a medical emergency or a vehicle problem played a role, or whether investigators have identified any contributing roadway or campus conditions. those questions should not be filled with speculation. the early police description and the prosecutor’s update establish the result of the crash, but they do not assign fault or provide a final account of the driver’s actions. the sequence also illustrates why a collision near a hospital can affect more people than those directly involved. a pedestrian was killed, the vehicle occupants needed care, emergency workers were assessed for exposure, a campus building was cleared, and utility crews had to isolate a damaged gas line while the main hospital remained open. each part of that response was reported by officials or hospital representatives through local news coverage; northeast news did not witness the crash or independently inspect the scene. for now, the confirmed update is mcgrath’s identity and the status of the case, not a final explanation of the crash. boston police and the suffolk county district attorney’s office have not announced charges in the reports reviewed for this article. further information about the investigation, the injured occupants, the gas-line repair or the belkin house’s operating status would need to come from those agencies or the hospital. until then, the oct. 1 collision remains a fatal crash under investigation on the faulkner hospital campus. massachusetts public-safety public safety ma boston jamaica plain, boston, massachusetts massachusetts boston jamaica plain faulkner hospital traffic crash public safety

ma-great-barrington-housatonic-water-eme.excerpt: The private utility says a fiscal crisis has put its manganese-treatment construction on hold, while town officials work to preserve emergency water service and continue a possible municipal acquisition.
ma-great-barrington-housatonic-water-eme.text: housatonic water works pauses treatment project as great barrington weighs takeover the private utility says a fiscal crisis has put its manganese-treatment construction on hold, while town officials work to preserve emergency water service and continue a possible municipal acquisition. great barrington’s emergency water fight has entered a new phase. the town is still working to keep service running for housatonic water works customers, but a treatment project that was supposed to address the system’s manganese problems is now on hold. the development leaves the private utility facing immediate financing pressure while the town and state agencies try to keep an emergency connection operating and consider who should control the system in the future. the company’s construction pause was reported by the berkshire edge after hww filed a sept. 30 report with the massachusetts department of public utilities. hww treasurer james mercer said the company’s financial condition and negative cash flow, worsened by a payment dispute with the great barrington fire district, meant it could not draw on existing loan facilities to pay for the manganese-treatment project. the company said the work is paused indefinitely while it seeks rate relief. the [berkshire edge report](https://theberkshireedge.com/housatonic-water-works-puts-manganese-treatment-plant-construction-on-hold-demands-emergency-rate-increase-from-dpu/) described the filing and the company’s position; the dpu has not been described as approving the requested increase. hww’s request comes after a 2024 dpu rate decision that allowed customer rates to rise by 90% over five years, according to the berkshire edge, with completion of capital projects including the treatment plant tied to that agreement. the company now says it needs an emergency increase to restore positive cash flow, cover amounts owed to the fire district and continue necessary work. those are hww’s claims in filings and letters, not an independent finding that the requested rate change is warranted. the company’s attorneys have also suggested accelerating a possible sale of hww’s assets to the town. under the proposal described by the berkshire edge, great barrington could assume the company’s debt and pay nothing for the franchise, property and corporate rights. that is a proposal, not a completed transaction or a purchase price set by regulators. the town’s existing valuation proceeding with the dpu remains active, and the town says it is evaluating legally and financially responsible options for a long-term solution. the immediate operational problem is the temporary connection between hww and the great barrington fire district. in an oct. 1 statement, the town said the connection is supporting hww while the company addresses filtration problems in its own system. continued use requires an agreement for continuous service between hww and the fire district, and massachusetts department of environmental protection officials told the town that massdep cannot compel the fire district to keep supplying hww through the link. massdep will not approve continued use until the two entities reach an agreement and hww incorporates that agreement into its operating procedures, the town said. if the connection ends and hww cannot otherwise meet the requirements of a sept. 15 massdep order, the company is required to provide one gallon of bottled water per person per day to affected customers, according to the [town’s public statement](https://www.townofgb.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/224). that is a contingency in the order, not an announcement that the system has already switched to bottled-water distribution. great barrington said it is coordinating with massdep on logistics in case service is interrupted and is prepared to assist state agencies if residents need help. the treatment project matters because it was intended to address recurring discoloration associated with manganese. massdep said in june that a 2025 consent order required hww to complete the plant by june 1 after an earlier march 1 deadline was extended. hww sought another extension, but massdep denied it and demanded $2,500 in partial payment from a suspended penalty. the [massdep notice](https://www.mass.gov/news/massdep-penalizes-housatonic-water-works-company-for-failure-to-comply-with-consent-order) said the penalty cannot be passed on to ratepayers and that the agency would continue tracking compliance. hww serves more than one community. the state’s [water-distribution-company directory](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/water-distribution-companies) lists 847 connections for housatonic water works in parts of great barrington, stockbridge and west stockbridge. the company says it has served the area since 1897 and provides water to housatonic village and surrounding neighborhoods. earlier reporting by wamc, based on an interview with berkshire eagle reporter talia lissauer, described discolored water and about 16 miles of aging pipe that ultimately need replacement. the [wamc report](https://www.wamc.org/news/2026-09-03/mass-utility-company-faces-scrutiny-residents-face-chronic-issues-with-discolored-water) said lissauer was aware of no health impacts from the discoloration, while residents continued to seek a durable fix. residents have some financial help while the dispute continues. great barrington’s reimbursement program can cover eligible bottled-water purchases, laundry costs and filters or other filtration products, with reimbursement capped at $1,500 per household. customers who previously received money may apply for additional funds up to the new maximum, the town says on its [housatonic water works information page](https://www.townofgbma.gov/371/housatonic-water-works-information-resou). the program recognizes costs residents have incurred, but it does not resolve the utility’s financing, treatment or emergency-connection problems. the next near-term test is whether hww and the fire district can document continuous emergency service that satisfies massdep. beyond that, regulators and town officials must decide how to finance the unfinished treatment plant, address the distribution system and move the valuation process forward. great barrington says it will provide more updates as information can be released. for customers, the stakes are practical: the taps need to keep running now, while the legal and financial decisions that could make the system reliable for the long term remain unresolved. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma great barrington great barrington, massachusetts
