ma-hadley-russian-plutonium-plea-2026-10.excerpt: Jacob D. Miller admitted importing plutonium and selling it through a South Hadley business; federal prosecutors say about 67 plutonium customers and 71 thallium customers received shipments before his arrest.
ma-hadley-russian-plutonium-plea-2026-10.text: hadley man pleads guilty to importing russian plutonium and mailing hazardous materials jacob d. miller admitted importing plutonium and selling it through a south hadley business; federal prosecutors say about 67 plutonium customers and 71 thallium customers received shipments before his arrest. a 44-year-old massachusetts man has pleaded guilty to importing plutonium from russia and sending radioactive and toxic materials through the mail from a business run out of his south hadley home. the plea, announced by the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of massachusetts, adds a new legal milestone to a case that began with a federal search and arrest in the pioneer valley in 2025. federal prosecutors identified the defendant as jacob d. miller of hadley. on monday, oct. 5, he pleaded guilty to charges involving unlawful importation of nuclear material, mailing hazardous materials, possession of ammunition and explosive materials as a convicted felon, and possession of child sexual abuse material. the [justice department’s massachusetts office](https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/massachusetts-man-pleads-guilty-illegally-importing-and-selling-plutonium-russia) said u.s. district court judge mark g. mastroianni set sentencing for jan. 21, 2027. a guilty plea resolves the charges, but sentencing has not yet occurred. the case centers on an online business called collect the periodic table, or ctpt. prosecutors said miller sold samples of chemical elements directly and through the bonanza marketplace, operating the company from his residence in south hadley. according to the federal account, the business was presented as a way to buy element samples, but the materials at issue included plutonium, which is highly radioactive, and thallium, which is highly toxic. the justice department said miller imported plutonium from russia and arranged for it to be mailed to his home. from about dec. 30, 2020, through march 31, 2025, prosecutors said he sold plutonium to approximately 67 customers in the united states and abroad, then shipped it from south hadley through the u.s. mail even though the material was prohibited from being mailed. the department did not identify the customers or say in its announcement whether anyone was injured or exposed. the same release said miller sold thallium to about 71 customers between october 2017 and april 2025 and mailed that material in the same way. the [boston globe’s report](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/05/metro/hadley-russian-plutonium-thallium-online-sales/) added local background from earlier reporting, including that massachusetts’ radiation control program sent miller a cease-and-desist letter in 2014 after learning he was selling depleted uranium on ebay. that earlier regulatory action is separate from the federal charges resolved by monday’s plea. investigators searched miller’s home in april 2025, according to prosecutors. they recovered bottles of explosive powder, ammunition and six rifles, which the justice department said he could not lawfully possess because of his prior felony convictions. agents also found child sexual abuse material on his laptop and phone. miller had been held in federal custody since his april 9, 2025, arrest, and a grand jury indicted him later that month, the department said. the potential penalties vary by count. the nuclear-material importation charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, while the ammunition and explosive-material counts each carry up to 15 years. the mailing charge carries up to one year. because prosecutors say miller had a prior conviction for possessing child sexual abuse material, that count carries a statutory minimum of 10 years and a maximum of 20 years. those figures are limits set by law, not a prediction of the sentence judge mastroianni will impose. for the communities around hadley and south hadley, the case illustrates how a specialized online business can create public-safety and regulatory questions far beyond a single home. the public record now confirms the plea and the approximate number of customers identified by prosecutors, but it does not establish what happened to every shipment or whether any customer faces charges. the next major development will be the january sentencing hearing, where the court will weigh the applicable statutes, sentencing guidelines and the facts presented by both sides. massachusetts public-safety public safety ma hadley hadley and south hadley, massachusetts massachusetts hadley south hadley federal court plutonium hazardous materials public safety

ma-harvard-medical-school-explosion-sent.excerpt: A federal judge sentenced Logan Patterson and Dominick Cardoza to probation and restitution for setting off a commercial firework inside a Harvard Medical School research building during Halloween weekend 2025.
ma-harvard-medical-school-explosion-sent.text: two massachusetts men avoid prison after harvard medical school explosion a federal judge sentenced logan patterson and dominick cardoza to probation and restitution for setting off a commercial firework inside a harvard medical school research building during halloween weekend 2025. two massachusetts men will not serve prison time for an explosion inside a harvard medical school building, but a federal judge has placed both on probation and ordered them to repay the medical school for the damage. logan david patterson, 19, of plymouth, and dominick frank cardoza, 21, of bourne were sentenced thursday in federal court in boston, according to the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of massachusetts. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-sentenced-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus) u.s. district judge angel kelley gave each defendant three years of probation and ordered the pair to pay $28,517 in restitution to harvard medical school. the sentence resolves a case that began after an early-morning blast on nov. 1, 2025, at the goldenson building on the school’s longwood medical area campus. the defendants had pleaded guilty in april to one count each of conspiring to damage a building by means of an explosive. the government’s account, summarized in the sentencing announcement, places the men near the campus shortly after 2:20 a.m. surveillance video showed two people in face coverings and dark clothing walking toward the medical school, then lighting what appeared to be roman-candle fireworks. prosecutors said the pair climbed into a construction area, used scaffolding to reach the roof and entered the building. at about 2:45 a.m., harvard campus police received a fire-alarm alert tied to an explosion on the fourth floor. the device was a large commercial firework placed inside a wooden locker in a fourth-floor research laboratory within harvard medical school’s department of neurobiology, federal prosecutors said. video later showed the defendants on the fifth floor before they left through a first-floor emergency exit and ran in different directions. the u.s. attorney’s office said they discarded clothing associated with the incident and returned to the nearby wentworth institute of technology, where they had been visiting for halloween social activities. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-plead-guilty-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus) no one was injured, but the blast triggered a major police response and public alarm around a boston medical and academic campus. boston.com reported that the men had been in the area for college halloween events and that prosecutors argued the nighttime break-in, face coverings, property damage and flight warranted a period of home confinement. judge kelley declined that request, saying the felony convictions and other consequences were sufficient deterrence. (https://www.boston.com/news/crime/2026/10/02/mass-men-sentenced-harvard-explosion/) the sentence also carries obligations beyond probation and restitution. boston.com reported that each man was ordered to complete 300 hours of community service, and that the pair must write apology letters to harvard. patterson apologized in court, the outlet reported. the defendants had no prior criminal records, according to the report, but the felony convictions will continue to affect them after the case ends. the case is significant locally because it turns a highly visible campus-security incident into a completed federal criminal proceeding without a prison term. the goldenson building houses a research laboratory, and the episode involved a construction area, a roof entry and an explosive device inside an occupied university complex, even though the building was empty when the firework was detonated. those details explain why prosecutors sought additional restrictions despite the defendants’ guilty pleas and lack of prior record. the defendants originally faced a statutory maximum of five years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of as much as $250,000, according to the april plea announcement. the confirmed next phase is therefore supervision, community service and restitution rather than incarceration. the federal sentencing release does not announce any further criminal hearing or a change to harvard’s campus operations. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-plead-guilty-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus) massachusetts public-safety public safety ma boston longwood medical area, boston, massachusetts massachusetts boston harvard medical school federal court public safety

ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.excerpt: The awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside Boston and Cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting.
ma-life-sciences-tax-incentives-2026-09-.text: massachusetts awards nearly $40m in life-science tax incentives tied to 1,644 jobs the awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside boston and cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting. massachusetts has awarded nearly $40 million in tax incentives to 38 life-science companies that collectively pledged to create 1,644 new jobs, putting a statewide economic-development program behind expansions in research, therapeutics, diagnostics and manufacturing. gov. maura healey announced the awards sept. 28 at smc ltd. in devens. the figures describe company commitments, not jobs already filled or money paid directly to workers. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the geographic distribution is a central feature of this round. the massachusetts life sciences center said 31 of the 38 awardees are expanding outside boston and cambridge, and those projects account for 71% of the expected new jobs. that puts communities such as acton, andover, bedford, burlington, chelmsford, devens, framingham, marlborough, milford, northbridge, sudbury, waltham and woburn in the direct path of the announced hiring commitments, rather than limiting the benefit to the state's traditional laboratory hubs. the agency described the program as a way to use massachusetts' broader network of life-science assets for growth and retention. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) the largest individual award goes to acton-based insulet corporation: $10 million tied to a 250-job commitment. lila sciences in cambridge received $3.6 million for 200 jobs, while vertex pharmaceuticals in boston received $3.025 million for 121 jobs. other sizable awards include $2.875 million for bristol myers squibb's 125-job commitment in devens, $1.86 million for transmedics in andover, and $1.35 million for smc's 54 jobs in devens. the boston business journal reported that the full list also includes astrazeneca, vericel, zoll medical, rentschler biopharma and dozens of smaller firms. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the awards are tax incentives administered through the massachusetts life sciences center's tax incentive program jointly with the department of revenue. the program is open to companies doing research and development, commercialization or manufacturing in massachusetts, and the commitments are meant to be new, long-term positions. awardees must maintain their job commitments for three years and file regular reports documenting the jobs created as a result of the incentives. that structure makes the announced 1,644 jobs a measurable target that can be checked over time, rather than an immediate headcount. the state release also says the program has supported commitments for more than 22,300 jobs since the center was established. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs) demand for the program was stronger than the award total. the boston business journal reported that companies submitted $58 million in applications this year, compared with a previous year when the center needed two rounds to allocate the full $40 million authorization. the outlet also reported that, since 2009, the center has made 519 awards to nearly 300 distinct companies totaling about $422 million and tied to more than 22,300 jobs. those figures show both the scale of the state's strategy and the competitive choices behind this year's list: the program is not an open-ended subsidy for every applicant, and some proposals were not funded in this cycle. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html) the current ceiling comes from the 2024 mass leads act, which raised the annual statutory cap for life-science tax incentives from $30 million to $40 million and broadened the eligible field to include areas such as medical technology, preventative medicine, biosecurity and life-science-related artificial intelligence. massachusetts' technical tax guidance describes the program as a collection of tax incentives available to qualifying companies, rather than a single grant pot. that distinction matters when evaluating the public return: the state is trading foregone tax revenue for promised hiring and investment, while the companies still have to execute their expansion plans. (https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-25-5-tax-provisions-in-certain-massachusetts-legislation-enacted-in-2024) for workers and municipalities, the next test is delivery. companies must meet the hiring and retention conditions attached to their awards, and the state must report whether projects translate into sustained employment across the commonwealth. the announcement includes activity in artificial intelligence, women's health, therapeutics, diagnostics, medical technology, research and development and biomanufacturing. if the commitments hold, the round will distribute new positions across a wider geography and reinforce massachusetts' life-science supply chain; if projects fall short, the reporting and tax-administration process will determine how the state responds. the award announcement establishes the targets, but future compliance records will show how many jobs actually materialize. massachusetts massachusetts massachusetts ma massachusetts massachusetts life sciences tax incentives jobs economic development biotechnology

ma-lithium-battery-fire-prevention-week-.excerpt: State fire officials say local departments logged 22 battery fires last month, twice the year-earlier total, as Massachusetts urges safer charging during Fire Prevention Week.
ma-lithium-battery-fire-prevention-week-.text: massachusetts reports record september for battery fires as safety week begins state fire officials say local departments logged 22 battery fires last month, twice the year-earlier total, as massachusetts urges safer charging during fire prevention week. massachusetts fire departments reported 22 battery fires in september, the highest monthly total since the state began tracking the incidents, state fire marshal jon m. davine said monday. the figure was double the number reported a year earlier, according to the massachusetts department of fire services, which released the data as gov. maura healey declared oct. 4-10 fire prevention week. the new count gives a statewide measure to a hazard that is increasingly part of ordinary household life. lithium-ion batteries power phones, laptops, earbuds, power tools, e-bikes, scooters and other rechargeable devices. the department of fire services says damaged batteries or improper charging can cause overheating, fire or explosions. the department's [fire prevention week announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-declares-october-4-10-fire-prevention-week) does not identify the individual september fires, their causes, the number of injuries or the amount of property damage, so the monthly total should not be read as a measure of severity. the september result also arrives after a warning from fire officials across new england. the [boston globe reported](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/25/metro/big-e-fairgoers-fire-safety-tips/) that fire marshals from massachusetts, connecticut, new hampshire and vermont used a big e appearance in west springfield to emphasize safe charging and working smoke alarms. the globe reported that massachusetts battery fires had risen from fewer than 20 to more than 130 in a few years and quoted davine saying the state was on track for a record month. the newer state announcement supplies the final september count. for residents, the advice is specific: use the cord and charger supplied with a device or one approved by its manufacturer; charge on a hard, flat surface rather than a bed, couch or pillow; and unplug the device when it is fully charged. the [concord fire department](https://concordfirenews.com/2026/10/01/national-fire-prevention-week-is-october-4-10-steps-to-charge-devices-safely/) separately advises charging while awake and nearby, keeping larger devices outside when possible, and never blocking an exit with an e-bike, scooter or power tool. officials also want people to recognize signs of a failing battery. a device that becomes unusually hot, swells, smokes or develops a strange smell should no longer be used, the state says. residents should leave and call 911 if a device catches fire. the massachusetts guidance says used batteries do not belong in household trash or recycling, where they can be crushed or damaged in collection and transfer equipment; instead, residents should use a household hazardous-waste event or a battery-recycling location. the risks extend beyond homes. the [national park service](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/nps-structural-fire-program-observes-fire-prevention-week-2026.htm), which is observing the same oct. 4-10 week, documented 2026 battery incidents involving a boat at glen canyon national recreation area, an audio-tour player at alcatraz and an e-bike at grand canyon national park. those examples are outside new england and do not establish a massachusetts trend, but they illustrate why agencies are focusing on charging practices rather than only on a particular product category. fire prevention week is a public-education observance, not a new massachusetts restriction on rechargeable devices. the 2026 theme is “charge into fire safety: safe charging is a superpower,” coordinated nationally by the national fire protection association. massachusetts officials say residents should look for recognized safety certification marks such as ul or intertek/etl when buying devices, keep large battery-powered equipment away from doors and stairs, and make sure smoke alarms can be heard wherever people sleep. the immediate takeaway is practical, while important questions remain open. the state has not published a september incident list in the announcement, and the release does not say how many fires involved e-bikes, scooters, chargers or other equipment. those details would help explain the record month. for now, fire officials are using the available statewide count and the start of fire prevention week to push habits that can reduce heat, overcharging and blocked escape routes before a battery problem becomes a structure fire.
