nh-bethlehem-landfill-closure-2026-10-01.excerpt: Casella says its North Country Environmental Services landfill will stop accepting municipal waste on Dec. 31, bringing an earlier transition for host-town services and disposal planning across the state.
nh-bethlehem-landfill-closure-2026-10-01.text: bethlehem landfill will close a year early, reshaping new hampshire waste plans casella says its north country environmental services landfill will stop accepting municipal waste on dec. 31, bringing an earlier transition for host-town services and disposal planning across the state. casella waste systems will stop accepting municipal solid waste at its north country environmental services landfill in bethlehem on dec. 31, 2026, moving the facility’s expected end of operations forward by a year. the company disclosed the new date in an oct. 1 [form 8-k](https://ir.casella.com/sec-filings/sec-filing/8-k/0000911177-26-000052) filed with the u.s. securities and exchange commission, saying the decision followed an evaluation of remaining permitted airspace, current and projected fill rates and other operating factors. the filing identifies dec. 31 as the final day the landfill will accept municipal waste for disposal. the change does not mean the site disappears at midnight or that all waste services end immediately. it means the landfill will no longer take new municipal solid waste; closure and post-closure obligations will continue under applicable permits and environmental requirements. casella said the earlier timing will increase landfill amortization expense in the fourth quarter, but the company does not expect the change to materially affect its 2026 quarterly or full-year financial results. those are the company’s projections, not an independent assessment of the site’s long-term costs. the regional question is where material will go next. [waste dive reported](https://www.wastedive.com/news/casella-mulls-early-landfill-closure-announcement-bethlehem-dalton-new-hampshire/832123/) that the bethlehem facility serves about 200 new hampshire communities, as well as contractors and other haulers, according to casella. the company did not identify a single replacement destination, but casella vice president of communications jeff weld told the publication that near-term options exist through the company’s transfer and disposal network and third-party sites. that leaves municipalities and private haulers to determine how those arrangements will affect transportation distances, contract prices and disposal capacity after december. bethlehem faces a more direct transition because the landfill has supported local services as well as disposal. in a [february letter to residents](https://www.casella.com/media/sk3izqru/2026-2-19-bethlehem-residents-letter.pdf), the nces general manager said the facility’s planned 2027 closure would end host-community benefits worth about $1.3 million a year. the letter listed curbside trash and recycling collection, transfer-station operations, property-tax payments, annual host fees, community donations and household hazardous waste day among the services or payments tied to the landfill. because the closure is now scheduled for the end of 2026, the town has less time than residents were told to expect when that notice was issued. the effect will vary by community. [new hampshire public radio, republishing concord monitor reporting](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-05/casella-bethlehem-landfill-closing-earlier), said concord already sends its collected waste to the wheelabrator waste-to-energy facility in penacook under a 2024 agreement, rather than hauling it to bethlehem. adam clark, a division manager for concord general services, told the outlet that the bethlehem closure should not affect concord residents. that example shows why the announcement cannot be translated into one statewide service change: some communities have alternate contracts, while others may rely more directly on the landfill’s capacity or casella’s transfer network. the closure also lands in the middle of a long-running debate about landfill regulation and environmental oversight. [nhpr reported](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-05/casella-bethlehem-landfill-closing-earlier) that casella agreed in january to pay $1.9 million in civil penalties tied to state allegations involving the bethlehem operation. the reported allegations included placing waste beyond permitted boundaries, mishandling leachate, failing to report facility damage, drilling gas wells through a protective liner and failing to apply required daily cover. those enforcement matters provide context for the facility’s history, but the company’s oct. 1 filing attributes the new timetable to capacity and operating considerations; it does not say the penalty caused the closure. the state’s next disposal options are unsettled. new hampshire has debated casella’s proposed granite state landfill in dalton as a possible future source of capacity, while residents and environmental groups have opposed that project. [waste dive reported](https://www.wastedive.com/news/casella-mulls-early-landfill-closure-announcement-bethlehem-dalton-new-hampshire/832123/) that the dalton proposal and a new state law placing a temporary limit on landfill-capacity expansion are part of the broader backdrop to the bethlehem decision. the policy debate matters because closing an existing facility earlier than expected compresses the time available to approve, build or contract for alternatives. for now, the firm date is dec. 31. casella’s filing establishes when municipal-waste intake ends, but it does not provide a public, community-by-community map of replacement disposal routes or a final schedule for bethlehem’s host-town services. local governments, haulers and state regulators will need to settle those questions before the last loads arrive. northeast news has not independently reviewed casella’s permits, municipal contracts or the company’s projected post-closure costs; those documents will be important for measuring the practical and financial effects of the accelerated shutdown. new-hampshire environment environment nh bethlehem north country environmental services landfill, 581 trudeau road, bethlehem, new hampshire new hampshire bethlehem landfill waste management north country environmental services casella waste systems environmental regulation

nh-bobcat-poaching-guilty-2026-10-02.excerpt: Federal prosecutors say at least 41 bobcats were illegally killed in New Hampshire, falsely tagged in New York and shipped to Canada for sale.
nh-bobcat-poaching-guilty-2026-10-02.text: three men plead guilty in new hampshire bobcat-poaching scheme federal prosecutors say at least 41 bobcats were illegally killed in new hampshire, falsely tagged in new york and shipped to canada for sale. three new hampshire men pleaded guilty this week in a federal case that prosecutors say involved the illegal killing of at least 41 bobcats and the shipment of their pelts to canada. the pleas add a major development to a long-running wildlife investigation spanning new hampshire, new york and canada. the [u.s. attorney’s office for the district of new hampshire](https://www.justice.gov/usao-nh/pr/three-men-plead-guilty-poaching-more-40-bobcats-and-exporting-them-canada) announced the pleas friday. sherwood dubrey jr., 48, and randy inman, 49, pleaded guilty to conspiring to violate the federal lacey act. sherwood dubrey sr., 72, pleaded guilty to a lacey act violation. all three appeared before u.s. district judge joseph n. laplante, and the court scheduled their sentencings for january 2027. the younger dubrey and inman each face a maximum of five years in prison and up to three years of supervised release. the elder dubrey faces a maximum of one year in prison and up to one year of supervised release. those are statutory maximums, not predictions of the sentences the judge will impose. according to the federal account, dubrey jr. and inman killed bobcats in new hampshire from 2018 through 2022, then moved the pelts to new york. dubrey sr. allegedly obtained false cites tags there so the animals would appear to have been legally taken in a state with a bobcat hunting season. the pelts were then exported to canada and offered at a fur auction. prosecutors say the scheme involved at least 41 illegally exported pelts. [new hampshire public radio](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-02/poaching-bobcats-nh-newhampshire-operation-night-cat) independently reported the same sequence and described the case as one of the state’s largest recent poaching investigations. the case matters because new hampshire does not allow bobcat hunting or trapping. the justice department says the lacey act, enacted in 1900, prohibits wildlife violations that cross state or international borders. a lawfully harvested bobcat pelt also requires a tag under the convention on international trade in endangered species, or cites. new york has a legal bobcat season and an export program, while new hampshire has neither because taking the animals is unlawful. the alleged movement of pelts across state lines therefore was not a paperwork technicality; it was central to making illegally taken wildlife appear eligible for international trade. investigators say the animals were lured with bait piles placed on the men’s property and on state land before being shot. the justice department said text messages and photographs or videos from rifles with scopes documented the conduct, and that messages showed the defendants knew the killings were illegal. new hampshire fish and game conservation officers and the u.s. fish and wildlife service led the investigation, with assistance from agencies in new york, canada and massachusetts as well as the fbi. the federal release attributes those details to the public record and investigative evidence; northeast news has not independently reviewed the underlying files. nhpr reported that the federal pleas are part of operation night cat, a new hampshire fish and game investigation that previously produced state convictions in 2024 for related hunting violations. inman and dubrey jr. are former corrections officers at the new hampshire state prison for men, according to nhpr. the public radio report also said the broader investigation uncovered allegations of potential crimes by prison staff that authorities reviewed but did not charge. those separate allegations are not part of the federal bobcat pleas and should not be treated as proven conduct. the wildlife backdrop is unusually clear in state records. new hampshire fish and wildlife’s [2023-24 furbearer report](https://www.nhfishandwildlife.com/assets/performance-reports/w89r21-projects%205-8%20combined%20final%202024.pdf) says the bobcat season remained closed; trappers reported 36 incidental captures that were released and one bobcat reported killed. that dated report is not a current population estimate, but it explains why the state treats unauthorized killing as a conservation and enforcement issue rather than an unregulated harvest. federal officials also said the case threatened the tagging system used to keep wildlife trade legal and sustainable. the next formal step is sentencing in january. the justice department says the investigation involved cooperation across multiple jurisdictions, underscoring why wildlife cases can become federal matters when animals or pelts cross borders. the guilty pleas resolve the defendants’ responsibility for the charges to which they admitted, but the judge will still determine penalties. for new hampshire, the case leaves a concrete reminder that the state’s closed bobcat season applies even when a pelt is later moved somewhere that has different hunting rules—and that false origin documents do not erase where protected wildlife was actually taken. new-hampshire environment environment nh concord new hampshire new hampshire bobcats wildlife conservation poaching lacey act nh fish and game

nh-cfi-settlement-2026-10-05.excerpt: The proposed four-year agreement would require provider-network reviews, contingency plans and a new aide directory for people who rely on the Choices for Independence Medicaid waiver.
nh-cfi-settlement-2026-10-05.text: new hampshire home-care lawsuit settlement would tighten oversight for disabled residents the proposed four-year agreement would require provider-network reviews, contingency plans and a new aide directory for people who rely on the choices for independence medicaid waiver. new hampshire has reached a proposed settlement in a five-year federal class-action lawsuit over whether people with disabilities and older adults can reliably receive the in-home services authorized through the state’s choices for independence program. the agreement would add oversight and reporting requirements for the department of health and human services, but it is not final: a federal judge must approve it before the reforms take effect. the new hampshire department of justice announced the settlement in a [statement published oct. 5](https://www.pubt.io/view/0ef56086574a0d5c5ab85b84ca1728a04b8d6676). choices for independence, commonly called cfi, is a medicaid-funded waiver designed to help people who meet a nursing-facility level of care remain in their homes and communities. the program helps participants obtain services such as personal care and other support from in-home aides. the lawsuit, fitzmorris v. new hampshire department of health and human services, was filed in 2021 and later converted into a class action. plaintiffs argued that staffing shortages and service gaps left some participants without the care the state had authorized, putting them at risk of institutional placement. the state agreed to the settlement without admitting wrongdoing, legal violations or liability, according to the [new hampshire bulletin’s account of the agreement](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/06/state-plaintiffs-agree-to-settle-lawsuit-over-nh-in-home-care-program-after-five-year-court-battle/). the proposed agreement focuses first on measuring the gap between approved care and delivered care. dhhs would hire an independent consultant to examine the provider network, including whether there are enough workers to meet participant needs in each county. the first review would be due within 180 days after the settlement is finalized, followed by annual reviews. the settlement notice from the [disability rights center–new hampshire](https://drcnh.org/litigation/cfi-class-action-notice/) says the state would consider reimbursement-rate changes when those reviews show that the available workforce is not meeting demand. the agreement also calls for a backup plan for every participant who is not receiving approved services. under the terms described by the bulletin, dhhs would identify people receiving less than half of their authorized services in a month and require the responsible case-management agency to activate a contingency plan. that provision matters because a missed aide visit can affect basic daily needs, not merely convenience. it also creates a clearer point at which the state must respond instead of treating an unresolved staffing problem as an individual household’s burden. provider pay is another part of the proposed remedy. dhhs would review the reimbursement methods and rates used for cfi services and ask the legislature for inflation-related increases when the review supports them. the state would also revise its specialized-rate policy, which can provide extra payment when the ordinary rate is not attracting a worker for a particular participant. the plaintiffs’ lead counsel told the bulletin that the special-rate process had been used only sparingly in the past. the settlement sets a framework for using it more quickly when a service gap is identified, but it does not itself guarantee a wage increase or an immediate aide for every participant. participants would also get new tools for finding and challenging services. the agreement would create an online directory of aides with contact information, the counties they serve and whether they are accepting new clients. dhhs would expand its grievance process to include missed services, and it would issue a compliance report every six months. those changes are intended to make the system more transparent: a participant could see where provider capacity exists, report a failure to receive authorized care and track whether the state is meeting its obligations. the legal timeline is still active. the [settlement notice](https://drcnh.org/litigation/cfi-class-action-notice/) says the proposed agreement would last four years and would not provide individual damages. it also says class members can object in writing by dec. 7, 2026, or appear at a federal court hearing in concord on jan. 21, 2027. the disability rights center and new hampshire legal assistance plan public information sessions in november for people affected by the agreement. a participant who does not object does not need to file anything, but the notice says the settlement would limit separate lawsuits over the same issues during the four-year term if the court approves it. for new hampshire, the settlement shifts the cfi debate from whether service shortages exist to how the state will document and correct them. the doj says the agreement strengthens accountability; advocates say implementation will require close monitoring. the next decisive step belongs to the federal court, followed by dhhs’s first network review and the state’s response to whatever gaps that review identifies. until approval and implementation occur, the existing cfi rules remain in place and the proposed reforms should not be treated as a guarantee of new services. new-hampshire health health nh concord new hampshire new hampshire choices for independence medicaid disability rights home care aging health policy

nh-drought-persists-after-noreaster-2026.excerpt: The latest U.S. Drought Monitor update says 96.05% of the state remains abnormally dry, with more than half in moderate drought after the weekend storm.
nh-drought-persists-after-noreaster-2026.text: new hampshire drought lingers despite nor’easter rain the latest u.s. drought monitor update says 96.05% of the state remains abnormally dry, with more than half in moderate drought after the weekend storm. a weekend nor’easter delivered at least an inch of rain to most of new hampshire, but it did little to change the state’s drought picture. as of oct. 1, 96.05% of new hampshire was at least abnormally dry and 53.33% was in moderate drought, according to the latest update summarized by [wmur](https://www.wmur.com/article/new-hampshire-drought-noreaster-report-101/73982475). the figures describe the share of the state’s land area in each category, not the percentage of residents or individual properties affected. the limited change matters because a single storm can improve surface moisture without repairing longer-term deficits in streams, reservoirs, groundwater and soils. wmur reported that the rainfall brought few gains to northern new england, while wetter conditions farther south improved portions of connecticut, massachusetts and rhode island. maine and new hampshire remained broadly dry, although maine’s conditions were more severe in the report’s regional comparison. the u.s. drought monitor classifies abnormally dry conditions as d0. d0 is not technically drought, but it can describe a landscape that is unusually dry or recovering from drought. moderate drought is d1, the first formal drought category. the monitor says d1 can bring some damage to crops and pastures, higher fire risk, low streams, reservoirs or wells, and developing or imminent water shortages in some places. those are broad indicators; they do not mean every new hampshire community or household is experiencing the same conditions. more information is available through the [u.s. drought monitor’s current map and data tools](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/). the latest statewide percentages also mask a sharp geographic contrast. wmur reported that just under 4% of new hampshire had no drought conditions, concentrated in a small area in southwestern hillsborough county and part of cheshire county. in other words, a resident may see a different situation depending on the watershed, soil, elevation and water source serving a particular town. the statewide map is useful for tracking the regional pattern, but local water managers and emergency officials are the authorities for specific restrictions or well concerns. new hampshire’s current conditions are nevertheless better than they were at this point last year. wmur reported that nearly the entire state had been in severe or extreme drought in late september 2025, with central new hampshire among the hardest-hit areas. the comparison shows why the current report should be read as a measure of ongoing stress rather than a declaration that the state is facing the same level of crisis as last fall. the u.s. drought monitor is updated weekly from a combination of precipitation, soil-moisture, streamflow, groundwater and other indicators. its maps are released on thursdays after a tuesday morning data cutoff, so the oct. 1 assessment captures conditions through the latest reporting cycle rather than every hour of rainfall. that timing also means a future wet period could change the map, while a short burst of rain may not be enough to move deeper hydrologic measures. for residents, the next developments to watch are not just the next rain total but whether water levels recover across the systems that supply farms, forests, fire departments and homes. people who rely on private wells should use their town or state notices for local guidance instead of treating a statewide percentage as a diagnosis of their own supply. the immediate message from the latest report is narrower: the nor’easter offered some rain, but it did not end new hampshire’s dry spell, and more sustained moisture will be needed for a broader recovery. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh manchester new hampshire new hampshire drought weather water supply climate

nh-ev-charging-grants-tourism-2026-10-06.excerpt: The new program will reimburse up to 80% of eligible costs for public Level 2 chargers at places such as ski areas, parks and downtown districts, with the first application window closing Nov. 15.
nh-ev-charging-grants-tourism-2026-10-06.text: new hampshire opens $1 million grant program for chargers at tourism destinations the new program will reimburse up to 80% of eligible costs for public level 2 chargers at places such as ski areas, parks and downtown districts, with the first application window closing nov. 15. new hampshire is offering about $1 million to help build public electric-vehicle charging stations at places that draw visitors, a move state officials say can support both tourism and cleaner transportation. the recharge the adventure new hampshire program focuses on travel- and tourism-oriented locations rather than limiting awards to government property. the new hampshire department of environmental services and department of business and economic affairs announced the program tuesday, according to the [new hampshire bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/06/nh-announces-1m-program-to-boost-spotty-ev-charger-network/). the eligible settings are broad enough to reach communities across the state: parks, ski areas, beaches, downtown districts and other attractions can apply if a proposed project meets the program requirements. public agencies, private organizations and nonprofits are eligible applicants. that structure gives municipalities and regional destinations a path to add charging where visitors already stop, while also allowing privately operated tourism businesses to participate. the grant is designed as a partial reimbursement. it can cover as much as 80% of eligible project costs, up to $10,000 for each level 2 charging port, according to the [southern new hampshire planning commission’s program notice](https://www.snhpc.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/30). applicants will have to finance the work initially and seek reimbursement under the grant agreement. the program also sets a $100,000 cap for projects within any one municipality, although the published program information says the state may consider exceeding that cap for a compelling project or one with substantial public or economic benefits. the state is also reserving at least $40,000 for each of new hampshire’s nine regional planning commission areas. the geographic set-aside matters because charging availability is uneven: the bulletin reported that a february 2025 analysis by clean energy new hampshire and ski new hampshire counted 597 charging ports in the state, the lowest total among new england states in that report. the analysis said new hampshire represented about 5% of the region’s charging infrastructure and linked the shortage to lost tourism dollars. the money comes from new hampshire’s volkswagen environmental mitigation trust, which holds settlement funds from volkswagen’s clean air act case. using that source ties the new awards to air-quality goals while directing part of the money toward a practical barrier for electric-vehicle travelers. level 2 chargers are slower than highway fast chargers, but they are suited to places where visitors may remain for an hour, an afternoon or an overnight stay. a charger at a trailhead, town center or ski-area property can therefore serve a different purpose from a short highway stop. the application process is rolling rather than built around one single deadline. the first monthly window closes nov. 15, and later applications will be considered until the available funding is committed, according to the regional planning commission notice. a webinar for prospective applicants is scheduled for oct. 14. applicants will need to show that their sites are publicly accessible and that the proposed equipment and location fit the program’s tourism and transportation goals. for new hampshire communities, the program offers a relatively modest but targeted way to improve the visitor experience before winter travel and the next tourism seasons. it does not create a statewide fast-charging network, guarantee an award to every applicant or resolve the larger question of how quickly charging infrastructure should expand. it does give destinations a chance to add ports with state-backed cost sharing, and it spreads a portion of the funding across every regional planning commission area. the next important steps are the oct. 14 applicant webinar and the nov. 15 first submission window. until awards are announced, the number and locations of new chargers remain unknown. state officials’ stated goal is to make it easier for electric-vehicle drivers to explore new hampshire while helping local businesses and communities capture spending from those visitors. new-hampshire transportation transportation nh new hampshire new hampshire electric vehicles ev charging tourism clean air grants infrastructure

nh-fema-firefighter-grants-2026-10-03.excerpt: The grants will help 27 Granite State jurisdictions buy protective gear, medical equipment, radios, training and a new tanker, according to the state’s congressional delegation.
nh-fema-firefighter-grants-2026-10-03.text: fema awards $3.67m to new hampshire fire and ems agencies the grants will help 27 granite state jurisdictions buy protective gear, medical equipment, radios, training and a new tanker, according to the state’s congressional delegation. fire departments and emergency medical organizations across new hampshire are set to receive $3,670,649.05 in federal assistance to firefighters grants, funding that will pay for protective equipment, training, communications gear and emergency vehicles, according to a sept. 25 [announcement from the state’s congressional delegation](https://www.shaheen.senate.gov/news/press/new-hampshire-congressional-delegation-celebrates-more-than-36-million-in-federal-funding-to-support-granite-state-firefighters). the awards cover 27 jurisdictions and agencies, from the north country to the seacoast. the largest single grant is $500,000 for training equipment at the new hampshire department of safety in concord. hancock is slated to receive $428,571.42 for a tanker, while seabrook is set to get $390,946 for paramedic training. colebrook’s 45th parallel emergency medical services is listed for $298,384.76 for cpr devices and cardiac monitors, and keene is listed for $198,181.81 for power cots and power-lift systems. other awards are aimed at needs that are less visible to the public but central to safe emergency response. goshen is slated for $180,523.80 for firefighter breathing apparatus, hebron for $162,680.95 for the same type of equipment, and weare for $125,047.61 for portable radios. meredith’s $37,819.42 award is designated for wildland-firefighting personal protective equipment, while rumney and surry are each slated to buy equipment to wash and dry contaminated protective clothing. the delegation’s announcement came from u.s. sens. jeanne shaheen and maggie hassan and reps. chris pappas and maggie goodlander. because the release was issued by elected officials, the award totals and descriptions are attributed to that announcement. [wmur](https://www.wmur.com/article/fema-first-responder-grants/73895544) separately reported that the federal emergency management agency’s awards were approaching $4 million statewide and highlighted training equipment for the department of safety, breathing devices for littleton and wildland equipment for meredith. [news radio keene](https://www.newsradiokeene.com/news/new-hampshire/keene-spofford-and-surry-secure-federal-firefighting-money/) separately reported the awards for keene, spofford and surry. the assistance to firefighters grants program is administered by fema and is intended to improve the ability of fire departments and other eligible organizations to protect firefighters and the public. the [u.s. fire administration](https://www.usfa.fema.gov/a-z/grants/) says the program can support equipment, apparatus, training and other resources, including efforts that improve firefighter health and safety. that makes the new hampshire awards more than a one-time equipment purchase: they can reduce the burden on local departments that must maintain specialized gear and medical-response capacity with limited municipal budgets. the list also shows how uneven emergency-service needs can be across the state. some awards target traditional fire suppression, such as turnout gear, breathing apparatus and thermal-imaging cameras. others support the medical side of calls, including paramedic education, power cots, cpr devices and cardiac monitors. vehicle and communications awards address the practical problem of moving personnel and equipment quickly across rural roads and between communities that rely on mutual aid. the money will not put every project into service immediately. local governments and agencies must accept the awards, follow federal grant requirements and complete the purchases or training described in their applications. the delegation’s published list identifies intended uses and dollar amounts; it does not establish a single statewide completion date. residents should look to their own fire department, ambulance service or town government for updates on when equipment arrives or training begins. for new hampshire residents, the immediate impact will vary by community, but the intended result is statewide: better-equipped responders arriving at fires, medical calls and other emergencies. the awards also give local officials a concrete funding source at a time when departments face rising equipment prices, training demands and the continuing need to protect responders from hazards encountered on the job. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh new hampshire new hampshire firefighters fema public safety emergency services

nh-heating-assistance-oil-prices-2026-10.excerpt: Community-action agencies say more working families are seeking help, while federal forecasters expect heating-oil households to spend more this winter than last.
nh-heating-assistance-oil-prices-2026-10.text: new hampshire heating-aid providers see more first-time applicants as oil costs rise community-action agencies say more working families are seeking help, while federal forecasters expect heating-oil households to spend more this winter than last. new hampshire community-action agencies are seeing more residents seek heating assistance for the first time as a costlier fuel season approaches. providers described a rise in new applicants and questions about overdue balances during a monday roundtable in concord, according to reporting by the [new hampshire bulletin](https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/oil-prices-soar-more-nh-residents-fall-behind-their-heating-bills). the early applications are a warning that the state's fuel-assistance program is being asked to cover households whose budgets were already strained before the first sustained cold weather arrives. the pressure is being amplified by the outlook for heating oil. the u.s. energy information administration said oct. 6 that homes primarily using heating oil are expected to pay about 21% more for the fuel this winter than last winter. eia also forecasts roughly a 30% increase in heating-oil prices, partly offset by an expectation of milder northeast weather. the agency said tight distillate markets are keeping oil costs elevated, while higher inventories are giving natural-gas customers a somewhat different price outlook. those are national forecasts, not a promise about any individual new hampshire delivery. a separate estimate cited by the bulletin, from the national energy assistance directors' association, puts the typical northeast heating-oil season at about $2,300, or more than $500 above last year. the estimates use different methods and should not be added together: eia is forecasting fuel spending for oil-heated homes, while neada is describing a regional seasonal-cost estimate. a household's actual bill will depend on the home's size and insulation, thermostat settings, equipment efficiency, weather and the price charged by its supplier. the impact is already showing up at local agencies. staff with community action partnership belknap-merrimack counties told the bulletin that inquiries about overdue fuel accounts are running ahead of last year's pace. southwestern community services reported many applicants who are working and new to the program. that does not establish how many households statewide are in crisis, but it does show that the higher costs are reaching beyond the residents who have traditionally used fuel assistance. new hampshire's program is the state version of the federally funded low income home energy assistance program, or liheap. the [community action partnership hillsborough and rockingham](https://www.caphr.org/services/fuel-assistance) program page says eligible homeowners and renters may receive grants from $188 to $2,500 for heating, with payments covering qualifying deliveries of oil, kerosene, propane, wood or coal from oct. 1 through april 30. electric and natural-gas assistance follows a different billing schedule. the benefit is assigned to the fuel vendor or, in some cases, the landlord; it is not a cash payment that a household can use for any expense. the program is limited by eligibility and available funds. the bulletin reports that new hampshire generally serves households with income up to about 60% of the state's median household income. the community-action program says priority pre-applications for the 2026-27 season became available after july 1 for certain households, including older or disabled residents and families with young children, while other households could pre-apply after sept. 1. its page lists april 30, 2027, as the application deadline, but residents should confirm current income rules and local appointment requirements with their administering agency. federal action is still uncertain. u.s. rep. chris pappas has proposed increasing liheap support and expanding eligibility, according to his [sept. 25 announcement](https://pappas.house.gov/media/press-releases/pappas-introduces-new-legislation-to-lower-energy-costs), but a bill or proposal is not the same as enacted funding. new hampshire providers told the bulletin they want more money and timely federal disbursements because assistance may not cover a full delivery, and one winter can require several deliveries. for residents, the immediate whether congress changes the federal program, and how severe the winter becomes, will determine how much of the gap families must absorb themselves. new-hampshire energy energy nh concord new
