nh-londonderry-firefighter-flashover-202.excerpt: Lt. Mike England suffered a broken leg and minor burns while searching a Rockingham Road house where crews feared people might still be inside. All residents and animals escaped safely.
nh-londonderry-firefighter-flashover-202.text: londonderry firefighter recovers at home after flashover injury lt. mike england suffered a broken leg and minor burns while searching a rockingham road house where crews feared people might still be inside. all residents and animals escaped safely. a londonderry firefighter is recovering at home after a flashover engulfed him during a search of a burning house, a close call that left him with a leg fracture and minor burns. lt. mike england was taken to a hospital after the oct. 2 fire on rockingham road and had been released by the time [wmur-tv reported](https://www.wmur.com/article/londonderry-firefighter-who-caught-fire-now-recovering-at-home/74015010) on oct. 4. the station said england described himself as fortunate given the severity of the conditions and the limited injuries. the incident began at about 10:07 p.m. when londonderry’s fire communications center received a report of a structure fire at 83 rockingham road. crews arrived to find smoke and flames coming from the home. early information indicated that someone could still be inside, so firefighters entered to conduct a primary search while other crews advanced a hose line. [whdh reported](https://whdh.com/news/watch-nh-firefighter-recovering-after-catching-fire-at-home-in-londonderry/) that england was using a thermal-imaging camera when the conditions changed without warning. a flashover is the near-simultaneous ignition of exposed combustible materials in an enclosed space. in this case, the sudden increase in heat and fire caught england inside the building. he escaped quickly while flames engulfed his protective gear, and other firefighters put out the fire on his clothing before he was evaluated and taken to the hospital. the sequence was also described in the local [patch account](https://patch.com/new-hampshire/nashua/amp/34945674/fiery-flashover-injures-firefighter-during-evening-house-fire-in-londonderry), which reported that the injured firefighter was treated at the scene before transport. the search was prompted by concern that residents and pets might be trapped, but the people inside had already made it out. wmur reported that five occupants evacuated on their own and declined medical treatment. whdh and patch both reported that the other occupants and animals were safely evacuated. no resident injury was reported in the accounts reviewed for this story, although the house suffered a serious fire and the cause remained under investigation. the response expanded as the danger became clear. patch reported that the fire grew to a second-alarm incident after the flashover, bringing additional crews from bedford, windham, salem and litchfield, along with earlier assistance from derry and manchester. firefighters knocked down most of the fire and then worked through salvage and overhaul operations to deal with remaining hot spots. the mutual-aid response allowed londonderry to add personnel while maintaining coverage for other calls in the town and neighboring communities. england’s recovery has given the incident a different ending than the video of his escape might suggest. wmur reported that he was home and recovering, while whdh said londonderry fire chief james young credited england’s training and experience and expressed relief that the injuries were not more severe. the reporting does not provide a detailed medical timeline or say when england will return to duty. northeast news has not independently reviewed medical records or the department’s incident report. for londonderry, the next confirmed step is the fire investigation. officials had not announced a cause in the reports reviewed through oct. 6, and the available accounts do not identify a final damage estimate. the incident illustrates why an apparently routine primary search can become life-threatening in seconds: firefighters were acting on a report of possible occupants, and the interior conditions shifted before the search was complete. the town’s [fire department](https://www.londonderrynh.gov/366/fire-department) remains the local agency responsible for fire response and public updates as the investigation and england’s recovery continue. new-hampshire public-safety public safety nh londonderry 83 rockingham road, londonderry, new hampshire new hampshire londonderry firefighter safety house fire flashover fire department public safety

nh-loon-fourth-peak-proposal-2026-10-06.excerpt: The Lincoln resort says the plan would add 280 acres, four lifts and two lodges, but the project still faces a federal environmental review and has no construction timetable.
nh-loon-fourth-peak-proposal-2026-10-06.text: loon mountain proposes fourth peak in expansion that could reshape lincoln ski traffic the lincoln resort says the plan would add 280 acres, four lifts and two lodges, but the project still faces a federal environmental review and has no construction timetable. loon mountain resort has submitted a proposal to add a fourth lift-served peak overlooking downtown lincoln, a long-range plan that would substantially enlarge one of new hampshire’s most visible ski destinations if it clears federal and local reviews. the resort says the concept would add 280 acres of skiable terrain and bring its potential total to 955 acres, a 137% increase over the terrain now available. the proposal was announced oct. 6 by [loon mountain resort](https://www.loonmtn.com/latest-news/pr-peak-4) and independently reported by [wcvb](https://www.wcvb.com/article/loon-mountain-fourth-peak-expansion/74057822). the new terrain would sit west of the resort’s current south peak footprint, with views toward lincoln’s town center. the announcement is important for the region because it describes a possible new visitor draw and a direct relationship between a major mountain expansion, downtown access and the future shape of tourism in the pemigewasset valley. loon’s concept calls for 145 acres of traditional trails and another 135 acres of tree-skiing areas. four aerial lifts would serve roughly 1,500 vertical feet, and the resort proposes a summit lodge at an elevation of about 2,324 feet with dining, sightseeing and event space. a second lodge is envisioned at mid-mountain. the resort says the layout is meant to give skiers and snowboarders more room to progress beyond beginner terrain while also adding winding trails, open cruisers and more challenging woods skiing. that design would make the project more than a simple trail cut. it would create a separate operating area with new lifts, buildings and connections to the existing resort network. the ski-industry publication [peakrankings](https://www.peakrankings.com/content/loon-proposes-massive-fourth-peak-expansion) described the proposal as an unusually large eastern resort expansion, while also emphasizing that the drawings are conceptual and could change. loon has not announced a project cost, a first construction phase or an opening season. the immediate next step is a federal environmental assessment because most of the proposed terrain lies within the white mountain national forest. loon says the u.s. forest service has accepted the proposal for review and that the assessment is expected to take about 12 months. the review will be followed by additional federal and local permitting decisions; acceptance for review is not approval to build. the process is where questions about forest impacts, water, wildlife, visual changes, transportation and public access can be examined before any construction schedule is set. land ownership adds another layer. loon says the project area includes both national-forest land and private property owned by south peak resort, an independently operated business. neither loon nor south peak owns all of the land involved, so the proposal depends on coordination among the resort, the private landowner, the forest service and local authorities. the resort says any buildout would be phased and adjusted in response to public feedback, operating needs and environmental findings. for lincoln, the potential payoff is a larger year-round tourism asset, but the impacts would not be limited to the slopes. a new peak facing downtown could send more visitors through local businesses and create demand for lodging, food and services. it could also intensify longstanding practical questions about parking, road congestion, employee housing and the balance between resort growth and the town’s capacity. those effects remain projections, not measured outcomes, because the resort has not submitted a final construction plan or visitor forecast. the announcement also sits within loon’s broader flight path: 2030 investment plan. the resort separately says a 272-acre black ridge tree-skiing expansion is planned for the 2027-28 winter season, along with projects involving lifts, summer activities and snowmaking. peak 4 is distinct from that work and is much less certain. loon says the fourth-peak concept grew from 1960s drawings associated with founder and former new hampshire gov. sherman adams, but the historical vision does not reduce the modern project’s permitting requirements. for now, skiers have a proposal, not a new mountain. the environmental assessment, public process and local approvals will determine whether the concept changes, moves forward in phases or stops. the next meaningful milestones will be the forest service’s review materials and opportunities for public comment, followed by any formal permit applications. until those steps occur, the most defensible description is a significant expansion under consideration—one that could change lincoln’s winter economy, but is still years from a possible opening and may never be built as currently drawn. new-hampshire business business nh lincoln loon mountain resort, lincoln, new hampshire new hampshire loon mountain lincoln skiing tourism white mountain national forest development

nh-medicaid-premiums-federal-approval-20.excerpt: A premium system that was expected to start July 1 has no new launch date while the state waits for federal approval and answers about how it fits with new Medicaid cost-sharing rules.
nh-medicaid-premiums-federal-approval-20.text: new hampshire medicaid premiums remain on hold awaiting federal guidance a premium system that was expected to start july 1 has no new launch date while the state waits for federal approval and answers about how it fits with new medicaid cost-sharing rules. new hampshire’s planned medicaid premium system remains on hold because the state is still waiting for federal guidance on how the charges would interact with changes made by congress. the department of health and human services has not begun collecting the premiums and has not announced a new start date, according to an oct. 1 report by the [new hampshire bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/01/lacking-federal-approval-new-hampshire-forced-to-hold-off-on-new-medicaid-premiums/). jake leon, a dhhs spokesperson, told the bulletin that the situation is “status quo” and that the department is still waiting for guidance on the impact of h.r. 1, the federal law commonly called the one big beautiful bill act. the premiums had been expected to take effect july 1. the delay means eligible granite advantage members are not currently receiving bills under the new system, even though the state law authorizing the charges remains in place. new hampshire law directs dhhs to seek a medicaid waiver and, if necessary, a state-plan amendment to charge premiums to granite advantage participants with household income at or above 100% of the federal poverty level. the statute sets monthly amounts of $60 for a one-person household, $80 for two people, $90 for three people and $100 for a household of four or more during the biennium ending june 30, 2027. it also requires the department to develop hardship criteria. the [new hampshire general court’s text of rsa 126-aa:2-a](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/x/126-aa/126-aa-2-a.htm) makes the charges subject to federal limits on cost sharing and eligibility. that federal condition is central to the delay. medicaid is jointly administered by the states and the federal government, so new hampshire needs approval from the u.s. centers for medicare and medicaid services before the premium structure can operate. the bulletin reported that state officials have been weighing whether the planned premiums can coexist with h.r. 1 provisions that create cost sharing for some medicaid enrollees. the law’s cost-sharing provisions are scheduled to take effect in 2028, but the state is waiting for the federal government to clarify how the programs should be coordinated before it spends money to launch the collection system. a dhhs presentation to state lawmakers lists the conflict in its implementation timeline. the agency’s [medicaid changes from hr 1 document](https://gc.nh.gov/statstudcomm/committees/72/documents/medicaid%20changes%20from%20hr%201.pdf) says the state budget requires granite advantage premiums in state fiscal year 2027, while the federal cost-sharing requirement is scheduled for oct. 1, 2028. the same document says dhhs planned to submit a waiver by july 1, 2026; the current status reported by the department’s spokesperson shows that submission has not yet produced an approved launch path. the policy would affect more than a small administrative group. the [new hampshire fiscal policy institute](https://nhfpi.org/resource/the-state-budget-for-fiscal-years-2026-and-2027/) estimated that about 11,000 adults in granite advantage would be subject to the adult premiums. its review of the state budget said monthly charges would range from $60 to $100 depending on household size. the budget also includes a separate premium structure for households with children enrolled through the children’s health insurance program, with monthly amounts ranging from $190 to $270 for families above the applicable income threshold. supporters have described the premiums as a way to preserve broad eligibility while generating revenue for the program. opponents argue that even modest monthly charges can discourage enrollment or care, especially for people whose incomes sit just above the poverty line. a [new hampshire legislative analysis](https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/legacy/bs2016/hearingreport.aspx?id=11706&sy=2026) of a bill that would have repealed the premiums recorded both the planned july 1 start for medicaid expansion enrollees and the concern that the state could spend on a collection system that federal law may soon make obsolete. the bill was later listed as inexpedient to legislate and did not become the current governing law. for now, the practical answer for granite advantage members is that the new premiums have not started. the next major decision belongs to dhhs and federal medicaid officials: they must determine whether the state can secure approval, revise the design or wait for the federal cost-sharing framework. until that process produces a new authorization and timeline, new hampshire residents should not assume that the amounts listed in state law are current bills or that a launch date has been set. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh concord new hampshire new hampshire medicaid granite advantage health care costs dhhs federal approval public benefits

nh-medicaid-trans-care-tro-2026-10-05.excerpt: A federal judge rejected a temporary restraining order sought by four New Hampshire families, leaving the Oct. 13 coverage cutoff in place for now while a preliminary-injunction fight moves toward an Oct. 30 hearing.
nh-medicaid-trans-care-tro-2026-10-05.text: new hampshire judge denies emergency bid to pause medicaid transgender-care rule a federal judge rejected a temporary restraining order sought by four new hampshire families, leaving the oct. 13 coverage cutoff in place for now while a preliminary-injunction fight moves toward an oct. 30 hearing. a federal judge in new hampshire has rejected an emergency request from four families who are challenging a federal rule that would end medicaid and children’s health insurance program funding for gender-dysphoria treatment for young people. the oct. 5 order did not decide whether the rule is lawful. it denied only the families’ request for a temporary restraining order while their broader request for a preliminary injunction proceeds. the [u.s. district court order](https://litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/goe_2026.10.05_order-on-motion-for-preliminary-injunction.pdf) says the case is goe et al. v. u.s. department of health and human services, civil no. 26-cv-803-sm-tsm. the plaintiffs filed suit oct. 1 under pseudonyms to protect their privacy. the [aclu of new hampshire](https://www.aclu-nh.org/cases/goe-et-al-v-u-s-department-of-health-and-human-services-et-al/) says the case represents four new hampshire teenagers and their families and was brought with glad law and the national center for lgbtq rights. the groups are challenging a rule issued in august by the centers for medicare and medicaid services. they say it will cut off federal medicaid and chip funding on oct. 13 for medications and other treatment for gender dysphoria, including care that a patient’s doctor has determined is medically necessary. the families asked for a preliminary injunction stopping enforcement of the rule and added that, if the court could not decide that motion before oct. 13, it should issue an emergency temporary restraining order protecting the named plaintiffs. judge steven j. mcauliffe wrote that the filing did not address the specific requirements for a temporary restraining order under federal rule of civil procedure 65(b). in particular, the plaintiffs did not submit an affidavit clearly showing that immediate and irreparable harm would occur before the government could respond. the judge also wrote that the facts presented did not suggest the kind of emergency required for that form of relief. that ruling leaves the case’s central legal questions open. the order does not validate the federal rule, reject the families’ arguments about medicaid law or equal protection, or resolve what treatment any plaintiff will ultimately receive. it means only that the court will consider the preliminary-injunction request on the ordinary schedule rather than imposing an immediate, temporary shield before the government files its response. the coverage change remains scheduled to take effect oct. 13 unless another court order or administrative action changes the timetable. a scheduling order entered oct. 6 sets the next milestones. the federal defendants’ response to the preliminary-injunction motion is due oct. 15, the families’ reply is due oct. 22, and the court has set a hearing for 10 a.m. oct. 30. the [georgetown university health care litigation tracker](https://litigationtracker.law.georgetown.edu/litigation/goe-et-al-v-department-of-health-and-human-services-et-al/) lists briefing as ongoing and identifies the case as a challenge to federal health-funding policy. those dates give the litigation a defined path even though the federal funding deadline arrives before the hearing. the dispute has a specific new hampshire dimension. [new hampshire public radio](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-10-02/nh-families-sue-trump-administration-medicaid-funding-transgender-services) reported that the four families are low-income households and that the teenage plaintiffs are transgender girls who use services that would no longer be covered under the change. nhpr described puberty-blocking medication and hormone therapy as examples of care affected by the medicaid rule. because the families are proceeding anonymously, public filings identify them through pseudonyms rather than names. nhpr also reported that new hampshire is the only new england state with a law banning most gender-affirming health care for transgender youth. that state law, signed by gov. kelly ayotte last year, included an exception for young people already receiving care before the state restriction took effect, according to the station. the federal case presents a different question: whether federal funding rules can prevent medicaid and chip from paying for care even when state policy and a patient’s doctors would otherwise allow it. another lawsuit brought by 22 state attorneys general is challenging the same federal medicaid rule in massachusetts, but nhpr reported that case did not seek emergency relief. for the new hampshire families, the immediate issue is whether coverage can continue through the federal government’s oct. 13 deadline. the next concrete answers will come from the defendants’ oct. 15 filing, the oct. 30 hearing and any subsequent order on the preliminary injunction. until then, the temporary-restraining-order denial is a procedural ruling, not a final judgment on the policy’s legality or the families’ claims. new-hampshire health health nh concord u.s. district court for the district of new hampshire, concord new hampshire medicaid chip transgender health care gender dysphoria federal courts lgbtq rights

nh-public-colleges-tuition-waiver-promis.excerpt: The New Hampshire Promise will cover standard tuition for qualifying residents and community-college transfer students, but not every cost of attending college.
nh-public-colleges-tuition-waiver-promis.text: new hampshire public colleges to waive tuition for eligible students starting in 2027 the new hampshire promise will cover standard tuition for qualifying residents and community-college transfer students, but not every cost of attending college. new hampshire residents from families earning up to $100,000 a year will be eligible for tuition waivers at the state’s public universities and colleges beginning in fall 2027, under a new program announced by the university system of new hampshire. the program is aimed at incoming first-year students and certain community-college transfer students, opening another path into the state’s public higher-education system as families face rising college costs. the new hampshire promise covers standard tuition for eligible students at the university of new hampshire in durham and manchester, plymouth state university, keene state college and the university of new hampshire’s college of professional studies online program. the [official usnh program page](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) says the benefit is built from federal, state and institutional grant aid and applies to students who qualify for in-state residency. eligibility is narrower than the phrase ‘free college’ might suggest. students must be enrolled full time, pursuing a first undergraduate degree and meet the program’s academic and financial-aid requirements. usnh lists a minimum 2.7 grade-point average from a student’s prior school, submission of the free application for federal student aid and total family income of no more than $100,000 with typical assets. transfer students can qualify after earning an associate degree through the community college system of new hampshire. the program does not require a separate application. students must apply for admission to a participating usnh institution and complete the fafsa; the university system says eligible applicants will then be considered automatically as part of their financial-aid offer. awards will be reviewed annually based on the student’s fafsa, academic status and full-time enrollment, according to the system’s published guidance. that distinction matters for families planning a budget. the promise covers standard tuition, while students may still need loans or other aid for fees, books, housing and meals. the [university system of new hampshire’s eligibility guidance](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) also says the program does not apply to january or summer courses. the benefit is therefore a reduction of one major expense, not a guarantee that a student’s total cost of attendance will be zero. new hampshire public radio reported that the revised program is expected to broaden access compared with the previous version. tania deluzuriaga, a university of new hampshire spokesperson, told [nhpr](https://www.nhpr.org/education/2026-10-02/usnh-unh-plymouth-state-keene-state-tuition-waiver-higher-education-newhampshire) the system estimates 29% more of next year’s incoming class will qualify. under the earlier structure, students had to complete a more complicated federal pell grant process before learning whether they were eligible, a hurdle the new fafsa-based approach is intended to reduce. the announcement comes as new hampshire’s public colleges are managing financial pressure. nhpr reported that the system lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget and that unh cut $17.5 million from its budget, contributing to staff reductions and a hiring freeze while enrollment has also been declining. kimberly derego, the system’s chief enrollment officer, said the institutions will fund the waivers with endowment money and hope the program attracts donors who want to support lower-income students. for prospective students, the immediate next step is preparation rather than a new application deadline: watch the participating college’s admissions process, complete the fafsa for the relevant aid year and keep academic records current. the first cohort will not begin until fall 2027, and the system’s rules leave unanswered questions about how many students ultimately enroll, how the endowment-supported financing performs and whether the program changes enrollment patterns across the four campuses and online program. those results will determine whether the promise becomes a durable affordability tool for new hampshire families. new-hampshire education education nh new hampshire new hampshire higher education tuition financial aid

nh-september-revenues-business-tax-2026-.excerpt: The state collected $398.9 million for its General and Education funds in September, beating the monthly plan by $69.1 million as quarterly business-tax payments arrived.
nh-september-revenues-business-tax-2026-.text: new hampshire revenue surges on record september business-tax collections the state collected $398.9 million for its general and education funds in september, beating the monthly plan by $69.1 million as quarterly business-tax payments arrived. new hampshire's general and education funds received a major revenue lift in september, when the state collected $398.9 million in unrestricted receipts. the total was $69.1 million, or 21%, above the $329.8 million monthly plan, according to the [new hampshire department of administrative services monthly revenue report](https://www.das.nh.gov/accounting/fy%2027/fy2027_monthly_revenue_september.pdf). gov. kelly ayotte highlighted the results in a [statement issued oct. 5](https://www.governor.nh.gov/news/statement-september-revenues), saying the figures showed the state's economy was moving in the right direction. the biggest factor was business-tax revenue. collections from the business profits tax and business enterprise tax totaled $269.8 million in september, $69.4 million above the state's plan and $94.7 million higher than september 2025, the report says. the month's total also exceeded the previous september record of $226.4 million, set in 2024. the report attributes the increase to estimated payments, extension payments and returns, along with fewer refunds than a year earlier. september is an important checkpoint because many businesses make quarterly estimated payments during the month. the new hampshire fiscal policy institute had warned in a september analysis that july and august offered only a limited view of the fiscal year because the state's largest revenue source, business-profit taxes, arrives unevenly. the institute said september would provide a stronger indication of whether early 2027 fiscal-year collections could help support the next state budget. the new report covers the third month of the fiscal year, which began july 1. after three months, unrestricted receipts for the two funds were $74.9 million, or 12.5%, above the state's revenue plan, according to the governor's statement. that does not mean every part of the revenue picture is outperforming. the report shows the general fund was $54 million ahead of plan and the education fund was $20.9 million ahead after the first quarter, but transfers from the liquor commission were $7.4 million below the first-quarter plan and video-lottery-terminal receipts were $3 million short. other sources also helped. real-estate-transfer-tax collections reached $73.6 million in september, exceeding the plan by $8.3 million and the year-earlier total by $11.9 million. meals-and-rentals-tax receipts, after transfers for municipal revenue and school-building debt service, totaled $111.8 million for the quarter, up $4.3 million from the same period last year. the first-quarter transfer to the municipal revenue fund reached $43.9 million, according to reporting by [nh journal](https://nhjournal.com/gop-tax-cuts-record-receipts-nh-revenues-beat-projections/). the numbers are likely to feed new hampshire's continuing argument over tax rates and public spending. republican officials have pointed to the business-tax receipts as evidence that earlier rate reductions did not prevent revenue growth. democrats and other critics have argued that strong collections do not settle questions about whether the state is adequately funding schools, local services and other obligations. those are political interpretations of the report, not findings in the revenue data itself. the results also come with limits. the september report is a cash-basis fiscal update rather than a forecast of the full year, and one strong month cannot establish a long-term trend. business-tax collections can vary with corporate profits, payment timing, refunds and economic conditions. new hampshire's fiscal reports will therefore remain important as lawmakers and agencies watch whether the early surplus persists into months with different revenue patterns. for now, the report gives state budget writers more room than they had at the start of the fiscal year: the general and education funds are ahead of plan, while the state's largest monthly business-tax haul has offset weaker performance in several other streams. the next question is whether the surplus represents durable growth or a concentration of payments in one unusually strong quarter. new-hampshire business business nh concord new hampshire new hampshire state revenue business taxes state budget general fund education fund economy

nh-west-rattlesnake-hiker-death-2026-10-.excerpt: Richard Chateauneuf, 64, was found unconscious about three-quarters of a mile from the trailhead Saturday. Other hikers and first responders attempted CPR, but he could not be revived.
nh-west-rattlesnake-hiker-death-2026-10-.text: massachusetts hiker dies on west rattlesnake mountain in holderness richard chateauneuf, 64, was found unconscious about three-quarters of a mile from the trailhead saturday. other hikers and first responders attempted cpr, but he could not be revived. a 64-year-old massachusetts man died saturday after he was found unconscious on the old bridle path at west rattlesnake mountain in holderness, new hampshire, according to the [new hampshire fish and game department](https://nhfishgame.com/2026/10/05/deceased-hiker-on-old-bridle-path-on-west-rattlesnake-mountain/). richard chateauneuf of tyngsboro was about three-quarters of a mile from the trailhead when other hikers found him and began administering cpr, the department said. the call came at 11:22 a.m. on oct. 3, the agency said. holderness fire-rescue, center harbor fire-rescue, sandwich fire-rescue, plymouth ambulance and fish and game conservation officers responded to the trail. first responders continued efforts to revive chateauneuf, but he could not be revived. his body was carried back to the trailhead, according to the official account. independent reports from [nbc boston](https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/massachusetts-man-dies-while-hiking-in-nhs-lakes-region/4025511/) and [wmur](https://www.wmur.com/article/hiker-dies-holderness-trail/74008418) matched the department's account of the response and identified chateauneuf as a tyngsboro resident. neither report described a cause of death, and fish and game said no additional information was available. the circumstances should therefore be understood as an unexplained medical emergency, not as a reported fall, weather incident or trail accident. west rattlesnake mountain is in new hampshire's lakes region, near the town of holderness. [cbs boston](https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/hiker-dies-west-rattlesnake-mountain-new-hampshire/) reported that the old bridle path is a popular 1.8-mile route with about 396 feet of elevation gain that typically takes roughly an hour and a half. distance from a road still matters when a hiker needs urgent medical care: the location reported by officials, less than a mile from the trailhead, shows why a medical crisis on a modest outing can require a coordinated response rather than a routine ambulance call. the response depended on both public agencies and people already on the trail. hikers who found chateauneuf called for help and started cpr before emergency crews arrived. fish and game said the incident brought together local fire and rescue departments, an ambulance service and state conservation officers, with the patient then carried to the trailhead for removal from the mountain. the department used the release to renew its broader hiking-safety message. new hampshire fish and game describes itself as a self-funded agency that relies heavily on volunteer rescue groups for wilderness search-and-rescue work. it encourages hikers to prepare with the ten essentials: a map and compass, warm clothing, extra food and water, a headlamp, fire starter, a first-aid kit, a whistle, rain and wind protection, and a knife. the list appears in the department's current release about the holderness response. fish and game also promotes the voluntary [hike safe card](https://gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/fis1100.html), which supports the state's search-and-rescue fund. the card is not a substitute for preparation or a guarantee that a hiker will avoid responsibility for a response; state rules address circumstances involving negligence or reckless conduct. the department's message after saturday's death was practical: plan the route, account for changing conditions and carry equipment that can help until rescuers arrive. no investigation or medical finding explaining chateauneuf's death was announced in the official release. for now, the confirmed facts are the location, response time, identity, rescue effort and death. the incident is a reminder for residents and visitors using holderness trails that even a familiar, relatively short hike can become a medical emergency far enough from a road to test both a hiker's preparation and the region's rescue network. new-hampshire new-hampshire new hampshire nh holderness west rattlesnake mountain, holderness, new hampshire new hampshire holderness west rattlesnake mountain hiking search and rescue

nj-nuclear-task-force-2026-10-01.excerpt: The group’s first meeting created five subcommittees and a public information hub as New Jersey moves from lifting its nuclear moratorium toward planning new generation.
nj-nuclear-task-force-2026-10-01.text: new jersey nuclear task force maps next steps for 1,100-megawatt expansion the group’s first meeting created five subcommittees and a public information hub as new jersey moves from lifting its nuclear moratorium toward planning new generation. new jersey’s newly formed nuclear task force held its first meeting thursday, beginning a state effort to determine how next-generation nuclear power could fit into the state’s future electricity system. governor mikie sherrill’s office said the group reviewed a draft charter, created five subcommittees and launched nuclear nj, a public website for updates and background information. the meeting marks a shift from changing state policy to working out the practical questions that would come before a new reactor could be built. the administration says the task force is intended to coordinate work across government and with industry, labor, environmental groups and other stakeholders. it is not itself an approval for a plant, and the governor’s announcement did not identify a project site, developer or construction schedule. the five subcommittees divide that work into the areas most likely to shape any future proposal. one will examine regulatory and permitting requirements. others will study financing and power-sale arrangements, supply chains and technology, workforce development, and public trust. the last category is especially consequential for a technology that requires long-term safety oversight and community participation before construction could move forward. the task force has 14 members, according to its public roster. the group includes leaders from the governor’s office, the board of public utilities, the department of environmental protection, the economic development authority, the state treasurer’s office and the department of military affairs. it also includes representatives of pseg nuclear, holtec, the new jersey business and industry association, electrical workers, the laborers’ international union of north america and the natural resources defense council. that mix gives the panel access to industry and labor expertise, while also putting potential environmental and public-interest concerns inside the same planning process. the new group follows two major policy steps. sherrill’s executive order 2 established a nuclear power task force on her first day in office. in april, she signed legislation that ended new jersey’s roughly 50-year de facto moratorium on new nuclear development. the state later enacted the power nj act, which directs a competitive procurement program designed to support at least 1,100 megawatts of advanced nuclear generation. the bill describes that number as a program design parameter, not a guarantee that the state will ultimately buy that amount of power. new jersey already relies heavily on nuclear generation. the governor’s office says existing nuclear plants provide more than 40% of the state’s electricity and about 80% of its carbon-free power. supporters frame new reactors as a way to add reliable supply as electricity demand grows and to put downward pressure on utility costs. those are policy goals, not results that have been demonstrated by a new project; any cost, schedule, waste, safety and siting questions would have to be resolved through later regulatory and procurement decisions. independent reporting by new jersey 101.5 described thursday’s meeting as the start of planning for the 1,100-megawatt program and noted that the work is focused on permits, financing, workforce needs and public support. that account also underscored the distance between a planning target and operating power: the task force can organize the state’s next steps, but it cannot by itself make a reactor economical, secure federal approvals or settle questions about who bears construction risk. for residents, the immediate development is therefore an information and planning structure rather than a construction announcement. nuclear nj, developed with the board of public utilities, the economic development authority and the department of environmental protection, is intended to collect agency updates and explain the state’s approach. the next meaningful tests will be whether the subcommittees publish clear work products, how the state handles public input and whether any future procurement produces a proposal that can pass technical, financial, environmental and safety review. sources: [new jersey governor’s office](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/20261001b.shtml), [new jersey nuclear task force roster](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/about/task-force/), [new jersey department of environmental protection energy policy page](https://dep.nj.gov/cleanenergy/nj/), [new jersey 101.5 reporting](https://nj1015.com/new-jersey-nuclear-task-force-launches/), and [nuclear nj information hub](https://www.nj.gov/nuclear/). more misc misc. nj trenton trenton, new jersey new jersey nuclear energy electricity power nj act energy policy

nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.excerpt: The state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals.
nj-shbp-reform-working-group-2026-10-01.text: new jersey opens health-benefits reform group as public-plan costs climb the state, unions, health-care organizations and local-government representatives will study how to make coverage more affordable, but any changes will require further planning and approvals. new jersey has formally launched a working group to rethink the state health benefits program, putting labor, state officials, health-care organizations and public-employer representatives in the same process as the state begins its october enrollment season. the group is expected to produce advisory recommendations for gov. mikie sherrill on how to slow cost growth while preserving coverage for public employees, retirees and participating employers, according to the governor’s oct. 1 announcement (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20261001a.shtml). the launch fulfills a commitment in a sept. 2 agreement between the administration and 17 unions representing state employees. that agreement waived an increase in state workers’ health-benefit contribution rates for 2027 while giving labor a role in a broader review of the system. the state described the agreement as a response to structural cost pressures, not a final redesign of the plans. new jersey says its state, local-government and education health programs cover about 690,000 people combined (office of the governor of new jersey: https://nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260902b.shtml). the working group’s agenda reaches beyond the portion of premiums paid by employees. the governor’s office says members will examine how the state administers benefits, how insurers and providers are paid, the structure of provider networks, plan pricing, premium contributions, benefit design, participation rules, and the program’s governance and data systems. subcommittees will take up those subjects in more detail, and the administration says it may add outside experts and stakeholders as the review continues. that scope matters because new jersey’s public plans are not facing one uniform problem. state employees, local-government workers and school employees participate through programs with different plans, employers, governing bodies and legal requirements. independent reporting by the new jersey monitor found that a state commission approved an average 17.3% premium increase for local-government workers in september, while actuaries said the school employees’ plan needed an average 34.4% increase to fund claims, rebuild a month of surplus and repay a projected $90 million in state loans. the school-plan commission deadlocked, in part because one of its nine seats has been vacant (new jersey monitor: https://newjerseymonitor.com/2026/09/03/nj-panels-ok-rate-hike-for-public-worker-health-plans-deadlock-on-increase-for-teachers/). the dispute is therefore tied to more than household payroll deductions. higher premiums can affect municipal budgets, school districts and the state’s cost of employing and retaining workers. the new jersey monitor reported that state actuaries estimated the state workers’ plan would need to collect $397.2 million more in 2027 premiums than in 2026, although that figure includes increases that otherwise would have been paid by the state and employees. the state’s earlier budget materials also projected roughly $6.7 billion in fiscal 2026 health-benefit payments for active and retired enrollees for whom the state is responsible (new jersey treasury: https://nj.gov/treasury/omb/publications/26bib/bib.pdf). the timing puts members and employers in a transition period. the state health benefits program’s open-enrollment window for the 2026 plan year runs from oct. 1 through oct. 31, while the school employees’ health benefits program’s enrollment period is scheduled for oct. 26 through oct. 31, according to the state treasury’s benefits page (new jersey department of the treasury: https://www.nj.gov/treasury/pensions/documents/hb/oe2026/hb-sbc-state-active-26.shtml). the reform group’s recommendations will not change those windows or immediately alter anyone’s plan. the group’s first meeting is scheduled for oct. 16. the administration says it will continue detailed design and implementation planning in 2027, and any resulting changes could require collective bargaining, administrative action, procurement steps, commission votes, legislation or other legal approvals. that means the immediate result is a process and a set of questions, not a promised savings figure or a new benefit package. the central test will be whether the review produces changes that address provider and prescription-drug costs while giving workers, employers and taxpayers clearer information about how the system is financed. more misc misc. nj trenton trenton, new jersey new jersey health benefits public employees labor health care costs

ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.excerpt: The lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of New York households at risk.
ny-housing-counseling-hud-lawsuit-2026-0.text: new york sues hud over housing-counseling funds as $1m state award hangs in balance the lawsuit challenges the trump administration’s decision not to award federally approved housing-counseling money, putting services used by thousands of new york households at risk. new york attorney general letitia james sued the u.s. department of housing and urban development on wednesday, arguing that the agency unlawfully withheld federal housing-counseling money that supports homeowners, renters and prospective buyers across the state. the case was filed in the southern district of new york on the final day of the federal fiscal year, when the state said the underlying funds were scheduled to expire. the attorney general’s announcement is at https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-sues-trump-administration-protect-housing-counseling-0. new york is seeking to protect roughly $1 million it applied for through the new york state housing finance agency. the money would be distributed among 22 hud-certified counseling organizations, with individual grants historically ranging from $20,000 to $100,000. the programs provide guidance on home purchases, rent and mortgage finances, foreclosure prevention, property maintenance and other housing decisions. the state’s complaint says new york has received this federal support regularly for about 13 years and submitted a complete application on may 22, but never received an award or explanation from hud. the lawsuit challenges a broader funding decision. the complaint says congress made approximately $57.5 million available for hud’s national housing counseling program, but hud had not obligated at least $56.1 million by the time the case was filed. new york argues that federal law requires hud to make assistance available to approved housing agencies and that congress did not authorize the department to eliminate or reduce the program on its own. those are allegations in the state’s complaint, not findings by the court. the filing is available at https://ag.ny.gov/sites/default/files/court-filings/state-of-new-york-v-u.s-department-of-housing-and-urban-development-complaint-2026.pdf. the immediate dispute grew out of a september 25 announcement by president donald trump seeking to cancel nearly $1 billion in federal spending through a so-called pocket rescission. the associated press reported that the package included hud housing-counseling money along with other programs the administration criticized as unnecessary or ideologically driven: https://apnews.com/article/46b356590699e6225f783c74e7ee3597. in its complaint, new york says the administration’s public criticism focused on the perceived views of some grant recipients rather than the housing services the program funds. hud and the administration could contest that characterization in court. the potential impact is more concrete than the statewide grant total. new york’s attorney general says the state’s 2024 funding helped counseling organizations serve more than 7,000 households with one-on-one assistance, provide nearly 2,800 households with financial help to improve living conditions, prevent more than 250 evictions and nearly 300 foreclosures, and help almost 300 first-time buyers close on homes. those figures describe the prior year’s reported results; they do not establish how many households would lose services immediately if the 2026 grant is not restored. housing counseling is designed to help people navigate decisions that can determine whether they remain housed or can buy a home. hud’s current new york resource page directs residents facing foreclosure or seeking homeownership information to hud-approved counselors and related assistance: https://www.hud.gov/states/new-york?custom2=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f&og1=0968e9f6-512c-4705-af0f-eb20f79a820f. that background helps explain why the funding fight reaches beyond nonprofit budgets: counselors can work with borrowers and tenants before a missed payment, foreclosure filing or failed purchase becomes harder to resolve. james is asking the court to declare hud’s actions unlawful, require the department to maintain the program and preserve the unobligated money while the case proceeds. the complaint also asks the court to prevent the funds from being transferred, returned to the treasury or otherwise made unavailable in a way that would frustrate relief. the filing does not itself restore the grants. the next significant step is a court decision on whether to preserve the money and require hud to act; until then, new york’s 22 counseling organizations and the households they serve face uncertainty over the state’s expected federal support. new-york nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.excerpt: The citywide Halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to Open Streets and plazas across all five boroughs.
nyc-trick-or-streets-160-car-free-2026-0.text: nyc plans record 160 car-free trick-or-streets locations for october the citywide halloween program will bring free activities, school events and neighborhood walking tours to open streets and plazas across all five boroughs. new york city is expanding its trick-or-streets program to a record 160 car-free open streets and plazas this october, giving families in all five boroughs a month of halloween and fall events instead of a single-night celebration. the city says the locations will host trick-or-treating, face painting, live entertainment and games. the new york city department of transportation also plans to distribute about 75,000 pieces of candy. abc7 new york reported the same announcement wednesday, sept. 30, and described the program as the city's largest trick-or-streets event to date: https://abc7ny.com/post/mayor-mamdani-announces-nycs-largest-trick-streets-new-york/19892758/ the effort is designed around temporary changes to public space. community organizations, schools and cultural groups will turn selected streets and plazas into pedestrian-oriented gathering places, while the municipal art society of new york will offer free guided walking tours focused on neighborhood history, architecture and public spaces. street lab is also partnering with nyc dot and city schools on halloween-themed play and creative activities at selected school sites. five signature events anchor the schedule. brooklyn's hillel plaza celebration is set for oct. 22 from 2 to 6 p.m.; staten island's water street open street follows oct. 24 from noon to 5 p.m.; and queens' austin street open street is scheduled for oct. 25 from 2 to 7 p.m. manhattan's canal street open street and division plaza event is planned for oct. 28 from 3 to 7 p.m., while the bronx's james baldwin plaza event is scheduled for halloween, oct. 31, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. the department of transportation's event page lists additional neighborhood programs beginning oct. 3, including activities on vanderbilt avenue in brooklyn and castleton avenue on staten island. the calendar includes block parties, parades, dog events and school-linked programming throughout the month. nyc dot says individual events can be delayed or canceled because of weather, so families should check the official calendar before traveling: https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pedestrians/trickorstreets.shtml the month-long format matters because the program is also a test of how new york uses streets beyond their usual transportation role. the city's announcement says the participating groups will use the spaces for community celebrations and, in some cases, to support local foot traffic and neighborhood businesses. the setup gives organizers control over their own programming while the city coordinates the street closures and works with partner agencies. mayor zohran kwame mamdani and nyc dot commissioner mike flynn announced the expansion on sept. 30. this is the fifth year of trick-or-streets, according to nyc dot, which says the initiative is meant to add pedestrian space during one of the busiest periods for new york streets. the full map and schedule remain the best guide to what is happening on a particular block, because the 160 locations will not all be active at the same time. the primary announcement is available from the nyc mayor's office: https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-office/news/2026/09/mayor-mamdani-announces-largest-ever-trick-or-streets-with-160-c new-york new-york new york ny new york new york city, new york new york new york city halloween open streets nyc dot family events

ri-anchorhome-expansion-2026-10-06.excerpt: The third phase of RI AnchorHome expands the lender network after the state-backed program financed more than $45 million in first-home purchases, even as Rhode Island prices remain out of reach for many buyers.
ri-anchorhome-expansion-2026-10-06.text: rhode island adds three lenders to first-time homebuyer program after 119 purchases the third phase of ri anchorhome expands the lender network after the state-backed program financed more than $45 million in first-home purchases, even as rhode island prices remain out of reach for many buyers. rhode island is expanding its ri anchorhome mortgage program to three additional lenders after the initiative helped finance 119 first-time home purchases totaling more than $45 million, state treasurer james diossa announced tuesday. baycoast bank, bristol county savings bank and westerly community credit union will join the program as it enters a third phase. the announcement came from the [rhode island office of the general treasurer](https://treasury.ri.gov/press-releases/treasurer-diossa-announces-ri-anchorhome-expansion-after-helping-more-100-rhode). the expansion is aimed at widening access rather than replacing the private mortgage market. under ri anchorhome, an eligible first-time buyer applies through a participating bank or credit union. if the lender approves the mortgage, the state deposits matching funds at that institution. the lender still issues and services the loan; the state is not the borrower’s mortgage company. treasury says the structure gives participating institutions more room to offer affordable terms while keeping lending decisions with the financial institution. the program’s headline terms are a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage with a starting interest rate of 3.99%, subject to market conditions, and no private mortgage insurance. buyers may also use down-payment and closing-cost assistance, and homeownership counseling is required. those terms are significant for households trying to manage the upfront cost of a purchase, but the program is not a universal subsidy: buyers must meet the program’s first-time-homebuyer and lender requirements, and an advertised starting rate can change with market conditions. the three original participating institutions were navigant credit union, centreville bank and banknewport. the new lenders add geographic and institutional reach to a program that began in december 2025. [what's up newp](https://whatsupnewp.com/2026/10/states-first-time-homebuyer-program-adds-three-lenders-after-financing-119-purchases/) reported that the average ri anchorhome loan is about $383,000, while the average purchase price for the financed homes is just above $400,000. those figures describe the program’s borrowers to date; they are not a statewide home-price average or a promise that every applicant will receive the same loan size. the timing reflects the gap between the program’s growing use and rhode island’s broader affordability problem. housingworks ri executive director brenda clement, cited in the independent report, said the state’s median single-family home price had risen 5.3% to $499,900 and that average rent for a two-bedroom apartment had reached $2,358. the figures help explain why a lower-cost mortgage pathway may matter, while also showing its limits: a program that has financed 119 purchases is operating within a housing market where the typical home costs more than the average anchorhome purchase. ri anchorhome uses public deposits through the state’s community deposit program and operates under the oversight of the state investment commission. treasury’s program information says the deposits are collateralized and subject to safety, liquidity and reporting requirements. the state is leveraging its financial position to influence the terms available through private lenders, not directly taking ownership risk on the homes or guaranteeing that a buyer will be approved. for prospective buyers, the next step is to contact one of the participating lenders and review eligibility, income limits, loan limits and counseling requirements before relying on the advertised rate. treasury’s [program page](https://treasury.ri.gov/programs/anchorhome) says ri anchorhome is for first-time buyers purchasing a primary residence in rhode island and lists maximum loan amounts of $525,000 for a single-family home and $575,000 for a two-family home. it also says household income is capped at 110% of statewide income limits and that a borrower cannot own another residential property at closing. the state’s announcement did not set a deadline for the new lenders to begin taking applications, so availability may depend on each institution’s rollout. what is clear is the policy direction: rhode island is adding private partners after an initial group of lenders moved more than 100 buyers into homeownership, while officials present the state-deposit model as one tool for a market where rents and home prices continue to pressure working households. the program’s results will be measured not only by the number of additional lenders, but by whether qualified buyers can actually close on homes they can sustain over time. rhode-island housing housing ri providence rhode island rhode island providence homeownership first-time buyers mortgages housing affordability ri ri-arts-climate-grants-2026-10-02.excerpt: The new program will fund artist-led projects that make climate information more accessible, with applications due Nov. 2 and work scheduled for 2027.
ri-arts-climate-grants-2026-10-02.text: rhode island opens arts-and-climate grants with $5,000 maximum award the new program will fund artist-led projects that make climate information more accessible, with applications due nov. 2 and work scheduled for 2027. rhode island artists and artist groups can now apply for a new grant program intended to turn climate information into public-facing art, stories and experiences. the rhode island state council on the arts, working with the executive climate change coordinating council advisory board, opened applications oct. 1 for the arts and climate grant. the application deadline is nov. 2 at 11:59 p.m., according to risca’s [grant guidelines](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate). the program is designed for projects that help residents understand climate change and participate in conversations about how communities should respond. risca says eligible work can address mitigation topics such as energy-efficient buildings, renewable energy, public transit, electric vehicles and heat pumps, or resilience issues such as flooding, extreme heat, stronger storms, sea-level rise, wetlands and community resilience hubs. the goal is not simply to decorate a climate campaign; the agency says artists may act as community connectors who gather local perspectives and carry those experiences back to state climate planners. awards can be as large as $5,000, although the grant page warns that partial awards are common. a partial award must be at least half of the request or $1,000, whichever is higher. the money is intended for projects taking place in rhode island between jan. 1 and dec. 30, 2027. risca expects to notify applicants in mid-december, with final reports due jan. 31, 2028. the first cycle is backed by $40,000 that the ec4 advisory board allocated to its partnership with risca from an $80,000 climate-communication award, according to the [program description](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate). the eligibility rules place the emphasis on rhode island residents working as the primary artistic force behind their projects. applicants must be at least 18, have lived in the state for at least one year and be legally resident in the united states with a tax identification number. groups of artists may apply, but the work must be artist-instigated and organized outside an institution’s formal program. projects may include a public performance, exhibition, curriculum, video, mural, brochure or other format, but risca says a pilot or public sharing is required when the proposal involves planning or curriculum development. the program’s structure reflects a practical problem in climate policy: technical plans can be difficult to understand even when they describe changes that affect daily life. rhode island’s climate agencies are working across issues that residents encounter locally, from coastal flooding and stormwater to home energy costs, transportation and heat. risca says projects should prioritize frontline communities, include community voices and use two-way engagement. that gives artists room to work at a neighborhood scale rather than requiring a statewide campaign or a large institutional production. the funding also comes with limits. grants cannot pay for capital construction or renovations, debt, regranting, prizes or events that are inaccessible to the public. applicants cannot use the program for work that is part of an undergraduate or graduate degree, and they cannot seek support for the same project through another risca grant, except for the agency’s general operating support for artists. awardees must credit risca and the ec4 advisory board in their marketing materials. risca will offer an online information session oct. 6 from 3 to 4 p.m. and another oct. 14 from 6 to 7 p.m., followed by drop-in support hours later in october and on the deadline day. the oct. 6 session will include an overview, a walkthrough of the application and time for questions, according to the [event listing](https://arts.ri.gov/events/arts-and-climate-grant-information-session). applications are submitted through risca’s online grant system. questions about the program can be sent to risca.contact@arts.ri.gov. the grant is administered by risca, but its climate-policy connection runs through ec4, the state council established under rhode island’s climate laws to coordinate mitigation and adaptation work. the [ec4 advisory board](https://climatechange.ri.gov/ri-executive-climate-change-coordinating-council-ec4/advisory-board) includes municipal representatives and members with expertise in economic policy, workforce development, natural and cultural resources, energy, education, public health and housing. the new grant therefore creates a small but concrete channel for residents’ creative work to inform the state’s broader resilience conversation. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri providence rhode island rhode island providence arts climate change grants risca environmental resilience

ri-ccri-uri-rn-to-bs-program-2026-10-02.excerpt: The new RN-to-BS program lets eligible CCRI nursing alumni pursue a bachelor’s degree online while continuing to work, with lower tuition and scholarship opportunities highlighted by the schools.
ri-ccri-uri-rn-to-bs-program-2026-10-02.text: ccri, uri launch online degree path for rhode island nurses the new rn-to-bs program lets eligible ccri nursing alumni pursue a bachelor’s degree online while continuing to work, with lower tuition and scholarship opportunities highlighted by the schools. the community college of rhode island and the university of rhode island have launched a fully online pathway for registered nurses who want to earn a bachelor of science degree without stepping away from their jobs. the schools announced the rn-to-bs program after an oct. 1 signing ceremony in warwick, describing it as a response to the state’s need for a stronger and more flexible nursing pipeline. [uri’s announcement](https://www.uri.edu/news/2026/10/uri-ccri-announce-new-rn-to-bs-program-to-strengthen-rhode-islands-nursing-workforce/) was posted oct. 2. the program is aimed at graduates of ccri’s associate degree in nursing program and is designed around the schedules of practicing nurses. uri and ccri say the new track combines online coursework with a lower tuition rate for the rn-to-bs program and scholarship opportunities. that matters in a workforce where returning to school can otherwise require a nurse to reduce hours, commute to campus or delay further education until family and work responsibilities ease. the schools say the arrangement can begin before students finish their associate-level training. eligible ccri nursing students may receive conditional admission to uri after completing their first full semester in ccri’s nursing program, then move into uri’s bachelor’s curriculum after graduation. ccri graduates who are already working can apply through uri online; the program’s admissions page says applicants generally need an associate degree or diploma from an acen-accredited nursing program, a 2.6 minimum cumulative grade-point average and an active, unrestricted u.s. nursing license. ccri students in their final semester may apply before submitting that license, but must provide proof of licensure by the end of their first uri semester. [uri’s program page](https://web.uri.edu/online/programs/undergraduate/nursing-rn-to-bs/) says the degree is an education pathway and does not itself lead to professional licensure. uri’s published program information lists 24 core credit hours that can be completed in as little as 15 months, while the full bachelor’s degree requires 120 total credits after nursing, general education, statistics and pharmacology requirements are met. the school lists a current tuition figure of $631 per credit based on the 2025-26 academic year and notes that rates can change. students from rhode island, connecticut, massachusetts, new jersey and new york are currently eligible to apply through uri online, subject to the program’s other requirements. the partnership gives the state’s two public institutions a shared way to connect community-college nursing preparation with a four-year degree. uri nursing dean danny willis said in the university announcement that baccalaureate-prepared nurses are associated with improved quality and safety outcomes, including lower risks of mortality and hospital readmission in research cited by the program. those findings are presented by the university as part of the case for expanding the number of nurses with bachelor’s degrees; they are not a guarantee about outcomes for any individual hospital or graduate. [providence business news](https://pbn.com/ccri-uri-launch-online-degree-pathway-for-registered-nurses/) independently reported that the pathway will allow ccri associate-degree nursing graduates to move into uri’s bachelor’s curriculum online while continuing to work. the newspaper also identified rhode island gov. dan mckee, state sen. hanna gallo and state rep. david bennett among officials connected to the announcement. the next practical step for prospective students is to review uri’s admissions requirements and the nov. 24 application deadline listed on the program page for classes beginning jan. 5, 2027. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri warwick warwick, rhode island rhode island nursing higher education ccri university of rhode island

ri-domestic-violence-grant-ruling-2026-0.excerpt: A final ruling led by the Rhode Island Coalition Against Domestic Violence removes federal conditions that providers said threatened funding for shelters, crisis response and legal assistance nationwide.
ri-domestic-violence-grant-ruling-2026-0.text: rhode island federal court voids doj grant conditions in survivor-services case a final ruling led by the rhode island coalition against domestic violence removes federal conditions that providers said threatened funding for shelters, crisis response and legal assistance nationwide. a federal judge in rhode island has set aside u.s. department of justice grant conditions that domestic-violence and sexual-assault service providers said could restrict who they serve and how they operate. the sept. 29 summary-judgment ruling in providence gives a rhode island-led coalition of 25 state organizations a final judgment in a case that reached well beyond the state. the order by u.s. district judge melissa r. dubose says the department did not adequately explain its decision to attach the conditions to grants administered through the office on violence against women and the office of justice programs. rhode island current reported that the court found no sufficient, contemporaneous explanation showing that officials had meaningfully considered the conditions’ effects on providers and survivors. the [public court record](https://ecf.rid.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show%5fpublic%5fdoc?2025cv0279-78=) is the controlling document. the challenged requirements touched on politically contested issues including diversity, equity and inclusion programs, gender identity and service to immigrants. the rhode island coalition against domestic violence and its partners argued that the federal government was using grant eligibility to impose new policy requirements without the reasoning required by the administrative procedure act. the [aclu of rhode island’s case update](https://www.riaclu.org/news/rhode-island-court-rules-in-favor-of-domestic-violence-and-sexual-assault-survivors-protecting-crucial-grants-to-support-victims-of-violence-nationwide/) says later conditions also could have prevented providers from serving some noncitizen survivors or people unable to immediately prove citizenship. that distinction matters because these grants support practical services rather than only administrative projects. rhode island current described the federally funded work as including legal help, housing assistance and crisis counseling. the programs are rooted in the violence against women act, the 1994 federal law that established a continuing national role in supporting services for people affected by domestic and sexual violence. the doj’s [fiscal-year 2026 award guidance](https://www.justice.gov/ovw/award-condition-general-appropriations-law-restrictions-use-federal-award-funds-fy2026) separately shows how broadly the department applies conditions to grants made under its funding notices. the case began in 2025 after the coalition challenged the grant terms. a federal court first blocked an earlier set of restrictions, according to the aclu, and the department later added conditions involving immigration status and other subjects. in april 2026, the court issued preliminary relief while the claims proceeded. the september ruling now resolves the merits of the challenge by vacating the conditions rather than leaving providers to operate under a temporary pause. rhode island’s regional role is unusually broad. the plaintiff coalition includes the massachusetts coalition against sexual assault and domestic violence, the maine coalition to end domestic violence and the vermont network against domestic and sexual violence, along with organizations from other states. the [rhode island current report](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/09/29/ri-federal-judge-strikes-down-trump-grant-restrictions-for-domestic-violence-groups/) lists 25 plaintiff organizations representing 22 states and the district of columbia. the court’s remedy is also broader than a ruling limited to one rhode island provider. the order explains that setting aside the challenged conditions as a whole is necessary because a provider-by-provider remedy would be impractical. that means the decision addresses the grant terms themselves, while leaving the underlying federal programs and ordinary grant requirements in place. it does not decide every dispute over federal funding or guarantee that individual providers will receive a particular award. the immediate effect is to remove the disputed certifications and restrictions that the plaintiffs said could force a choice between accepting federal money and altering survivor services. the public sources reviewed for this report did not identify a government appeal or a new replacement policy after the judgment. providers and advocates will still have to follow the remaining statutory and grant-administration rules, but the contested conditions can no longer serve as the basis for withholding these awards under this case’s ruling. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri providence providence, rhode island rhode island domestic violence sexual assault federal court doj grants survivor services administrative procedure act

ri-fema-firefighter-grants-2026-10-05.excerpt: The awards will replace aging apparatus, upgrade breathing equipment and radios, and expand training in communities from Providence to Prudence Island.
ri-fema-firefighter-grants-2026-10-05.text: rhode island departments win $4.54m in federal firefighter grants the awards will replace aging apparatus, upgrade breathing equipment and radios, and expand training in communities from providence to prudence island. rhode island fire departments and a statewide training academy will receive $4,538,706 in federal grants for equipment, vehicles and instruction, a package that officials say will improve both firefighter safety and emergency response across the state. the awards were announced by rhode island's congressional delegation and detailed in reporting by [rhode island current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/05/fema-awards-more-than-4-5m-to-rhode-island-fire-departments/). providence received the largest award, $1,849,284. the city plans to spend nearly $1.5 million on new self-contained breathing apparatus, commonly called air-paks, according to city information reported by rhode island current. the remaining money will support nationally standardized supervisory training for lieutenants, captains and chief officers. the department expects to buy the breathing equipment within the next few months and put it into service in early 2027; it has two years to spend the award after accepting it. the grants also target apparatus that can determine how quickly a department reaches a fire or medical call. woonsocket will receive $1 million for a new aerial ladder truck to replace an obsolete vehicle that has become difficult and expensive to repair. coventry will receive $499,177 for an ambulance to replace a central coventry fire district vehicle with more than 250,000 miles, the delegation's [official announcement](https://www.whitehouse.senate.gov/news/release/ri-delegation-delivers-nearly-4-5-million-for-local-firefighters/) said. other awards are smaller but address specific gaps. west warwick will use $339,932 to update hose and nozzle equipment on a frontline engine and buy two cardiac monitors. the prudence island volunteer fire department will receive $255,015 for 34 portable radios. in lincoln, lime rock fire department will get $99,840 for cardiac monitor-defibrillators, while quinnville fire district will get $57,191 for four portable radios and a thermal-imaging camera. newport will receive $68,181 for three lucas mechanical cpr devices. the rhode island fire training academy will receive $370,086 for a fire-truck simulator, three forcible-entry doors, 15 self-contained breathing apparatuses and 40 reflective helmet covers. the simulator and practice equipment are intended for training rather than frontline deployment, but they matter to departments that need recruits and current firefighters to practice high-risk operations in a controlled setting. the award also gives the academy equipment that can be used by firefighters from multiple communities rather than a single department. the money comes through the federal assistance to firefighters grant program. the [u.s. fire administration](https://www.usfa.fema.gov/a-z/grants/) says the program supports eligible career and volunteer departments, emergency medical organizations and state fire-training academies with equipment, training, firefighter health and safety initiatives, and efforts to maintain a trained frontline workforce. the grants are competitive: the rhode island delegation said awards are evaluated based on need, project scope, community impact and application merit. the statewide announcement combines awards that fema released separately in late september and early october. that timing explains why the grant package includes a mix of purchases rather than one coordinated state project. providence's planned air-paks and woonsocket's ladder truck address the most visible equipment needs, while radios, cardiac monitors and thermal-imaging equipment can improve communication, patient care and scene awareness in smaller departments and volunteer organizations. the awards do not immediately put new vehicles or equipment into service. departments must accept the grants, complete purchasing and follow the program's performance requirements. providence has supplied the clearest schedule so far, with new breathing equipment expected early next year; the other communities' delivery dates were not announced in the sources reviewed for this report. the practical impact will depend on how quickly each recipient can complete procurement and training.
