the congressional announcement said rhode island fire departments and other first responders have received more than $43 million through fema's assistance to firefighters, staffing for adequate fire and emergency response, and fire prevention and safety programs over the last three years. it also said the current round was supported by $648 million in fiscal 2025 federal funding for competitive fire grants nationwide. for rhode island residents, the new awards translate that national program into more specific local changes: safer breathing gear in providence, a replacement ladder truck in woonsocket, a high-mileage ambulance replacement in coventry and updated communications and medical tools across the state. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri rhode island rhode island fema fire departments public safety emergency response

ri-first-circuit-nea-arts-funding-2026-1.excerpt: The appeal asks whether the federal arts agency may disadvantage grant applications it views as promoting ‘gender ideology’ after a Rhode Island judge found the policy violated the First Amendment and administrative law.
ri-first-circuit-nea-arts-funding-2026-1.text: first circuit weighs rhode island arts group’s challenge to nea funding restrictions the appeal asks whether the federal arts agency may disadvantage grant applications it views as promoting ‘gender ideology’ after a rhode island judge found the policy violated the first amendment and administrative law. a rhode island-led challenge to the federal government’s rules for arts grants reached the first circuit court of appeals on wednesday, putting a providence-based cultural organization at the center of a broader dispute over whether agencies may condition public funding on a project’s viewpoint. the court’s [official oral-argument record](https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/doar/search-results) lists rhode island latino arts v. national endowment for the arts as case 25-2113, argued oct. 7 in boston. the appeal concerns the national endowment for the arts’ response to an executive order directing federal agencies to ensure that federal funds are not used to promote what the order calls “gender ideology.” the nea initially required applicants to acknowledge that condition. after the organizations sued, the agency withdrew that first version and later adopted a process under which its chairperson could consider whether a proposed project promoted gender ideology when making the final funding decision. the policy said that factor would not be the sole reason to deny an application, but it could count against approval and could not count in the project’s favor, according to the [rhode island federal district court’s decision](https://www.riaclu.org/app/uploads/2025/03/decision-%e2%80%93-rila-v.-nea-1.pdf). u.s. district judge william e. smith ruled in september 2025 that the final policy violated the first amendment because it treated nea-funded art as private speech and assigned negative weight to a viewpoint about gender identity. he also ruled that the policy violated the administrative procedure act, finding that the agency had not adequately explained its decision or tied the restriction to the criteria congress gave the nea. the order enjoined the government from applying the viewpoint-based standard to the plaintiffs and vacated the plan. the court rejected the plaintiffs’ separate fifth amendment claim, so the ruling was only partly in their favor. rhode island latino arts is a statewide nonprofit based in providence and central falls that promotes and preserves latino art, history and culture. its programs include artists’ networks, public art, oral histories and community events. the group joined the case with national queer theater, the theater offensive and theatre communications group. in a [statement released after the hearing](https://www.riaclu.org/news/first-circuit-hears-arguments-in-case-challenging-viewpoint-based-penalties-in-federal-funding-for-the-arts/), rila executive director marta v. martínez said artists should not have to choose between access to public funding and telling their stories fully. that is the plaintiffs’ position, not a finding by the appeals court. the federal government is defending a different understanding of the grant program. the aclu of rhode island said the government argues that its funding decisions are government speech and that considering viewpoints is consistent with the law establishing the nea. a case summary from the [institute for free speech](https://www.ifs.org/podcast/free-speech-arguments-episode-55-can-the-government-withhold-arts-funding-based-on-viewpoint/) describes the government’s appeal as raising three questions: whether the district court misapplied the administrative procedure act, whether the policy is facially unconstitutional and whether the remedy was too broad. those arguments remain contested; the first circuit has not ruled on them. the dispute matters beyond one grant cycle because the nea is a national funding agency, while rhode island latino arts is a local organization whose work connects artists with schools, libraries, museums and community spaces. the lower court’s reasoning says the government may support private expression without turning the funded work into the government’s own message, but it may not then downgrade applications because officials disfavor a viewpoint. the government’s position would give the agency more room to treat the message of a proposed project as part of its funding judgment. the first circuit’s decision could clarify how first amendment and administrative-law limits apply when federal agencies distribute competitive grants. the aclu of rhode island said the ruling could affect funding restrictions in areas beyond the arts, while the case record shows that the panel is also considering the statutory and remedial questions separately from the constitutional issue. wednesday’s argument produced no immediate decision. the court will issue its ruling later, and the parties’ filings and the district court injunction—not campaign statements or predictions about the outcome—will determine what happens to the challenged policy in the meantime. rhode-island courts courts ri providence providence, rhode island rhode island providence first circuit national endowment for the arts arts funding first amendment federal courts

ri-general-election-registration-deadlin.excerpt: Eligible Rhode Islanders have until 4 p.m. Sunday to register or update a voter record for the Nov. 3 general election, with mail-ballot and early-voting deadlines close behind.
ri-general-election-registration-deadlin.text: rhode island voter registration deadline arrives sunday for november election eligible rhode islanders have until 4 p.m. sunday to register or update a voter record for the nov. 3 general election, with mail-ballot and early-voting deadlines close behind. rhode island’s deadline to register to vote or update a voter record for the nov. 3 general election arrives sunday, oct. 4. eligible residents must act by 4 p.m. to participate in the statewide election, according to the rhode island department of state and the state’s 2026 election calendar. the deadline applies 30 days before election day and covers local, state and federal contests on the november ballot. the state says residents can use the online voter-registration portal at [vote.ri.gov](https://vote.ri.gov/) or work with their local board of canvassers. the [rhode island board of elections registration guidance](https://elections.ri.gov/voter-resources) says an online registration or record update requires a rhode island driver’s license or state identification card. if an applicant does not have either document, the portal generates a form to print and mail to the local board. the board of elections also provides english and spanish paper forms. first-time applicants face an additional identification step under the federal help america vote act. the board of elections says applicants should provide a valid rhode island driver’s-license or state-id number, or the last four digits of a social security number if they have not been issued a rhode island license or id. people who cannot provide those numbers may still register, but the state says they will need to present an accepted identification document before registering, before voting or at the polls. the agency lists documents such as a passport, student or employee id, utility bill, bank statement, lease or government document. for people who need to file a paper form sunday, the department of state published a list of drop-off sites operating around rhode island. examples include the public safety complex in providence, the blackstone valley visitors center in pawtucket, cranston city hall, the newport city hall municipal drop box and police or town facilities in communities including barrington, bristol, cumberland, middletown, warwick and woonsocket. hours vary by location: some open in the morning, while others accept forms from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. the full list and local hours are in the [state’s deadline notice](https://www.sos.ri.gov/article?articleno=51498), and residents should check the listing before traveling. the deadline comes as rhode island’s electorate moves from the september primary into a general election that includes congressional, statewide and local races. more than 695,000 eligible voters were registered in september, according to data cited by [rhode island current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/09/30/voter-registration-deadline-is-sunday-oct-4/) and maintained by the department of state. about 52% were unaffiliated, 34% were democrats and 14% were republicans at that point, figures that describe the registration file rather than likely turnout or the outcome of any race. registration is the first of several fall deadlines. registered voters who want to vote by mail must submit an application by 4 p.m. tuesday, oct. 13, according to the [state election calendar](https://vote.sos.ri.gov/forms/elections/guides/2026eleccal.pdf). the application is available online or on paper. in-person early voting begins oct. 14 and continues through 4 p.m. monday, nov. 2, at locations designated by each city or town. the state says voters should confirm those locations and hours with their local board of canvassers or through the department of state’s election website. on election day, polls are scheduled to open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. across rhode island, except in new shoreham, where polls open at 9 a.m. anyone in line at closing time may still vote, according to the official calendar. residents can check their registration status and polling place at [vote.sos.ri.gov](https://vote.sos.ri.gov/) before heading to a registration site or making a voting plan. the state’s online resources remain the best source for any change to a deadline, address or local procedure. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri providence providence, rhode island rhode island elections voter registration 2026 general election voting access

ri-governor-campaign-cash-divide-2026-10.excerpt: New filings show independent Ken Block with $263,000 on hand, Democrat Helena Foulkes with $214,000 and Republican Aaron Guckian with just over $7,000 as early voting approaches.
ri-governor-campaign-cash-divide-2026-10.text: rhode island governor race enters final month with a stark campaign-cash divide new filings show independent ken block with $263,000 on hand, democrat helena foulkes with $214,000 and republican aaron guckian with just over $7,000 as early voting approaches. rhode island’s three major candidates for governor are entering the final month of the general-election campaign with sharply different financial positions. reports due tuesday to the [rhode island board of elections](https://elections.ri.gov/campaign-finance/public-info) show independent ken block with the most cash available for the closing stretch, democrat helena foulkes close behind and republican aaron guckian operating with a much smaller reserve. the figures offer a measurable look at the resources each campaign can use before voters begin casting ballots. according to [wpri’s review of the filings](https://www.aol.com/articles/block-leads-foulkes-campaign-cash-034332000.html), block reported about $263,000 in his account as of monday. that total included $190,000 in personal loans he made to his campaign during september. his report covered july 1 through oct. 5, during which he raised $63,000 and spent $80,000. the personal-loan figure is important context: cash on hand describes what a campaign can spend, but it does not mean all of that money came from outside donors. foulkes reported $214,000 on hand. her filing covered the shorter period from sept. 2 through oct. 5, after she won the democratic primary against gov. dan mckee. wpri reported that she raised $381,000 and spent $545,000 during that period, while her campaign has spent more than $5 million this year. the new balance suggests a campaign that has had access to substantial support but also has been spending heavily as it moved from a competitive primary into the general election. guckian, the republican nominee, reported a little more than $7,000 on hand after raising roughly that amount and spending about $12,000 during the same sept. 2-to-oct. 5 period, wpri reported. that leaves him with considerably less money for advertising, field organizing and voter contact than either of his two major opponents. the filing does not determine the election’s outcome, but it narrows the amount of paid communication his campaign can deploy without a major new infusion of money. the party accounts widen the gap. wpri reported that the rhode island democratic party had about $314,000 in its state account, compared with roughly $22,000 for the republican party. the democratic governors association also put $500,000 into an affiliated rhode island group supporting foulkes, according to a board of elections filing cited in the report. those party and outside resources are separate from the candidates’ own balances, but they can still affect the volume and reach of campaign activity voters see. the financial reports arrive as the race is also being shaped by the question of whether guckian should remain in the contest. [the boston globe reported](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/2026/10/06/metro/rhode-island-governor-race-foulkes-guckian-block-election/) that block and some of his supporters have pressed guckian to leave, arguing that block would have a stronger chance against foulkes in a two-way race. guckian has said he will stay in the race, and the globe noted that it is already too late to remove his name from the ballot. that dispute makes the cash figures part of a broader argument about whether the november contest is effectively three-sided or could become a one-on-one race. foulkes won the sept. 9 democratic primary over mckee by 62% to 38%, according to wpri’s account, and the report said she won all 39 cities and towns. since then, democratic leaders and organized labor have begun consolidating behind her, while block has tried to position himself as the principal alternative. the candidates’ fundraising reports cannot measure enthusiasm, volunteer strength or issue preferences, but they do show how much financial capacity each campaign brings into the period when many voters will first focus on the race. early voting begins oct. 14, and the general election is nov. 3. the three candidates are scheduled to take part in a televised debate on oct. 20 from rhode island college, according to wpri. between now and then, campaigns will be competing for attention across television, digital media, mail and local organizing. the next meaningful test will be whether block can turn his cash advantage into broader support, whether foulkes can maintain her lead while rebuilding her account, and whether guckian can raise enough to remain visible through election day. rhode-island elections elections ri providence rhode island rhode island governor helena foulkes ken block aaron guckian campaign finance early voting 2026 election

ri-newport-hellewell-cold-case-arrest-20.excerpt: William Morton, 61, was held without bail after Rhode Island investigators charged him in the killing of Hillary Hellewell, whose death had gone unsolved for more than four decades.
ri-newport-hellewell-cold-case-arrest-20.text: dna investigation leads to arrest in 1985 newport murder case william morton, 61, was held without bail after rhode island investigators charged him in the killing of hillary hellewell, whose death had gone unsolved for more than four decades. a 41-year-old newport murder investigation has produced an arrest after rhode island authorities used new dna analysis and investigative work to identify a potential suspect. william morton, 61, of smithfield was arraigned tuesday in newport county district court and charged with the 1985 murder of hillary hellewell, a 22-year-old woman from jamestown. the rhode island attorney general’s office announced the case with newport police and emphasized that the charge is an allegation; morton is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. the [attorney general’s release](https://riag.ri.gov/press-releases/former-newport-man-charged-alleged-1985-murder-following-cold-case-investigation) says morton was held without bail and is scheduled for a status conference oct. 20. court documents cited by the attorney general’s office say hellewell was killed on or about may 19, 1985, in newport. [rhode island current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/06/ags-cold-case-unit-cracks-1985-newport-murder-case/) reported that her body was found early that morning on anthony street, near the newport public library. the case went cold after the initial investigation, leaving hellewell’s family without a criminal defendant for decades. the arrest does not resolve the case in court, but it changes the practical posture of an investigation that had remained open without a publicly identified suspect. the investigation was reopened in 2023 by the newport police department and the attorney general’s cold case unit. according to the state, investigators used new forensic dna analysis and investigative techniques to develop morton as a potential suspect. rhode island current’s [account](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/06/ags-cold-case-unit-cracks-1985-newport-murder-case/), based on an affidavit filed in district court, describes a process that moved from older biological evidence to family-related dna leads and then to a sample allegedly recovered from a water bottle morton left at a woonsocket concert. the affidavit says the state department of health later found that the bottle’s dna profile was consistent with evidence from the 1985 case. those are allegations presented in court documents, not findings after a trial. the forensic work illustrates why older cases can change even when the original investigation produced no arrest. [rhode island current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/06/ags-cold-case-unit-cracks-1985-newport-murder-case/) reported that evidence had been tested before but did not generate a match in the national dna database. later testing by a private laboratory produced relatives’ partial genetic links, investigators followed those leads, and a sample collected during surveillance supplied another comparison. the state has not said that dna evidence alone proves the charge; prosecutors will have to present the evidence and its chain of custody as the case moves forward. the case also highlights the role of rhode island’s cold case unit, which was created after attorney general peter neronha sought state funding in 2023. the unit includes prosecutors, investigators and a forensic genealogist who work with local police departments on unsolved homicides and unidentified-remains cases. the [unit’s public overview](https://riag.ri.gov/coldcase) says its work includes reexamining evidence, developing witnesses and applying modern technology to old cases. the attorney general’s office says the unit has documented more than 150 cold cases and assisted on 13 cold-case homicide investigations since its creation. the prosecution now turns to the courts. morton was ordered held without bail and has a status conference set for oct. 20, according to the state. [rhode island current](https://rhodeislandcurrent.com/2026/10/06/ags-cold-case-unit-cracks-1985-newport-murder-case/) reported that he entered no plea at the district court arraignment, as the felony case is expected to move to superior court. the public record will have to establish what happened in 1985, what the dna evidence can reliably show and whether the state can prove every element of murder beyond a reasonable doubt. until then, the arrest is a major investigative development, not a conviction. for newport and jamestown, the announcement connects a current criminal proceeding to a case that has shaped the memory of two communities for more than 40 years. the attorney general said hellewell’s family has asked for privacy. that request, and the presumption of innocence, are central to covering the case responsibly: the new evidence may offer a path toward an answer, but the legal process still has to test the accusation in open court. rhode-island public-safety public safety ri newport newport and jamestown, rhode island rhode island newport jamestown cold case dna evidence hillary hellewell criminal justice

ri-opioid-treatment-audit-medicaid-2026-.excerpt: A review of 100 sampled medication-assisted-treatment claims found every claim missed at least one federal or state requirement, while a separate billing review identified 6,347 potentially improper payments.
ri-opioid-treatment-audit-medicaid-2026-.text: rhode island audit finds gaps in opioid treatment records and $875,696 in potential medicaid overpayments a review of 100 sampled medication-assisted-treatment claims found every claim missed at least one federal or state requirement, while a separate billing review identified 6,347 potentially improper payments. a rhode island performance audit released wednesday found widespread documentation and service-delivery problems in the state’s opioid treatment programs, with every one of 100 sampled medication-assisted-treatment claims failing at least one federal or state requirement. the same review identified $875,696 in potential medicaid overpayments tied to daily methadone billing that should have been submitted as weekly bundled claims. the [rhode island office of the auditor general report](https://www.oag.ri.gov/reports-performance/opioidprovidercompliance-20261003.pdf), prepared with the u.s. department of health and human services office of inspector general, examined the state’s oversight of opioid treatment services from jan. 1, 2023, through dec. 31, 2024. five providers submitted claims for 274,412 medication-assisted-treatment services totaling $25.54 million during that period. auditors selected 100 services for detailed testing; the sample was designed to evaluate compliance, not to establish that every service delivered statewide was deficient. the problems covered core parts of treatment. auditors recorded 99 instances in which the sampled claims did not satisfy medication-assisted-treatment requirements, 95 problems with intake or five-year biopsychosocial assessments, 75 missing or incomplete six-month treatment-plan reviews and 70 failures involving required counseling sessions. they also found deficiencies in annual assessments, treatment plans, medical examinations and toxicology screening. the audit said 22 of the 100 client cases did not meet the minimum annual toxicology-testing requirement, and seven had no toxicology tests documented. the report describes opioid treatment programs as federally certified and state-licensed providers that dispense methadone and other medications while also providing counseling, medical evaluation and recovery support. rhode island rules require patients in maintenance treatment to receive random toxicology testing at least eight times per year, annual medical examinations and documented treatment planning. those records are not merely administrative paperwork: the auditor said missing examinations, counseling notes or safety instructions can make it harder to identify medical problems, monitor relapse risks, coordinate care and manage medication safely. the audit also estimated that 274,412 medication-assisted-treatment services during the review period, totaling $24.92 million, did not meet enough documented requirements to support medicaid reimbursement. that estimate is different from the $875,696 figure, which concerns a specific billing problem. auditors and federal investigators validated 6,347 claims in which providers billed daily methadone encounters instead of the required single weekly bundled claim. in some cases, providers submitted five to seven daily claims for one beneficiary in the same week, causing medicaid to pay more than the established bundled rate. the report calls the amount potential overpayments, not a final fraud finding. rhode island’s executive office of health and human services said a full investigation and data analysis of the relevant billing code had been completed and that corrective-action plans involving recoupments were under review. the agency also said it was reassessing its medicaid system configuration with gainwell technologies, updating billing guidance and planning quarterly surveillance of the code. the audit recommends reviewing all adjudicated and pending claims, recovering amounts determined to be improper and returning the federal share. the state behavioral-health department outlined a separate response to the clinical-documentation findings. it plans to keep biennial audits but add six-month post-audit reviews, routine unannounced visits and standardized documentation samples from all five providers. the department also said providers will conduct internal audits at least every six months, receive mandatory training and eventually be measured through a centralized compliance dashboard. providers that remain below a compliance threshold or show recurring deficiencies may be required to submit correction plans and face licensing or administrative action. providence business news independently reported the audit’s finding of 100 out of 100 sampled claims with compliance failures and the potential overpayment total. the report’s release comes after a separate june settlement in which journey to hope health and healing and its former chief executive agreed to pay $10.2 million to resolve federal and state allegations involving treatment services and medicaid claims; the justice department said that case concerned conduct from 2015 through 2021 and is not the same matter as the new audit. the next measurable test for rhode island will be whether the promised claims review, billing controls and provider monitoring produce recoveries and better documentation without disrupting access to treatment. the audit does not identify the individual patients whose records were sampled, and its findings do not mean every rhode island treatment provider or every patient encounter failed. they do show that the state’s existing oversight did not provide the assurance auditors expected across the sampled claims. for patients and families, the practical issue is whether the corrective steps improve continuity and safety in programs that play a central role in treating opioid-use disorder. for taxpayers, the open questions are how much of the potential overpayment is confirmed, how much is recovered and whether new system edits prevent the same billing pattern from recurring. rhode-island health health ri providence rhode island office of the auditor general, providence, rhode island rhode island opioid treatment medicaid methadone audits behavioral health public health

ri-providence-mother-toddler-stabbing-20.excerpt: Nelson Blanco faces two counts of assault with intent to commit murder after the Broad Street attack; police say investigators do not believe he knew the victims.
ri-providence-mother-toddler-stabbing-20.text: providence man charged after mother and 2-year-old daughter are stabbed nelson blanco faces two counts of assault with intent to commit murder after the broad street attack; police say investigators do not believe he knew the victims. a 46-year-old man has been charged after a mother and her 2-year-old daughter were stabbed wednesday afternoon near broad street and public street in providence, a case that sent both victims to a hospital and prompted a public pursuit of the suspect. the child was reported in critical condition wednesday night, while the mother was expected to recover, according to [the boston globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/07/metro/mother-and-toddler-stabbed-south-providence-police-say-ri/). providence police identified the defendant as nelson blanco. officers responded to the south providence area after the stabbing, which local reports placed at about 1:30 p.m. or shortly before 2 p.m. on wednesday. the [boston 25 news account](https://www.boston25news.com/news/local/suspect-taken-into-custody-after-mother-2-year-old-daughter-stabbed-providence/3kwvjqlmhvdrzesmxvq6w3o7tu/?outputtype=amp) said police chief oscar perez described the victims as a woman in her late 20s and a 2-year-old girl suffering from stab wounds. the arrest followed more than an immediate police response. [wcvb](https://www.wcvb.com/article/mother-child-stabbed-providence-rhode-island-october-8/74076432) reported that newly released video showed witnesses chasing a man down a nearby street after the attack. police said the suspect went into the basement of a home, where he was arrested. the account gives residents a clearer outline of how blanco was located, but it does not establish what happened inside the residence or how the attack began. the victims’ medical status has not been described consistently across the early reports because officials were still updating the case. the globe reported wednesday night that the toddler was in critical condition and that the mother was expected to be ok. wcvb said thursday morning that police had not released a new official condition update, while [whdh](https://whdh.com/news/man-charged-with-stabbing-mother-2-year-old-child-in-providence-ri/) reported that both victims had been taken to a hospital without listing their conditions. northeast news is not independently confirming either patient’s status. blanco faces two counts of assault with intent to commit murder, one involving the adult victim and one involving the child, according to police information reported by wcvb and whdh. the other listed charges are assault with a deadly weapon; breaking and entering into a dwelling occupied by a person over 60; possession of a knife during the commission of a crime of violence; and possession of a knife with a blade longer than 3 inches. those are allegations, not findings of guilt, and blanco is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. the charging documents’ breaking-and-entering count is listed alongside the stabbing charges, but police have not publicly explained how that allegation relates to the attack. investigators also said they had no evidence that blanco knew the mother or child. that leaves the relationship question, the reason for the encounter and the sequence of the violence unresolved. the globe reported that other children were nearby but were not injured. the case was scheduled to move into court thursday, with blanco expected to be arraigned in providence district court at 10 a.m. police also planned a morning update before the arraignment, according to wcvb. that proceeding should establish the formal charges presented to the court and provide the first public opportunity for information about custody and the next hearing, although it may not resolve the central investigative questions immediately. the location matters because the incident unfolded on a busy south providence corridor and witnesses, rather than police alone, were described as helping track the fleeing suspect. video and witness accounts may become part of the investigation, but their existence does not answer whether the victims were targeted or attacked at random. detectives still have to reconcile the public footage, statements from people at the scene, medical evidence and the defendant’s account. until those steps are complete, the most consequential facts remain the injuries, the charges and the unknown motive. rhode-island crime crime ri providence broad street and public street, providence, rhode island rhode island providence stabbing public safety criminal charges

ri-route10-i95-ramp-closure-october-2026.excerpt: RIDOT will shut the Route 10 South ramp to I-95 North from 9 p.m. Friday until before Monday’s morning commute, then shift the ramp entrance as the Providence-Cranston interchange rebuild continues.
ri-route10-i95-ramp-closure-october-2026.text: rhode island route 10-to-i-95 ramp closes friday night for interchange work ridot will shut the route 10 south ramp to i-95 north from 9 p.m. friday until before monday’s morning commute, then shift the ramp entrance as the providence-cranston interchange rebuild continues. drivers heading from route 10 south to interstate 95 north at the providence-cranston line should expect a weekend detour beginning friday night. the rhode island department of transportation says the ramp will close at 9 p.m. on oct. 2 and reopen before the morning commute on monday, oct. 5, while crews connect a newly built bridge to the roadway leading toward i-95 north. the schedule remains subject to weather and construction conditions, according to ridot’s [i-95 15 project update](https://www.dot.ri.gov/projects/the-i-95-15/). ridot’s signed detour sends drivers onto the ramp for i-95 south, then off at exit 31c for jefferson boulevard. from there, motorists will turn left onto jefferson boulevard and left again to reach the northbound i-95 on-ramp. that route adds decisions and turning movements to a connection many commuters use to move between cranston, providence and the broader interstate network, so drivers who normally make the route 10-to-i-95 north move will need to watch for temporary signs and allow extra time. the closure is only one step in the traffic plan. on friday, before the nighttime shutdown, ridot expects to shift the beginning of the route 10 south-to-i-95 north ramp about 100 feet from its current position. drivers will enter the ramp sooner after the shift, while the nearby on-ramp to i-95 south will not change. once the northbound ramp reopens, motorists will be using the new alignment rather than returning to the present entrance. more changes are planned for mid-october at the route 1, or elmwood avenue, northbound ramp to route 10 north. ridot says drivers will have to choose a lane based on where they are going after the merge: the right lane for i-95 north, or the left lane for route 10 toward providence and exit 1c for i-95 south. the department plans additional signs and pavement markings, and says that arrangement will remain through spring 2027. the providence journal reported sept. 25 that the work is part of a larger effort to turn the route 10 segment between park avenue and the i-95 interchange into a boulevard-style connection. the newspaper said the planned design is intended to create a direct link between elmwood avenue and park avenue, with a shared-use bike path and improved pedestrian connections to roger williams park. that broader street design means the current ramp closures are tied to a long construction sequence, not a short resurfacing job. the scale of the corridor helps explain why a weekend ramp closure can affect more than the immediate interchange. ridot says the i-95 15 project corridor between providence and warwick carries about 185,000 vehicles each day, including roughly 9,000 trucks and other heavy freight vehicles. the agency also identifies hospitals, businesses and universities along the route, making reliable access important for commuters, deliveries and regional trips even when the affected ramp is only one part of the highway system. the project is designed to address 15 bridges rated poor or fair but nearing poor condition along i-95 and route 10. ridot lists providence, cranston and warwick as the project locations, a projected cost of $779 million and a construction schedule running from 2024 through 2031. the department says a $251 million federal bridge investment program grant helps offset the cost. it also says the work will remove three of rhode island’s five most-traveled structurally deficient bridges from that list. for friday-night travelers, the immediate issue is the route 10 south ramp closure and the signed jefferson boulevard detour. for regular commuters, the more lasting change will be learning the shifted entrance and the later lane assignments near elmwood avenue. ridot says construction schedules and traffic patterns can change with weather, project needs and field conditions, so drivers should check the department’s travel information and follow the signs in place when they approach the interchange. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri cranston providence-cranston corridor rhode island providence cranston i-95 route 10 ridot road construction traffic

ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.excerpt: Fourteen districts and schools will use Rural Health Transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs.
ri-rural-health-cte-grants-2026-09-30.text: rhode island directs $5.48m to rural school healthcare career pathways fourteen districts and schools will use rural health transformation funds for healthcare training, from middle-school exploration to hands-on high school programs. rhode island is directing more than $5.48 million in federal rural health transformation program awards to 14 school districts and schools, creating or expanding healthcare career pathways in rural communities across the state. the rhode island department of education announced the awards wednesday at ponaganset high school in glocester. the department said the grants are designed to connect students with health careers in stages: career awareness in kindergarten through fifth grade, exploration in grades six through eight, and preparation for work or further study in grades nine through twelve. the announcement was also reported independently by [providence business news](https://pbn.com/foster-glocester-lands-largest-share-of-5-48m-rural-healthcare-cte-grants/). the money comes through the federal rural health transformation program, which is supported by the centers for medicare and medicaid services and the u.s. department of health and human services. rhode island says the broader program is intended to improve access to coordinated healthcare in rural communities. ride said its awards will reach the state’s 18 rural communities, while helping schools build relationships with healthcare providers and colleges. foster-glocester regional school district received the largest award, $1,360,343. the district plans to anchor its pathway at ponaganset with an on-campus physical therapy clinic, physical and occupational therapy programs, and a middle-school wellness initiative that introduces younger students to health careers. that design gives students a local setting to encounter the field before they have to choose a high school concentration or postsecondary program. other awards target distinct parts of the healthcare pipeline. burrillville schools received $928,574 for a biomedical sciences pathway and a new ems and health sciences learning center, with possible training in emergency medical services, nursing, phlebotomy, physical therapy and related fields. east greenwich public schools received $710,619 to launch what ride described as rhode island’s first pre-medicine career and technical education program, while modernizing learning spaces and adding work-based learning, medical simulation and ai-supported clinical tools. westerly public schools received $658,773 to improve its medical careers and ems pathway with simulation equipment, virtual-reality training, staffing and professional development. smithfield received $513,690 to expand biomedical sciences and add behavioral-health training. scituate received $318,191 to extend its biomedical pathway through the k-12 grades and add sports medicine, community health and emergency-response options. the remaining grants range from $25,604 for jamestown’s lawn school to $268,454 for narragansett high school, with projects also planned in chariho, exeter-west greenwich, little compton, north kingstown, north smithfield and at the greene school. the awards are arriving as rhode island expands its overall career-and-technical-education system. ride reported that the number of high-quality cte programs statewide has grown from 203 in 2019 to 365, while participation has increased from about 12,000 students to more than 20,000. those figures are the department’s comparison, not an independent evaluation of the new grants, and the announcement does not provide a single completion date for the 14 projects. the next phase will be local implementation: districts will have to turn the awards into courses, equipment, work-based learning and partnerships that students can actually use. for rural rhode island, the practical test will be whether the new pathways make healthcare careers visible earlier, provide meaningful clinical or technical experience, and create durable connections between schools, employers and the communities that need healthcare workers. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri glocester rural rhode island rhode island career and technical education rural health transformation program healthcare workforce public schools education funding

ri-tiverton-pfas-water-line-grant-2026-1.excerpt: The USDA award will help the North Tiverton Fire District begin extending public water to households whose private wells exceed Rhode Island's PFAS standard, while testing and the source investigation continue.
ri-tiverton-pfas-water-line-grant-2026-1.text: tiverton secures $1m grant for water line after pfas well contamination the usda award will help the north tiverton fire district begin extending public water to households whose private wells exceed rhode island's pfas standard, while testing and the source investigation continue. tiverton has secured $1 million in federal assistance to begin extending public water service to homes whose private wells have been contaminated with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or pfas. the money is being provided through the u.s. department of agriculture's emergency community water assistance program to the north tiverton fire district, according to a sept. 29 announcement from the offices of u.s. sens. jack reed and sheldon whitehouse and rep. gabe amo. the grant is aimed at the crandall road, bulgarmarsh road and stafford road areas, where rhode island officials are continuing to test private wells. the lawmakers' announcement said more than 100 wells tested so far had exceeded rhode island's 20-parts-per-trillion standard, with some results above 4,000 parts per trillion. the lawmakers had backed the district's application in a sept. 8 letter to agriculture secretary brooke rollins, asking for emergency funding to restore reliable drinking water to affected homeowners. the award does not resolve the wider water problem. [what's up newp](https://whatsupnewp.com/2026/10/tiverton-gets-1-million-in-federal-funding-for-emergency-water-line-after-pfas-contamination/) reported oct. 1 that the grant will start the public-water extension, while testing and planning continue for other households. the publication said the town's effort is focused on homes with the most serious contamination first. a separate providence journal report, republished by [aol](https://www.aol.com/articles/help-coming-tiverton-homeowners-contaminated-185020000.html), said town officials were seeking to put the first section in the ground before winter and had sent the project out to bid, but the full buildout will require additional money and coordination. tiverton's [municipal pfas information page](https://www.tiverton.ri.gov/363/pfas-information) identifies the crandall road area as the subject of continuing investigation and posts updates from sept. 15, sept. 22 and sept. 28. the town cautions that its concentration map shows the known or suspected area of impact, not a property-by-property finding. it tells residents to rely on rhode island department of environmental management laboratory results and state guidance rather than assuming a home is safe or contaminated based only on its location. ridem says on its [emerging-contaminants program page](https://dem.ri.gov/ecsdc-grants) that it detected pfas above the state maximum contaminant level in a private well near crandall road and offered free testing to homes within a quarter-mile of the fire station or the initial detection. the agency says it is providing filtration systems at no cost to homeowners whose results exceed 20 parts per trillion. in its statewide emerging-contaminants program, dem says it is testing more than 800 private wells in 26 communities and using activated-carbon or reverse-osmosis systems where eligible results are above the state standard. the suspected source in tiverton has not been established. local reporting has noted the investigation's proximity to tiverton fire station 3 and the historical use of pfas-containing firefighting foam, but the state has not confirmed that the station caused the contamination. that distinction matters as officials decide whether public water, household treatment or other remedies are appropriate for each property. for residents, the immediate change is a path toward a permanent water connection for at least the first phase of the response, rather than continued reliance on bottled water or individual treatment while results arrive. the lawmakers said construction is expected to be completed before the end of december, though the schedule remains dependent on design, bidding, permits and the district's work. tiverton says it will continue posting test results, water-delivery information and public updates as the investigation develops. rhode-island rhode-island rhode island ri tiverton tiverton, rhode island rhode island tiverton pfas drinking water private wells usda grants environmental health

vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.excerpt: Applications will open Oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000.
vt-ag-timber-disaster-aid-2026-10-01.text: vermont to open $31.7m disaster-aid program for farms and timber businesses applications will open oct. 26 for recovery payments tied to qualifying weather losses from 2023 and 2024, with first-phase awards covering up to 95% of eligible losses and capped at $75,000. vermont will begin accepting applications oct. 26 for a $31.7 million disaster-recovery program aimed at farms, forest landowners and logging contractors that suffered qualifying weather-related losses in 2023 or 2024. the state says the first phase will cover up to 95% of an applicant’s eligible losses, with a maximum payment of $75,000. [gov. phil scott’s office](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-317-million-vermont-agriculture-timber-disaster) announced the program sept. 30 with the vermont agency of agriculture, food & markets and the department of forests, parks and recreation. the program is built from federal block-grant funding authorized under the american relief act of 2025. vermont’s [legislative joint fiscal office](https://www.ljfo.vermont.gov/grants-reports/) separately lists a $31,771,557 usda farm service agency grant for compensation tied to crop, timber and livestock losses, including on-farm infrastructure and weather damage. the aid is designed for businesses that are still operating and can document both the loss and its connection to an eligible weather event. the state says applicants may seek reimbursement for damage that has already been repaired, rebuilt or replanted, or may commit to completing eligible restoration or replanting with the funds. the program is non-competitive: applicants who demonstrate eligible, otherwise-unmet losses are intended to receive a payment, subject to the program’s rules and available documentation. for agricultural producers, eligible categories may include damage to on-farm infrastructure, bare-ground practices needed after a weather event, future economic loss and market loss. for the forest economy, the program can cover standing-timber and harvested-timber losses, licensed-forester assessment costs, updates to forest stewardship plans and certain recovery costs for loggers reopening damaged harvest sites. those categories reflect the different ways floods, hard freezes, excessive moisture and other severe weather can disrupt a farm or a logging operation beyond the cost of one immediate repair. the program follows years of recovery pressure from vermont’s storms and floods. independent reporting by [vtdigger](https://vtdigger.org/2026/06/10/feds-approve-31-7-million-in-disaster-aid-for-flood-hit-vermont-farmers/) described the federal award as specialized relief for farmers with limited access to other federal disaster programs, including people facing infrastructure and market losses from the 2023 and 2024 events. the state’s current notice expands the practical reach to timber landowners and contracted loggers as well as agricultural producers. applicants should begin assembling ownership, lease or timber-sale records; parcel information; tax or business identification; descriptions of the damage; dated photographs; receipts, invoices, repair records or estimates; and records of other payments for the same loss. timber applicants may also need stand maps, forest-management information, timber-sale records, revenue documentation and a licensed forester assessment for some claims. the state says the online application window is expected to close dec. 31, with payments anticipated in early 2027. the first phase is not the entire program. vermont says a second phase will address larger infrastructure projects valued above $75,000 and up to $750,000 through a competitive grant process. receiving a phase-one payment will not by itself bar an applicant from phase two, but the second phase cannot pay for losses already covered by phase one or another funding source. the outstanding questions for producers are how many businesses will apply, how much documented loss the program will face and how quickly the state can turn the october filing window into payments. new-england new-england new england vt montpelier vermont vermont agriculture timber disaster assistance flood recovery weather losses farm economy

vt-agriculture-timber-disaster-assistanc.excerpt: The state program will reimburse up to 95% of eligible unmet losses from qualifying 2023 and 2024 weather events, with first-phase payments capped at $75,000.
vt-agriculture-timber-disaster-assistanc.text: vermont sets oct. 26 start for $31.7m farm and timber recovery program the state program will reimburse up to 95% of eligible unmet losses from qualifying 2023 and 2024 weather events, with first-phase payments capped at $75,000. vermont will begin accepting applications oct. 26 for a $31.7 million disaster-assistance program aimed at farms, forest landowners and logging contractors still recovering from qualifying weather-related losses in 2023 and 2024. the first phase will reimburse up to 95% of eligible unmet losses, with a maximum payment of $75,000, according to the [office of gov. phil scott](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-317-million-vermont-agriculture-timber-disaster). the vermont agriculture and timber disaster assistance program is designed for businesses that were operating in one of those two years, experienced a qualifying weather loss and are still operating now. applications are expected to remain open through dec. 31, and the state anticipates distributing payments in early 2027. the program is noncompetitive: applicants who document eligible unmet losses are to receive a payment, rather than competing for a limited pool of scored awards. the assistance is broad enough to reach several parts of a farm operation. the state says eligible agricultural losses may include damage to on-farm infrastructure, bare-ground practices, future economic loss and market loss. in a report on the launch, [wcax](https://www.wcax.com/2026/09/30/vermont-launches-31m-flood-recovery-fund-farmers-foresters/) described the program as a way to help agricultural and forestry businesses catch up on costs connected to flooding and recovery. that framing matters because the qualifying events are in the past; the program is intended to cover documented losses that may already have been repaired, rebuilt or replanted as well as approved work that has not yet been completed. timber applicants face a different documentation burden. the [vermont department of forests, parks and recreation](https://fpr.vermont.gov/forests/watershed-forestry/vermont-timber-disaster-assistance-program) says the program can cover standing-timber losses, harvested-timber losses, some costs of reopening damaged harvest sites and certain forest-management-plan updates. applicants should be prepared to provide proof of ownership or financial interest, stand maps, photos, a description of the weather damage and, where required, a licensed-forester assessment. public agencies and government organizations are not eligible for the timber component. the state is asking potential applicants to begin assembling records before the portal opens. the governor’s announcement lists ownership or lease documents, parcel information, tax or business identification, time-stamped photographs, receipts or repair estimates and records of other payments received for the same loss. those requirements are intended to prevent duplicate recovery payments, which means an applicant’s award may depend as much on the paper trail as on the original damage. the money comes from a federal block grant authorized under the american relief act of 2025. vermont announced the $31.7 million allocation in june, and [vtdigger](https://vtdigger.org/2026/06/10/feds-approve-31-7-million-in-disaster-aid-for-flood-hit-vermont-farmers/) reported at the time that the funding was aimed in part at farmers with limited access to other federal disaster programs. the september rollout supplies the application date and operating rules that were not yet settled in that earlier announcement. a second phase will address larger infrastructure losses. the state says projects valued above $75,000, up to a $750,000 maximum, will be handled through a competitive grant program. receiving a first-phase payment will not automatically disqualify an applicant from the second phase, but the same loss cannot be paid twice. vermont has not yet published the second-phase application schedule, so the immediate deadline for farms and forest businesses is the dec. 31 first-phase cutoff. for producers, landowners and loggers, the next step is preparation rather than immediate submission: identify the weather event, separate losses already covered by another program, gather dated evidence and check the state’s agriculture or forestry guidance as the portal launch approaches. vermont officials say additional application instructions and assistance will be released before oct. 26. vermont agriculture agriculture vt vermont vermont agriculture timber disaster assistance flood recovery forestry grants

vt-education-strategic-plan-2026-10-01.excerpt: The Agency of Education says the plan will guide work on college and career readiness, academic achievement, school climate and agency operations through 2030.
vt-education-strategic-plan-2026-10-01.text: vermont education agency unveils 2026-2030 plan built around four statewide priorities the agency of education says the plan will guide work on college and career readiness, academic achievement, school climate and agency operations through 2030. vermont’s agency of education has released a 2026-2030 strategic plan that sets a statewide direction for public education and lays out how the agency says it will measure progress. the plan was published oct. 1 after nearly two years of input from educators, students, families, school and district leaders and community partners, according to the [agency of education’s announcement](https://education.vermont.gov/press-release/vermont-agency-education-releases-statewide-strategic-plan) and a report by [vermont business magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/01/vermont-agency-education-releases-statewide-strategic-plan). the document arrives as vermont schools and state officials confront pressures that the agency identifies as declining enrollment, changing demographics, workforce strain and shifting expectations for graduates. those are statewide conditions rather than a promise that the plan will solve any one district’s budget or staffing problem. the agency describes its role as providing leadership, setting expectations, supporting schools and maintaining transparency and accountability for results. the plan organizes that work under four connected pillars. college and career readiness is intended to help students leave school with the knowledge, skills and experiences needed for what comes next. academic excellence for all focuses on teaching, meaningful learning and more equitable outcomes. safe and healthy schools covers the conditions that help students belong, engage and learn. operational effectiveness addresses the systems, data and capacity behind the agency’s work, according to the agency’s [strategic-plan webpage](https://education.vermont.gov/about/strategic-plan). the priorities are broad by design, but the agency says they will be translated into annual work. each year, officials plan to set priorities, identify milestones, measure progress and report on what they learn. the agency’s webpage also links to a 2026-27 implementation plan and a 2025-26 progress report, creating a structure for comparing the long-range goals with specific near-term actions. the plan’s development timeline shows how the agency assembled that framework. during a 2024 listen and learn tour, the agency says it heard from more than 1,000 education leaders, educators, parents, students and community members across vermont. in november 2025, it hosted more than 300 educators and other partners at a strategic-planning retreat. during 2026, participants from around the state met through steering committees to develop strategies tied to the agency’s vision. that process matters because the plan is not a new school-funding formula or a single mandate for local districts. it is an operating framework for the state agency, which oversees and supports vermont’s public education system while schools continue to make local decisions. its effect will depend on how the agency turns the four pillars into guidance, technical support, data reporting and decisions about where to direct its limited capacity. the agency’s announcement says the plan is meant to evolve as implementation produces new information. that gives the document a built-in review cycle, but it also leaves important questions for later reports: which student outcomes will be used as benchmarks, how milestones will be measured across districts with different circumstances, and whether the agency’s annual priorities match the needs heard during the public-input process. for now, the next step is the 2026-27 implementation plan and the reporting that follows it. vermont’s education agency says it will continue working with educators, families, students and community partners as the strategy moves from a published framework to yearly commitments. the plan’s value will ultimately be judged less by its four headings than by whether those commitments produce clearer support and better outcomes for students across the state. vermont education education vt vermont vermont education public schools education policy strategic planning student outcomes

vt-scott-leadership-appointments-2026-09.excerpt: The appointments put new deputies in Vermont’s human-services and commerce agencies, elevate a longtime budget official in human resources and move tourism leadership into an interim phase.
vt-scott-leadership-appointments-2026-09.text: scott names four leaders for vermont agencies as roles shift across state government the appointments put new deputies in vermont’s human-services and commerce agencies, elevate a longtime budget official in human resources and move tourism leadership into an interim phase. gov. phil scott has appointed four leaders to senior roles in vermont state government, changing the management teams at the departments responsible for human resources, human services, commerce and tourism. the announcement affects the state’s central administrative operations as well as agencies that shape services for families and the economy, according to the [governor’s announcement](https://governor.vermont.gov/press-release/governor-phil-scott-announces-leadership-appointments-5) and independent reporting by [vermont business magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/september/30/governor-scott-announces-leadership-appointments-kramer-nolan-pelham). nick kramer was named deputy commissioner of the department of human resources. scott’s office said kramer had been chief operating officer of the agency of administration, where he worked across the departments of finance and management, human resources, taxes, buildings and general services, libraries, financial services and the office of racial equity. before joining that role in 2024, he worked in the department of finance and management on state operating and capital budgets. shabnam nolan was appointed deputy secretary of the agency of human services, which coordinates major state programs serving vermonters. nolan has led king street center in burlington since 2021. the governor’s office said her work there included youth workforce development, mentoring, early-childhood and after-school programming, and family supports. nolan is scheduled to begin oct. 19, taking the position previously held by kristin mcclure, who is now commissioner of human resources. the two appointments connect administrative management with the state’s human-services system at a time when vermont agencies are managing workforce and service pressures. the announcement does not set out new programs or funding. its immediate effect is organizational: kramer brings experience in state budgeting and agency operations to the human-resources department, while nolan brings nonprofit and community-program experience into the agency of human services. scott also appointed heather pelham deputy secretary of the agency of commerce and community development. pelham had served as commissioner of the department of tourism and marketing since 2019. in that job, the governor’s office credited her with overseeing tourism promotion and the use of $10.4 million in federal eda-arpa travel, tourism and outdoor recreation funding intended to support economic recovery after the pandemic. the tourism department will be led on an interim basis by sara defilippi, who was named interim commissioner after pelham’s move. defilippi has spent eight years with the department and most recently served as director of partnerships and community engagement, according to the state. her duties have included outreach to tourism businesses and community organizations, relocation efforts through the grants for relocation outreach work program, and international marketing activities. the state’s public directory lists pelham under the agency of commerce and community development and identifies defilippi with the tourism department, providing a current administrative reference as the changes take effect. the directory also shows how the appointments fit into the existing structure: tourism remains a department within the broader commerce agency, while the human-resources and human-services roles sit in separate parts of state government. the [vermont business magazine report](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/september/30/governor-scott-announces-leadership-appointments-kramer-nolan-pelham) independently identifies the four appointments and their titles. the leadership changes will be measured by what the agencies do next, not simply by the appointments themselves. for human resources, that means how the department supports the state workforce and carries out administrative responsibilities. for human services, commerce and tourism, the practical questions include how leaders maintain ongoing programs, coordinate with local and nonprofit partners, and turn existing plans into services and economic activity. scott’s announcement provides the personnel changes; future agency updates will show their policy and operational effects. vermont government government vt montpelier montpelier, vermont vermont state government gov. phil scott appointments human services tourism economic development

vt-scott-refugee-cap-2026-10-02.excerpt: The governor says Vermont can accommodate up to 300 fully vetted refugees in the new fiscal year, more than twice the roughly 125 arrivals the state is preparing for under current federal policy.
vt-scott-refugee-cap-2026-10-02.text: scott asks trump administration to let vermont resettle more refugees the governor says vermont can accommodate up to 300 fully vetted refugees in the new fiscal year, more than twice the roughly 125 arrivals the state is preparing for under current federal policy. vermont gov. phil scott is asking the trump administration to expand the number and range of refugees the state can receive in the federal fiscal year that began oct. 1. vermont is preparing for about 125 arrivals under its current allocation, but state officials say the resettlement system has capacity for as many as 300 fully vetted refugees. the request comes as the federal government sets the rules that determine whether vermont’s capacity can be used. in a [statement carried by vermont business magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/02/scott-requests-president-increase-and-broaden-fully-vetted-refugee-admissions), scott’s office said the governor sent president donald trump a letter seeking broader admissions for people fleeing war and persecution. the governor framed the request around both humanitarian concerns and the contributions refugees make to vermont communities and the workforce. the timing is significant because the [federal register’s fy2027 presidential determination](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/02/2026-20318/presidential-determination-on-refugee-admissions-for-fiscal-year-2027) authorizes the admission of up to 17,500 refugees nationwide. the document says those admissions will be allocated primarily among afrikaners from south africa and remain subject to other federal restrictions and case-by-case requirements. that national ceiling is not a vermont quota, but it establishes the narrow federal pool from which state resettlement partners must work. independent reporting shows the practical gap vermont is trying to close. [wcax reported](https://www.wcax.com/2026/10/02/scott-asks-trump-administration-raise-vermonts-refugee-cap/) that scott’s letter seeks to roughly double vermont’s intake from 125 to about 250, while the governor’s announcement says the state could welcome up to 300. the difference reflects a distinction between the state’s current planning figure and its broader capacity: neither number guarantees that many people will arrive, because admission decisions and federal allocations remain outside vermont’s control. vermont’s [state refugee office](https://humanservices.vermont.gov/our-work/programs-services/state-refugee-office) coordinates with resettlement organizations that help newly arrived families find housing, enroll children in school, navigate health care and enter the workforce. the office describes its mission as helping refugees and immigrants participate in the state’s economic, social and civic life, working through providers including the u.s. committee for refugees and immigrants and the ethiopian community development council. that infrastructure is why the governor’s letter emphasizes capacity rather than asking vermont to accept arrivals without a plan. the issue also carries a local workforce and demographic dimension. wcax quoted state refugee director tracy dolan describing young people and families with children as quickly becoming part of local communities and the economy. [wptz’s report](https://www.mynbc5.com/article/vermont-scott-trump-refugee-limits/73999506) likewise said scott argued that refugees contribute to the state’s workforce and communities. those are state-level claims, not a guarantee that every community or employer will experience the same effect, and the available reports do not provide a forecast of how many workers or students a larger intake would add. the next decision belongs to federal officials. vermont can prepare case managers, housing partners and schools for more arrivals, but it cannot set the national ceiling or determine which applicants receive refugee admission. scott made a similar request in 2020, according to the governor’s office and wcax. for this fiscal year, the unresolved question is whether the administration will approve a broader vermont allocation consistent with the state’s stated capacity, and whether the federal admissions priorities will leave room for the mix of families vermont is asking to welcome. vermont government government vt montpelier montpelier, vermont vermont refugees immigration resettlement federal policy phil scott workforce

vt-teacher-apprenticeship-grant-2026-09-.excerpt: The new program will help educator-preparation providers build paid, debt-reducing routes to Vermont licensure, with applications due Feb. 23, 2027.
vt-teacher-apprenticeship-grant-2026-09-.text: vermont opens $300,000 grant path for teacher apprenticeships the new program will help educator-preparation providers build paid, debt-reducing routes to vermont licensure, with applications due feb. 23, 2027. vermont is making $300,000 available to expand teacher registered-apprenticeship programs, a new funding opportunity aimed at helping educator-preparation providers build debt-reducing routes into the profession. the [vermont agency of education](https://education.vermont.gov/news/grow-your-own-teacher-registered-apprenticeship-expansion-grant) announced the competitive subgrant sept. 29 with the vermont department of labor and the national center for grow your own, which will administer the application and award process. the grant is intended for programs that combine educator preparation with employment and supervised classroom experience. the agency of education says the opportunity is designed to create or expand teacher registered apprenticeship programs across the state, with particular attention to rural, high-need and underserved communities, including areas beyond vermont's current apprenticeship model. that focus matters in a state where recruiting and retaining licensed teachers is harder for small districts that compete across long distances and have fewer preparation options nearby. individual awards may reach $100,000 per distinct proposal. vermont-approved educator-preparation providers may lead an application, including approved colleges and universities and approved alternative-route providers that have a university or credit partner. out-of-state providers may participate as well. each proposal must include at least one vermont local education agency that will employ the apprentices and their assigned mentors, according to the agency of education's grant notice. the money is not a general scholarship pool for people who want to become teachers. it is intended to cover approved apprentice tuition, required fees and books for a complete pathway to initial vermont licensure. the state says grant funds and other available resources must ensure that selected apprentices pay nothing out of pocket for those costs. the arrangement can allow a school employee, such as a paraeducator, to earn while receiving training and moving toward a teaching license, although the grant notice does not promise a job or admission to any particular preparation program. the new round builds on a vermont apprenticeship system that has already tested teacher pathways. in its [2024 workforce report](https://legislature.vermont.gov/assets/legislative-reports/workforce-investment-system-registered-apprenticeship-program-annual-report-2024.pdf), the department of labor said a federal state apprenticeship expansion fund grant helped the vermont rural education collaborative work with school districts, the agency of education and other partners. that effort registered seven pre-k through grade 12 teacher-apprenticeship programs and had 28 apprentices in the program as of summer 2024. the same report said the agency of education had identified more than 1,300 teachers working on provisional or emergency licenses in april 2023, a dated measure of the staffing challenge rather than a current count. the prior model centered on vermont's northeast kingdom and used a hybrid structure: apprentices with bachelor's degrees in fields other than education worked under provisional or emergency licenses, received mentoring and completed online coursework and competency-based portfolios. the new grant is statewide and can support both new and existing programs, so its effect will depend on which providers apply and which districts are prepared to employ and mentor apprentices. prospective applicants can attend a pre-proposal conference oct. 7 from 2 to 3 p.m. eastern, with additional sessions scheduled for oct. 21, nov. 4 and jan. 13. applications are due feb. 23, 2027. the agency of education directs questions to the [national center for grow your own](https://ncgyo.org/vermont), whose grant page says the $300,000 allocation comes from an education grant to the organization from ascendium education group. the immediate next step is therefore planning: providers and districts must decide whether they can meet the partnership, licensure and no-out-of-pocket requirements before submitting a proposal. vermont education education vt vermont vermont education teacher apprenticeships teacher shortage registered apprenticeships rural schools grants

vt-uvm-drink-spiking-investigation-2026-.excerpt: A Sept. 30 alert says the reports involve off-campus locations, a cash reward is available for information, and temporary weekend screening support will be offered to students in October.
vt-uvm-drink-spiking-investigation-2026-.text: uvm police investigate alleged drink-spiking reports in burlington a sept. 30 alert says the reports involve off-campus locations, a cash reward is available for information, and temporary weekend screening support will be offered to students in october. university of vermont police services is investigating reports that people may have been given incapacitating drugs without their knowledge at off-campus locations in burlington, prompting a campus safety alert and a request for information from students and the broader community. the sept. 30 alert says uvm police and safety teams received reports of alleged incapacitating or so-called date-rape drug incidents in the burlington area. it does not identify the locations, disclose what substances may have been involved or say how many people reported incidents. the alert says criminal investigations are ongoing and that uvm is offering a substantial cash reward for information that leads to the apprehension of a suspect or suspects. anyone with information is asked to call uvm police at 802-656-3473. ([uvm police alert](https://content.getrave.com/artifacts/api/v1/riki/alert/2645895/moreinfofile/3e2e5059-d183-4ba2-a0d6-d4fc2bc6acd8)) local reporting adds limited context but does not resolve those unknowns. [wcax reported](https://www.wcax.com/2026/09/30/uvm-police-warn-drink-spiking-offer-reward-information/) that sources described three or four incidents at different locations. [wptz reported](https://www.mynbc5.com/article/uvm-police-investigate-alleged-date-rape-drug-incidents/73967944), citing uvm chief safety and compliance officer michael schirling, that officials believed the reports involved multiple distinct events, multiple people and more than one location. those descriptions are part of an active investigation, not a court finding that a crime occurred in any particular case. burlington police told wcax they had not seen a trend of these incidents. that distinction matters: uvm’s alert is a warning about allegations under investigation, not a declaration that a citywide pattern has been established. the reports also concern off-campus places, so the alert reaches beyond the university’s property and asks anyone who may have information to come forward. uvm urged people attending parties or visiting bars and restaurants to avoid leaving drinks unattended, reject open drinks from others and seek help quickly if they feel suddenly weak, confused or otherwise unwell. uvm’s existing [incapacitating-drug screening initiative](https://www.uvm.edu/dsc/incapacitating-drug-screening-initiative), operated with uvm medical center, is designed for students who believe they were drugged but do not necessarily suspect a sexual assault. the university says testing is most useful when obtained promptly because some substances leave the body quickly. the program says student health services can provide screening, and that testing may be tracked anonymously on request. if sexual assault is suspected, uvm directs people to the uvm medical center emergency department for examination and treatment. the new alert adds a short-term change for october: weekend on-call support will be available for screening, giving students an option besides going directly to an emergency department. uvm says students can contact police services and be connected with a student health services medical provider through the center for health and well being. the university also says reporting does not force a person into a full investigation; its screening guidance describes options ranging from a full report to sharing only basic timing and location information that may help investigators identify patterns. the next steps are investigative. uvm police are seeking tips, but the alert does not announce an arrest, identify a suspect or establish whether the allegations are connected. students and community members who feel unsafe or witness a crime in progress should call 911; people seeking confidential support can contact hope works, which uvm lists as a 24-hour resource at 802-863-1236. until investigators release more information, the confirmed public facts are the alert, the request for tips and the temporary screening support—not a confirmed count of victims or a proven explanation for what happened. new-england new-england new england vt burlington burlington, vermont vermont burlington university of vermont
