public safety campus safety crime investigation

vt-uvmmc-support-staff-tentative-deal-20.excerpt: A tentative two-year agreement could avert a walkout by roughly 3,300 support and technical workers, but the contract terms remain private until members vote.
vt-uvmmc-support-staff-tentative-deal-20.text: uvm medical center labor deal heads to ratification vote after strike threat a tentative two-year agreement could avert a walkout by roughly 3,300 support and technical workers, but the contract terms remain private until members vote. a tentative two-year labor agreement at the university of vermont medical center is headed to a ratification vote, putting a possible strike on hold at vermont’s largest hospital while workers review a contract whose terms have not been released. the agreement was announced tuesday by aft vermont, according to [vermont public’s report](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-10-06/support-staff-techs-reach-tentative-deal-with-uvmmc). union members are scheduled to vote from wednesday through sunday, oct. 11. the deal covers two bargaining groups representing roughly 3,300 employees at the burlington medical center. the [vtdigger account](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/06/uvm-medical-center-unions-reach-tentative-agreement-in-contract-negotiations/) describes the support-staff unit as including licensed nursing assistants and schedulers, while the technical-professionals unit includes jobs such as laboratory and sterilization technicians. those positions are not interchangeable with doctors or registered nurses, but they are part of the day-to-day workforce that keeps patient care, testing, cleaning, transport and scheduling moving through a large academic hospital. the agreement follows months of bargaining that began in april. last week, 82% of voting members authorized union leaders to call a strike, a step that gave negotiators leverage but did not itself start a work stoppage, [vermont public reported](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-10-02/support-staff-techs-at-uvmmc-authorize-a-strike). the two sides reached the tentative deal before the unions issued a formal 10-day strike notice, according to [vermont business magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/06/unions-and-uvmmc-administration-reach-tentative-agreement). safe staffing and job security were central issues in the negotiations. union representatives sought more say in determining how many employees are assigned to hospital floors, while workers across the university of vermont health network have experienced three rounds of layoffs in two years, vermont public reported. the hospital and unions have not disclosed whether the tentative contract changes staffing rules, protects particular positions or alters wages and benefits. that missing detail is important. a tentative agreement is not a ratified contract, and the public announcement does not establish what members will receive or what management agreed to change. [vtdigger reported](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/06/uvm-medical-center-unions-reach-tentative-agreement-in-contract-negotiations/) that representatives on both sides declined to provide the terms before the vote. until members approve or reject the deal, the labor dispute remains unresolved even though the immediate prospect of a strike has receded. the negotiations also unfolded during a difficult financial period for the medical center. vermont public reported that hospital chief executive stephen leffler recently told regulators the medical center could lose about $75 million this year. the same report said the hospital has faced pressure from regulators and lawmakers to reduce health-care costs, while its expenses continue to rise. those financial claims come from the hospital’s own statements to regulators and do not, by themselves, explain the terms of the tentative agreement. for patients and families, the near-term effect is continuity: the tentative deal means the support and technical workers are not preparing an announced walkout while the ratification process runs. it does not guarantee that staffing levels will improve, that layoffs will stop or that service costs will fall. those outcomes depend on the contract language, the membership vote and the hospital’s broader financial decisions. the ratification vote is the next decision point. a yes vote would turn the tentative agreement into the governing contract for the two units, while a no vote would leave the parties to determine their next bargaining step. the agreement’s wage, staffing and job-security provisions are expected to become clearer only after the union membership has completed its vote, making the result and the eventual contract terms the next developments to watch in burlington. vermont labor labor vt burlington university of vermont medical center, burlington, vermont vermont burlington university of vermont medical center uvm medical center health care workers vt-voting-accessibility-2026-10-04.excerpt: A state task force and community partners are focusing on disability access, nursing-home voting, homelessness, survivor safety and ballots for incarcerated Vermonters.
vt-voting-accessibility-2026-10-04.text: vermont groups push to close voting-access gaps before november election a state task force and community partners are focusing on disability access, nursing-home voting, homelessness, survivor safety and ballots for incarcerated vermonters. vermont officials and voting-rights advocates are working to remove barriers that can keep eligible residents from participating in the november general election. the effort is broader than making a polling place physically accessible: it includes clearer information, transportation, privacy and assistance for people in nursing homes, people without fixed housing, survivors of domestic or sexual violence and people in state custody. [vtdigger reported](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/04/vermont-officials-and-advocates-tackle-voting-accessibility-concerns-ahead-of-november-election/) on the work oct. 4. the work is being coordinated through a voting-accessibility task force launched by secretary of state sarah copeland hanzas in 2025. the task force’s working groups address people with disabilities, people experiencing homelessness, incarcerated vermonters and survivors of domestic violence. the secretary’s office says the goal is to identify barriers and develop practical ways to help eligible voters use the systems already available to them. nursing homes are a particularly immediate focus. a september guide from the vermont health care association, developed with input from vermont legal aid’s long-term-care ombudsman, explains how facilities can protect residents’ voting rights while avoiding pressure or interference. the guide says residents may register with assistance if they want it, receive mail ballots, vote in person or use vermont’s accessible voting equipment. it also tells facilities to document a resident’s permission when staff help with registration or voting. the [association’s guidance](https://www.vhca.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/172/2026/09/overview-nh-voting-rights-final-2026-1.pdf) says a resident’s choice—not a staff member’s judgment about disability or cognition—should control unless a court has ruled the person legally incompetent. that guidance followed a july memo from the federal centers for medicare and medicaid services. cms said the memo did not create new regulations, but reminded nursing facilities that residents retain the right to vote and to decline participation. facilities cannot coerce, discriminate against or improperly influence residents, and people who need help should be able to choose an assistant when state law permits. cms also encouraged facilities to coordinate with election officials and, where authorized, use bipartisan election workers to reduce the risk of undue influence. the [cms memo](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/qssam-26-04-nh-original-release-2026-07-20.pdf) described those reminders as enforcement of existing residents’ rights. for vermonters with disabilities, the state already offers an accessible voting system at every polling place. the tablet-based system can mark selections on the same paper ballot used by other voters and is intended to let people vote privately and independently. the secretary of state’s [accessibility page](https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/accessible-voting) also says voters may request help from an election official, bring a person of their choice into the booth, ask for a ballot to be brought to their car or request a replacement ballot if they make a mistake. the remaining challenge is that statewide tools do not erase local barriers. vtdigger reported that vermont ranks poorly on disability voting access in an analysis of census data, and advocates identified gaps in accessible voter information, transportation and the accessibility of some municipal and school-election buildings. copeland hanzas told the publication that smaller communities may not have the money to add ramps or elevators or to move an election to another site. those limitations can matter most in local elections, where a town meeting or school vote may be held in a building that was not designed for every resident who has a right to participate. the task force is also trying to make voting safer and more practical for people whose circumstances can make a public voter record risky. a voter guide developed with the vermont network against domestic and sexual violence addresses confidentiality and housing concerns for survivors. the secretary’s office is working with the department of corrections to forward mail ballots to incarcerated vermonters and plans to send a voter guide to households statewide. people without a fixed address can register using a shelter or another location where they live, according to the secretary of state’s [voting-rights information](https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/vermont-voting-rights). the policy questions are not all settled. copeland hanzas told vtdigger she would like to pilot a secure electronic voting option for some municipal elections, but that would require legislative action and a change in state law. in the meantime, the state is emphasizing the options available now: accessible equipment, mail voting, local-clerk assistance and support chosen by the voter. vermonters who encounter a problem can contact their town or city clerk, the secretary of state’s elections division or the attorney general’s office. the practical test before november will be whether those pathways are easy to find and usable in every community, not simply whether they exist on paper. vermont government government vt montpelier vermont vermont elections voting access disability rights nursing homes voting rights

vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.excerpt: Five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the Vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer.
vt-williston-ice-protest-federal-charges.text: federal charges widen legal fight over williston ice facility protests five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer. federal prosecutors have charged five people accused of repeatedly blocking access to an immigration and customs enforcement facility in williston, opening a new legal track in a protest campaign that has already produced separate state trespass cases. the u.s. attorney’s office for the district of vermont said sept. 30 that peter booth, 58, of jericho; lexington kennedy, 22, of new york city; henry prensky, 80, of burlington; roan wade, 23, of red hook, new york; and sherri wormser, 57, of colchester were charged by information with obstructing access to the ice national criminal analysis and targeting center. the facility is in the white cap business park in williston, according to the [department of justice announcement](https://www.justice.gov/usao-vt/pr/five-people-charged-obstructing-access-federal-facility-williston-vermont). the allegations involve three protest dates. prosecutors say all five entered the building’s atrium on feb. 9 and used their bodies to block doors leading to the federal facility after warnings to disperse. the justice department says booth and prensky did so again on may 14, while kennedy and wade repeated the conduct on july 24. in each instance, the release says, access was restored after law enforcement removed protesters from the building. the federal case is narrower than a general challenge to protest activity: the charging document alleges obstruction of entrances and exits, not simply opposition to immigration policy. first assistant u.s. attorney jonathan ophardt said the blockades created safety risks for people working at the facility and required a substantial police response. those are the government’s allegations, not findings by a court. the defendants have not yet been scheduled for initial appearances. the justice department said each faces up to 30 days in prison and a fine of up to $5,000 if convicted, with any sentence to be set by the court under the applicable factors. the agency also said the five had not retained or been appointed counsel when the announcement was issued. all five are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. the charges add to a separate vermont prosecution arising from a july 24 demonstration at the same office complex. vermont attorney general charity clark filed unlawful-trespass cases against 13 people arrested during that sit-in; twelve pleaded not guilty at a sept. 24 arraignment, and the case of an 18-year-old was transferred to family court. [vermont public’s reporting](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-09-24/vermont-attorney-general-charges-protesters-for-trespassing-at-ice-surveillance-facility) said the state charge carries a maximum of three months in prison, a $500 fine, or both. vermont public reported oct. 1 that three of the five people named in the federal case also face state charges. the outlet described the federal action as an escalation after chittenden county state’s attorney sarah george previously declined to prosecute some protesters arrested during sit-ins, while clark’s office later took up the july cases. that split has made charging decisions part of the local debate over how vermont should respond to civil disobedience at the facility. for williston, the immediate issue is practical as well as legal. the white cap complex has become a recurring site of demonstrations, arrests and competing claims about public safety, federal immigration enforcement and protest rights. the next concrete step in the federal matter is the defendants’ initial court appearance; until then, the charging information establishes what prosecutors allege but does not resolve whether the conduct violated federal law or how the cases will affect future demonstrations. new-england new-england new england vt williston williston, vermont vermont williston immigration enforcement protests federal courts public safety

vt-wrightsville-dam-drilling-2026-10-05.excerpt: The three-week study will examine the 115-foot flood-control dam, its foundation and an auxiliary spillway as the state weighs future safety work.
vt-wrightsville-dam-drilling-2026-10-05.text: vermont engineers to drill wrightsville dam above montpelier this week the three-week study will examine the 115-foot flood-control dam, its foundation and an auxiliary spillway as the state weighs future safety work. vermont dam engineers are scheduled to begin drilling at wrightsville dam above montpelier on monday, oct. 5, starting a three-week examination of the structure, the soil beneath it and the bedrock around its auxiliary spillway. the work is expected to continue through about oct. 23, according to a [vermont daily chronicle report](https://vermontdailychronicle.com/dam-protecting-montpelier-2-on-safety-priority-list-drilling-starts-oct-5/) citing the vermont department of environmental conservation. wrightsville is a 115-foot earthen dam on the north branch of the winooski river in middlesex. it holds back a reservoir upstream from montpelier and was built in the 1930s as part of a flood-control system created after the devastating 1927 flood. a vermont agency of natural resources presentation to lawmakers lists the dam at 1,525 feet long, with storage capacity of about 36,000 acre-feet, and identifies flood control, recreation and hydropower among its purposes. the [state dam safety program](https://dec.vermont.gov/water-investment/dam-safety) says its mission is to reduce risks to life, property and the environment from dam incidents and failures. the drilling is an assessment, not a repair project. the chronicle reported that crews will take samples from inside the earthen embankment, from
